The mutated gene encodes one of the three proteins that assemble into a complex in response to DNA damage and activate ATM. A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATM

choices.label: B
choices.text: BRCA2

choices.label: C
choices.text: MRE11

choices.label: D
choices.text: NBS1

choices.label: E
choices.text: RAD50

explanation.summary: NBS1 mutation causes Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome; each MRN component has its own genomic instability syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: MRE11, RAD50, and NBS1 form the MRN complex in response to DNA damage and then activate ATM. Loss of any component compromises cell life. Mutations in MRE11, RAD50, and NBS1 cause Ataxia-Telangiectasia-like disorder (A-TLD), NBS-like disorder (NBSLD), and Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome (NBS), respectively. Improper neural development in these syndromes generally causes microcephaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATM is activated downstream of the MRN complex; its mutation causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia itself, not Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRCA2 regulates RAD51 in homologous recombination and is not part of the MRN complex; its mutation predisposes to breast and ovarian cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MRE11 is an MRN component, but its mutation causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia-like disorder (A-TLD).
whyWrongByChoice.E: RAD50 is an MRN component, but its mutation causes NBS-like disorder (NBSLD), a distinct entity from NBS.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A neurologist explains to a family that the brain, as the body's largest consumer of oxygen, is especially vulnerable to DNA damage from reactive oxygen species, and that genomic instability can disrupt genes involved in neurogenesis. In children with genomic instability syndromes, the ataxia is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cerebellar defects with malfunction of Purkinje cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degeneration of dopaminergic basal ganglia neurons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Demyelination of peripheral motor nerves

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired cerebrospinal fluid absorption with hydrocephalus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular engorgement within the spinal cord

explanation.summary: Ataxia in genomic instability syndromes reflects cerebellar defects and Purkinje cell malfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the brain is the biggest oxygen user in the body, undesirable ROS can damage DNA and lead to neurological disease. In genomic instability syndromes, improper neural development generally causes microcephaly during brain development, and ataxia is regarded as a consequence of cerebellar defects and the malfunction of Purkinje cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Basal ganglia degeneration is not the mechanism described for ataxia in these syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral neuropathy can occur in ataxia-telangiectasia, but the ataxia itself is attributed to cerebellar Purkinje cell dysfunction, not peripheral demyelination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrocephalus is not part of the described pathophysiology; the developmental brain finding is microcephaly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telangiectasias in ataxia-telangiectasia are benign vessel engorgements in the skin and eyes; they do not cause the ataxia.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman tells her dermatologist that she uses a tanning bed several times per week because she believes it is safer than direct sun exposure. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consistent tanning bed use before age 35 raises melanoma risk by about 75%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tanning bed damage is reversed by photolyase in human skin cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tanning beds emit less UV-A than the sun and therefore carry lower risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tanning beds emit mainly ionizing radiation that produces double-strand breaks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tanning beds increase melanoma risk only when use begins after age 35

explanation.summary: Tanning beds are as dangerous or more dangerous than the sun, and early consistent use raises melanoma risk by 75%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatologists know that tanning beds are as dangerous or more dangerous than sun exposure. Tanning beds can emit 10-15 times more UV-A than the sun, and consistent tanning bed use prior to age 35 can increase the risk of developing melanoma by 75%.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans do not possess photolyase; UV-induced pyrimidine dimers must be removed by nucleotide excision repair.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tanning beds emit 10-15 times more UV-A than the sun, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tanning beds emit UV light, which forms pyrimidine dimers; double-strand breaks are the hallmark of ionizing radiation such as X-rays.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The increased melanoma risk is specifically tied to consistent use prior to age 35, not after.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A guanine residue in a hepatocyte becomes abnormally methylated at its O6 position and the lesion is not corrected before the cell enters S phase. Because methylation blocks one of guanine's hydrogen bonds, the replication machinery perceives a base capable of forming only two hydrogen bonds. Which base is most likely inserted opposite the methylated guanine in the new strand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytosine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guanine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uracil

explanation.summary: Methylated guanine presents only two hydrogen bonds, so the cell inserts thymine instead of cytosine, creating a substitution mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal base pairing depends on hydrogen bonding: A and T share two hydrogen bonds while C and G share three. When guanine is abnormally methylated, one of its hydrogen bonds is blocked, so the cell sees only two hydrogen bonds and inserts the wrong base during replication. The pyrimidine that pairs with two hydrogen bonds is thymine; if not repaired, this becomes a substitution mutation (a change in one DNA base).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenine is a purine and would not be inserted opposite a purine; it normally pairs with thymine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytosine is the normal partner of guanine via three hydrogen bonds; methylation blocks one of these, so cytosine is no longer correctly recognized.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanine is a purine that does not pair with another guanine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uracil is not normally used in DNA; its introduction during replication is a separate lesion corrected by base excision repair.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with lymphoma is treated with a nitrogen mustard, a structural analog of the chemical warfare agent sulfur mustard. Which of the following best describes the DNA damage produced by this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of an alkyl group to purine and pyrimidine bases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coordination of a metal ion to the N7 position of guanine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deamination of cytosine residues to uracil

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of cyclobutane dimers between adjacent thymines

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removal of a purine base leaving an abasic site

explanation.summary: Nitrogen mustards are alkylating agents that add alkyl groups to the nitrogenous bases of both purines and pyrimidines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrogen mustard is a structural analog of sulfur mustard. Both agents form adducts and crosslinks with DNA, RNA, and proteins. The DNA damage results from an alkyl group being added to the nitrogenous base of both purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, making them interstrand crosslinking (ICL) agents.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Metal coordination at N7 of guanine describes platinum drugs such as cisplatin, not nitrogen mustards.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deamination is an endogenous alteration of a nucleotide's base, not the action of an alkylating agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cyclobutane thymine dimers are produced by UV light, not by alkylating agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Depurination is an endogenous hydrolytic lesion corrected by base excision repair.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A pharmacologist quantifies the platinum-DNA adducts present in tumor cells after carboplatin exposure. Which of the following adduct types is expected to be the most abundant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abasic sites from depurination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interstrand crosslinks between opposite strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intrastrand crosslinks within the same strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mono-adducts at the N7 position of adenine

explanation.summary: Intrastrand crosslinks are the most abundant platinum adducts, whereas interstrand crosslinks drive antitumor activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cisplatin and carboplatin first form mono-adducts, mostly covalently at N7 of guanine. The mono-adduct then evolves via a covalent bond into either intrastrand (same strand) crosslinks, which are the most abundant platinum adducts, or interstrand (opposite strand) crosslinks, which are responsible for the antitumor activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abasic sites arise from depurination, an endogenous lesion unrelated to platinum chemistry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyrimidine dimers are produced by UV light, not by platinum drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interstrand crosslinks cause the drug's antitumor activity but are not the most abundant adduct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The initial mono-adduct forms mostly at N7 of guanine, not adenine, and the mono-adduct evolves into crosslinks.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with epithelial ovarian cancer had a complete response to a carboplatin-containing regimen 2 years ago. She now presents with relapsed disease. Which of the following best describes the expected response of her tumor to re-treatment with a platinum-containing drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete response to the platinum-containing drug, identical to the initial course

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced sensitivity due to accumulated adducts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resistance to subsequent platinum-containing treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Response limited only by MGMT-mediated adduct removal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Response restored by switching to oxaliplatin

explanation.summary: Epithelial ovarian cancer is initially platinum-responsive, but relapsed tumors are resistant to further platinum therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is the most lethal gynecological cancer. Platinum drugs (cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin) are part of combined regimens for ovarian, lung, gastrointestinal, and germ-cell cancers. While EOC is initially responsive to cisplatin and carboplatin, in patients who relapse the tumor is resistant to subsequent treatment with platinum-containing drugs. Cisplatin and oxaliplatin also carry significant neurotoxic potential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Relapsed EOC does not reproduce the initial response; it has become resistant to platinum-containing drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Relapsed tumors show resistance, not heightened sensitivity, to platinum drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MGMT removes anomalous methyl groups from guanine; it is not the mechanism governing platinum adduct response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxaliplatin is itself a platinum-containing drug, so resistance to platinum-containing treatment applies to it as well.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A toxicologist lecturing on tobacco smoke explains that its at least 70 carcinogens fall into two categories: direct DNA-damaging carcinogens and procarcinogens. Which of the following best characterizes the procarcinogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They act exclusively through aldehyde-DNA adducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: They become active only after a metabolic reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: They damage DNA directly without any chemical change

choices.label: D
choices.text: They enhance DNA repair capacity in lung tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: They reverse pyrimidine dimers by photoreactivation

explanation.summary: Procarcinogens in tobacco smoke require metabolic activation before they can damage DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tobacco smoke contains at least 70 different carcinogens. The two types of mutagens and carcinogens in tobacco smoke are (a) direct DNA-damaging carcinogens and (b) procarcinogens, which are activated only after a metabolic reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldehydes such as acrolein and crotonaldehyde are the major driving force of tobacco-smoke DNA damage, but procarcinogens are defined by their need for metabolic activation, not by adduct type.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Damaging DNA directly without chemical change describes the direct DNA-damaging carcinogens, the other category.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tobacco smoke reduces DNA repair rather than enhancing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Photoreactivation is a repair process performed by photolyase, which humans lack; carcinogens do not repair DNA.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes asks whether vaping protects his DNA. Which of the following best describes the DNA damage associated with e-cigarette use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acrolein-DNA and methyl-dG adducts in lung and bladder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers in oropharyngeal epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depurination abasic sites in the bladder urothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double-strand breaks in alveolar epithelium and bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platinum-like interstrand crosslinks in liver and kidney

explanation.summary: E-cigarettes are not a safe alternative; they induce acrolein-DNA and methyl-dG adducts in the lungs and bladder.
explanation.whyCorrect: While originally thought to be a better smoking option, e-cigarettes also damage DNA by inducing acrolein-DNA and methyl-dG adducts in the lungs and bladder. This parallels tobacco smoke, whose DNA damage is driven mainly by aldehydes forming acrolein- and crotonaldehyde-DNA adducts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyrimidine dimers result from UV light exposure, not from inhaled aldehydes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Depurination is a spontaneous endogenous lesion, not the adduct-based damage attributed to e-cigarettes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Double-strand breaks are characteristic of ionizing radiation, not of e-cigarette aerosol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interstrand crosslinks at N7 of guanine are the signature of platinum drugs, not e-cigarettes.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: During mitochondrial electron transport, a molecule of oxygen (O2) accepts a single extra electron. Which of the following reactive species is produced by this event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen peroxide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydroxyl ion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyl radical

choices.label: D
choices.text: Superoxide anion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Water

explanation.summary: Oxygen that accepts an extra electron becomes the superoxide anion, a reactive oxygen species.
explanation.whyCorrect: ROS can be created from endogenous sources such as enzyme-catalyzed reactions, the mitochondrial electron transport chain, Fenton reactions, or an immune response, or induced by exogenous sources such as ionizing radiation. When oxygen (O2) accepts an extra electron, it becomes a superoxide anion, an ROS. Because ROS have unpaired electrons, they are extremely reactive toward DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrogen peroxide is a separate species; it is the precursor that is reduced to form hydroxyl radicals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hydroxyl ion is a stable species without an unpaired electron, not the product of O2 accepting an electron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyl radicals are produced from the reduction of hydrogen peroxide, not directly from O2 gaining one electron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Water is the fully reduced, stable end product of oxygen metabolism, not a reactive oxygen species.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A patient with a germ-cell tumor receives cisplatin. In tumor cells that survive treatment, the most abundant platinum lesions, which covalently join two adjacent bases on the same strand and distort the helix, are recognized and removed. Which repair pathway is principally responsible for removing these intrastrand crosslinks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair (BER)

choices.label: B
choices.text: MGMT direct reversal repair

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mismatch repair (MMR)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair

explanation.summary: Bulky adducts and intrastrand crosslinks are helix-distorting single-strand lesions handled by nucleotide excision repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nucleotide excision repair recognizes a broad range of helix-distorting single-strand lesions that involve more than one nucleotide and removes a stretch of nucleotides containing the lesion. In the overview of damage and repair mechanisms, bulky adducts and intrastrand crosslinks are assigned to NER, whereas double-strand breaks and interstrand crosslinks are assigned to double-strand break repair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair corrects lesions affecting only a single nucleotide (uracil, oxidized bases, abasic sites), not a crosslink spanning two bases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MGMT removes O6-methyl groups from guanine directly without cutting the backbone; it cannot remove a platinum crosslink.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertions or deletions introduced during replication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks; interstrand crosslinks, not intrastrand crosslinks, are routed to double-strand break repair.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A medical student on a radiology rotation is handed a 20-lb lead apron before a fluoroscopy-guided procedure. Which of the following best explains why lead is the appropriate shielding material for this exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lead absorbs alpha particles that would otherwise penetrate deep tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lead blocks the UV-A component emitted by the fluoroscope

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lead is the only material capable of stopping neutron radiation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lead neutralizes free radicals generated by beta particles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thick lead stops high-energy gamma and X-ray radiation

explanation.summary: X-rays and gamma rays are penetrating ionizing radiation stopped by thick lead, which protects DNA from double-strand breaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroscopy provides continuous real-time imaging using X-rays and carries risk of inducing double-strand breaks, especially during prolonged procedures. In terms of penetration, alpha rays are stopped by paper, beta rays by thin aluminum, gamma and X-rays by thick lead, and neutron rays by water or concrete. A lead apron is therefore a good shield for the ionizing radiation used in fluoroscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper; they do not penetrate deeply and are not the concern in fluoroscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroscopy uses X-rays, a form of ionizing radiation; UV-A is emitted by tanning beds and the sun, not fluoroscopes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutron radiation is stopped by water or concrete, not lead, and fluoroscopy does not use neutrons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta particles are stopped by thin aluminum; lead's role is physical shielding of X-rays, not chemical neutralization of radicals.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: In a quiescent neuron, a single nucleotide spontaneously loses its purine base entirely, leaving the sugar-phosphate backbone intact. Which repair pathway is best suited to correct this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination

choices.label: C
choices.text: MGMT direct repair

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair

explanation.summary: Depurination, the complete loss of a base from a nucleotide, is corrected by base excision repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: If DNA lesions affect only a single nucleotide, cells can use base excision repair. Lesions amenable to BER include the introduction of uracil during replication, damage from reactive oxygen species, deamination (an alteration to a nucleotide's base), and depurination (where a nucleotide loses its base entirely). The resulting abasic site is processed by an endonuclease and lyase, then filled by DNA polymerase and sealed by ligase.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous chromosome; there is no strand break here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MGMT direct repair specifically removes anomalous methyl groups; it cannot replace a missing base.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining fuses severed DNA ends after a double-strand break, which has not occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair addresses helix-distorting lesions spanning more than one nucleotide, such as pyrimidine dimers.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: In a cell-free system reconstituting base excision repair, uracil DNA glycosylase has already recognized a misincorporated uracil and removed its base, creating an AP site. Which of the following must occur next to generate the single-nucleotide gap that DNA polymerase will fill?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An endonuclease cleaves the 5' bond and a lyase cleaves the 3' bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase unwinds and excises an oligonucleotide containing the AP site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds on both sides of the AP site

choices.label: D
choices.text: MGMT transfers the abasic sugar residue onto itself

choices.label: E
choices.text: Photolyase cleaves the abasic sugar using light energy

explanation.summary: After glycosylase creates the AP site, an endonuclease cuts the 5' phosphodiester bond and a lyase cuts the 3' bond to open a one-nucleotide gap.
explanation.whyCorrect: BER proceeds in ordered steps: a DNA glycosylase specific to the lesion removes the base to create an AP (apurinic/apyrimidinic) site; an endonuclease then cleaves the 5' phosphodiester bond while a lyase cleaves the 3' bond, creating a single-nucleotide gap; DNA polymerase fills the gap and ligase seals the nicks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase-mediated removal of an oligonucleotide segment is a step of nucleotide excision repair, which excises a stretch of nucleotides rather than a single one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligase acts last, sealing the nicks after the gap has been filled; sealing before excision would leave the abasic sugar in place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MGMT accepts a methyl group from O6-methylguanine in direct repair; it does not act on abasic sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Photolyase breaks pyrimidine dimers by photoreactivation, is absent in humans, and has no role in processing AP sites.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A bulky, helix-distorting lesion is detected on one strand of a fibroblast's DNA. Endonucleases encoded by three uvr genes have made incisions in the phosphodiester backbone upstream and downstream of the lesion. Which enzyme next removes the damaged segment from the helix before the gap is filled?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA glycosylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA ligase

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA polymerase eta

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helicase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lyase

explanation.summary: In nucleotide excision repair, helicase removes the incised oligonucleotide segment after the endonuclease cuts.
explanation.whyCorrect: NER is a remove-and-replace mechanism for helix-distorting single-strand lesions. Special endonucleases from three uvr genes sever the phosphodiester backbone upstream and downstream of the lesion, and helicase removes the segment. DNA polymerase then fills the gap and ligase seals it. NER occurs primarily in G1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA glycosylase removes a single damaged base to initiate base excision repair; it does not excise oligonucleotides.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA ligase acts at the end of NER, sealing the gap after polymerase has filled it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase eta replicates accurately across pyrimidine dimers as a means of circumventing damage; it does not remove the lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A lyase cleaves the 3' bond at an AP site during base excision repair, not during NER segment removal.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A researcher synchronizes a cell population and induces double-strand breaks at defined points in the cell cycle. Repair by homologous recombination is observed most robustly during which phases, and for what reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any phase, because the pathway does not require a homologous template

choices.label: B
choices.text: G1 and S, because checkpoints are most active before replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: G1 only, because chromatin is least condensed

choices.label: D
choices.text: M only, because the machinery resembles meiotic crossing over

choices.label: E
choices.text: S and G2, because a homologous chromosome template is available

explanation.summary: Homologous recombination requires a homologous chromosome as template and therefore occurs mainly in S and G2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as a template to process severed strands, reconnecting the complementary strands without loss of any nucleotide sequence. Because it requires a homologous chromosome, HR occurs mainly in the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle. The HR protein machinery is very similar to that involved in chromosomal crossing over during meiosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is nonhomologous end joining, not HR, that can occur in any phase because it does not require a homologous template.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Checkpoint activity does not drive HR; template availability does, and G1 precedes replication of the needed template.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G1 is the phase in which NER predominates; HR is limited in G1 because a homologous template is not yet available.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although HR machinery resembles meiotic crossing-over machinery, HR repair occurs mainly in S and G2, not M.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: During DNA replication, a DNA polymerase incorporates an incorrect base into the newly synthesized strand despite its proofreading capability. Which of the following proteins recognize this error and recruit endonucleases to initiate its correction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: BRCA1 and BRCA2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesion-specific DNA glycosylases

choices.label: C
choices.text: MRE11, RAD50, and NBS1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mut class proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: XPA through XPG proteins

explanation.summary: Mismatch repair begins when Mut class proteins recognize a replication error and recruit endonucleases.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA polymerases have high fidelity but are not perfect even with proofreading. When incorrect bases are incorporated into newly synthesized strands, they are recognized by the Mut class proteins, which recruit endonucleases. Mismatch repair then removes and replaces a stretch of nucleotide sequence containing the mismatch, similar to NER, and occurs primarily during S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 and BRCA2 function in homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA glycosylases recognize damaged single bases such as uracil to initiate base excision repair, not replication mismatches.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MRE11, RAD50, and NBS1 form the MRN complex that responds to DNA damage and activates ATM in the double-strand break response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XPA through XPG are nucleotide excision repair genes whose mutation causes xeroderma pigmentosum; they do not recognize replication mismatches.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with extreme photosensitivity and multiple early skin cancers is diagnosed with a variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum. Sequencing of the XPA through XPG genes is normal. A deficiency of which of the following is most likely responsible for his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA polymerase eta, which replicates accurately across pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: B
choices.text: MGMT, which removes anomalous methyl groups from guanine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Photolyase, which cleaves pyrimidine dimers by photoreactivation

choices.label: D
choices.text: RAD51, which is regulated by BRCA2 during recombination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uracil DNA glycosylase, which excises misincorporated uracil

explanation.summary: The XP variant results from deficiency of DNA polymerase eta, a polymerase that bypasses pyrimidine dimers rather than repairing them.
explanation.whyCorrect: NER activity is impaired by mutation in eight genes, XPA through XPG and XP variants. The variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum results from deficiency of a specific DNA polymerase. DNA polymerase eta is unique in that it can still accurately replicate DNA in the presence of pyrimidine dimers; it is not a repair mechanism so much as a means of circumventing the structural defects caused by UV light. Without it, UV damage accumulates and drives progression of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MGMT deficiency would impair direct repair of methylated guanine, not the handling of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Humans do not possess photolyase at all, so its absence cannot distinguish a variant XP patient from the general population.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RAD51 functions in homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks; its loss relates to BRCA-associated cancer risk, not photosensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uracil DNA glycosylase initiates base excision repair of misincorporated uracil and is unrelated to UV damage.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with colon cancer. His mother developed endometrial cancer at age 44 and a maternal uncle had colon cancer at age 38. Germline testing reveals a PMS2 mutation. Which of the following statements about this syndrome is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accounts for less than 4% of colon cancer cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: It accounts for the majority of colon cancer cases

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is associated with extreme photosensitivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It results from defective nucleotide excision repair

choices.label: E
choices.text: It typically presents after age 70

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is rare, causing under 4% of colon cancers, but presents early in patients under 50.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome (formerly HNPCC) results from a germline mutation in one of four MMR genes: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. Affected individuals have significantly increased risk of cancer within the gastrointestinal tract as well as ovarian and endometrial cancers. While Lynch syndrome is rare, accounting for less than 4% of colon cancer cases, it presents in patients under 50, with some diagnosed in their twenties. A detailed family history is a valuable component of diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lynch syndrome is rare and accounts for fewer than 4% of colon cancer cases, not the majority.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extreme photosensitivity is the hallmark of xeroderma pigmentosum, not Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lynch syndrome results from defective mismatch repair; defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lynch syndrome presents in patients under 50, with some individuals diagnosed in their twenties.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a germline BRCA2 mutation asks how her mutation differs at the molecular level from a BRCA1 mutation. BRCA2 specifically regulates the activity of which of the following proteins essential for homologous recombination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATM

choices.label: B
choices.text: MGMT

choices.label: C
choices.text: MSH6

choices.label: D
choices.text: RAD51

choices.label: E
choices.text: XPA

explanation.summary: BRCA2 specifically regulates RAD51, whereas BRCA1 signals DNA damage and repair across HR, NER, and possibly NHEJ.
explanation.whyCorrect: BRCA1 and BRCA2 play crucial roles in the homologous repair process, so mutations in either significantly increase breast and ovarian cancer risk. BRCA1 is involved in the signaling of DNA damage and repair by HR, NER, and possibly NHEJ, while BRCA2 specifically regulates the activity of RAD51, which is essential for homologous recombination. Together they maintain genomic stability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATM is activated by the MRN complex in the double-strand break response; it is not the protein regulated by BRCA2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MGMT performs direct repair of O6-methylguanine and is unrelated to homologous recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH6 is a mismatch repair gene associated with Lynch syndrome, not an HR effector regulated by BRCA2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XPA is a nucleotide excision repair gene associated with xeroderma pigmentosum.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections and is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency. Evaluation reveals a defect in a DNA repair mechanism whose inherent inaccuracy is normally exploited by B cells to generate diverse antibodies and receptors through V(D)J recombination. Which repair mechanism is defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mismatch repair

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair

explanation.summary: The error-prone nature of NHEJ enables V(D)J recombination, so NHEJ defects can cause SCID.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inaccuracy of nonhomologous end joining has physiological utility in the immune system: it allows B cells to undergo V(D)J recombination, the process by which novel antibodies and receptors are generated to detect foreign antigens. For this reason, NHEJ defects can result in severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Ataxia telangiectasia is another clinical consequence of NHEJ defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair replaces single damaged bases and plays no role in antibody diversification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologous recombination is accurate and template-dependent; the diversity-generating inaccuracy needed for V(D)J recombination is a property of NHEJ, and HR defects are linked to BRCA-associated cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects replication errors; its defect causes Lynch syndrome, not immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair removes helix-distorting lesions; its defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A dermal fibroblast in G1 phase sustains a single double-strand break from diagnostic X-rays. Which repair mechanism is the cell most likely to use in this situation, and what is the principal trade-off?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair; risk of an unfilled single-nucleotide gap

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination; risk of translocation because a template is copied

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mismatch repair; risk of mispairing when S phase begins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining; risk of mutation because homology is not required

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair; risk of oligonucleotide loss at the break site

explanation.summary: When HR is unavailable because of cell-cycle stage, the cell prioritizes NHEJ to rejoin the break even at the cost of genetic integrity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homologous recombination requires a homologous chromosome and occurs mainly in S and G2; NHEJ can occur in any phase. When HR is not possible, due to the degree of damage or the current status of the cell cycle, the higher priority for the cell is to use NHEJ to reconnect the severed strands, even at the risk of jeopardizing some genetic integrity. Because NHEJ connects any two severed strands without requiring homology, it is error-prone; HR is much more accurate, but NHEJ is more versatile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair replaces a single damaged nucleotide on one strand and cannot reconnect two severed strands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HR is not available in G1 because no homologous template is present, and HR restores sequence without loss rather than creating translocations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects replication errors during S phase and cannot rejoin a severed helix.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair addresses helix-distorting single-strand lesions, not double-strand breaks.

questions.topicName: DNA Damage and DNA Repair Mechanism

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is studying the components of a DNA nucleotide. She learns that each nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a nitrogenous base, and a pentose sugar. Which feature of the pentose sugar distinguishes a DNA nucleotide from an RNA nucleotide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydroxyl group on the 3' carbon

choices.label: B
choices.text: A methyl group replacing the base

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single hydrogen on the 2' carbon

choices.label: D
choices.text: A six-membered ring rather than a five-membered ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: An additional phosphate on the 5' carbon

explanation.summary: DNA uses deoxyribose, which lacks the 2' hydroxyl found in RNA's ribose.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA nucleotides have a single hydrogen attached to the 2' carbon of the pentose sugar instead of a hydroxyl group, which is why the sugar is called deoxyribose. RNA nucleotides carry a hydroxyl at the 2' position on ribose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both DNA and RNA sugars have a 3' hydroxyl; it is the phosphodiester linkage site, not the DNA/RNA distinction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The base is attached to the sugar in both DNA and RNA and is not replaced by a methyl group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both ribose and deoxyribose are five-membered (pentose) sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A phosphate group is part of every nucleotide and does not distinguish deoxyribose from ribose.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A researcher determines that a segment of double-stranded DNA is unusually resistant to strand separation, requiring a high melting temperature. Sequencing shows the region is rich in guanine-cytosine base pairs. Which molecular property best explains the elevated melting temperature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G-C pairs are joined by three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T pairs

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-C pairs eliminate the antiparallel orientation of the strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: G-C pairs form covalent phosphodiester bonds between strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: G-C pairs widen the diameter of the double helix

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purines pair only with other purines in G-C-rich regions

explanation.summary: G-C base pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds, making G-C-rich DNA more tightly bound.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guanine-cytosine pairs form three hydrogen bonds while adenine-thymine pairs form only two. More hydrogen bonds create stronger adhesion between the strands, so more thermal energy (higher melting temperature) is needed to separate G-C-rich DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: All double-stranded DNA is antiparallel regardless of G-C content.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphodiester bonds are covalent linkages within a single strand's backbone, not bonds between the two strands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrogen bond number affects binding strength, not the diameter of the helix.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Base pairing is always purine-to-pyrimidine (A-T, G-C); purines do not pair with purines.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: While reviewing the structure of a DNA strand, a student notes that each strand has a defined directionality described as a 5' end and a 3' end. Which type of bond is responsible for creating this directional backbone by linking one nucleotide to the next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Covalent phosphodiester bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disulfide bond between cysteines

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen bond between base pairs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ionic bond with histone proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Van der Waals stacking interaction

explanation.summary: Phosphodiester bonds covalently link nucleotides and establish 5' and 3' ends.
explanation.whyCorrect: A covalent phosphodiester bond links the phosphate group of one nucleotide to the hydroxyl group of the sugar of the previous nucleotide. This repeating linkage forms the backbone and creates the distinct 5' and 3' ends of each polynucleotide strand.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Disulfide bonds form between cysteine residues in proteins, not in the DNA backbone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrogen bonds hold the two complementary strands together, not the backbone within a strand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ionic bonds describe attractions such as histone-DNA binding, not the covalent backbone linkage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Van der Waals forces are weak transient interactions and do not form the covalent backbone.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A textbook figure shows two complementary DNA strands running in opposite directions so that the 3' end of one strand aligns with the 5' end of the other. This antiparallel arrangement is required for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of ribose to deoxyribose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of covalent bonds between the two strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Generation of a left-handed helix as the natural configuration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralization of the negative charge on the phosphate backbone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proper hydrogen bonding between paired bases

explanation.summary: Antiparallel orientation allows complementary bases to align and hydrogen bond correctly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complementary strands are oriented antiparallel, with the 3' end of one strand pairing with the 5' end of the complementary strand. This geometry is what permits the bases to align and form the hydrogen bonds that hold the double helix together.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sugar identity (deoxyribose) is fixed during nucleotide synthesis and is unrelated to strand orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The natural configuration of DNA is a right-handed helix, not left-handed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The exposed phosphates give DNA an overall negative charge; antiparallel orientation does not neutralize it.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A molecular biology lecture emphasizes that the naturally occurring DNA helix is right-handed, with about 10 base pairs per complete turn and roughly 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs. The helix also displays a major groove and a minor groove. What is the primary functional importance of these grooves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They convert heterochromatin into euchromatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: They join sister chromatids at the centromere

choices.label: C
choices.text: They neutralize the negative charge of the backbone

choices.label: D
choices.text: They provide surfaces where proteins bind

choices.label: E
choices.text: They store extra nucleotides for repair

explanation.summary: The major and minor grooves are protein-binding surfaces used in transcription and replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: The natural twist of the double helix creates a major and a minor groove. These grooves are important because various proteins use them to access the DNA for processes such as transcription and replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromatin state changes are driven by methylation and acetylation, not by the helical grooves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sister chromatids are joined at the centromere by cohesins, unrelated to the helical grooves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The exposed phosphates give DNA a net negative charge; the grooves do not neutralize it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The grooves are structural surface features, not storage sites for spare nucleotides.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: The human genome contains roughly 3 billion base pairs and, when stretched out, is 2 to 3 meters long, yet it must fit within a eukaryotic nucleus about 6 micrometers in diameter. The first step in condensing DNA involves winding it twice around a core of eight histone proteins. What property of histones allows them to bind DNA so tightly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histones are composed mainly of hydrophobic amino acids that bury themselves within the DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histones are large aromatic proteins that physically clamp the DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histones are rich in positively charged amino acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histones carry a strong negative charge that repels the DNA into a coil

choices.label: E
choices.text: Histones form covalent bonds with the DNA so it can never be separated

explanation.summary: Positively charged histones bind the negatively charged DNA backbone by electrostatic attraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histones contain an abundance of positively charged amino acids such as lysine and arginine. These bind tightly to the negatively charged phosphate groups of the DNA, allowing DNA to wind around the histone octamer to form a nucleosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The amino acids that matter are positively charged, not hydrophobic; hydrophobicity does not drive DNA binding here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding is due to charge attraction, not the bulky aromatic size of the amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histones are positively charged; a negative charge would repel rather than bind DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA-histone interactions are electrostatic (ionic), not covalent; covalent bonds would prevent replication and transcription.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A student is labeling a diagram of DNA packaging. DNA wraps twice around a core of eight histone proteins to form a nucleosome, giving chromatin its 'beads on a string' appearance. A ninth histone protein then secures the DNA onto the core, forming a chromatosome. Which histone protein performs this securing role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histone H1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histone H2A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histone H2B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histone H3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Histone H4

explanation.summary: The linker histone H1 secures DNA onto the histone core to form a chromatosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The nucleosome core is made of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. A ninth histone protein, H1, then secures the DNA around this core, forming the structure called a chromatosome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H2A is one of the eight core histones of the nucleosome, not the linker that forms the chromatosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2B is a core histone in the octamer, not the securing linker histone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H3 is a core histone; two copies help form the nucleosome core.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H4 is a core histone; it is part of the octamer, not the linker histone.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A pathologist explains that a region of a patient's genome is transcriptionally silent because it is packaged as highly condensed chromatin that polymerases cannot access. Which term best describes this state of chromatin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromatosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Euchromatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterochromatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solenoid fiber

explanation.summary: Heterochromatin is highly condensed and transcriptionally inactive.
explanation.whyCorrect: When DNA is highly condensed it is referred to as heterochromatin. Heterochromatin is inaccessible to polymerases, making it transcriptionally inactive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chromatosome is a nucleosome plus H1, a packaging unit, not the condensed silent state itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Euchromatin is loosely condensed and transcriptionally active, the opposite of what is described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nucleosome is a single DNA-histone unit, not a description of overall transcriptional accessibility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A solenoid fiber is an intermediate coiling structure, not the term for transcriptionally silent condensed chromatin.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A researcher studying epigenetic regulation observes that adding methyl groups to specific DNA sequences recruits repressor proteins and drives chromatin toward a tighter, more condensed configuration. What is the expected effect of this DNA methylation on the affected genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of thymine to uracil in the coding strand

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased gene expression by promoting condensation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate strand separation and replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased gene expression by opening chromatin

choices.label: E
choices.text: No effect, because methylation only alters the sugar backbone

explanation.summary: DNA methylation recruits repressors and condenses chromatin, decreasing gene expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nucleotides can be modified by adding methyl groups to specific DNA sequences. These methyl groups recruit proteins that repress gene expression and facilitate tighter condensation into heterochromatin, thereby decreasing transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methylation adds methyl groups; it does not convert thymine to uracil.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylation represses transcription and condenses chromatin rather than triggering strand separation and replication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetylation of histone tails opens chromatin and increases expression; DNA methylation does the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methylation modifies specific base sequences and recruits repressors; it does not merely alter the sugar backbone with no effect.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: In a study of chromatin dynamics, a compound is applied that adds acetyl groups to the tails of histone subunits. Which outcome is most consistent with histone acetylation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenine begins pairing with cytosine rather than thymine throughout the duplex

choices.label: B
choices.text: The centromere dissolves and the sister chromatids separate ahead of anaphase

choices.label: C
choices.text: The chromatin condenses further into tightly packed, transcriptionally silent heterochromatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The DNA forms covalent bonds with the acetylated histone tails, permanently silencing the region

choices.label: E
choices.text: The positive charge of the histones decreases, loosening the coil and opening the chromatin

explanation.summary: Acetylation reduces histone positive charge, decondensing chromatin and opening it for transcription.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acetylation of histone tails decreases the overall positive charge of the histones, weakening their attraction to the negatively charged DNA. This allows the DNA to relax its tight coil, decondensing and opening the chromatin toward the active euchromatin state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base pairing rules (A-T, G-C) are unaffected by histone tail modification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Centromere function and sister chromatid separation are cell-cycle events unrelated to histone acetylation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetylation opens chromatin; it is methylation that promotes condensation into heterochromatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA and histones interact through charge attraction, not covalent bonds, and acetylation opens rather than silences the region.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A cytogeneticist prepares a karyotype from a patient's cells and counts the chromosomes. She explains that humans have a diploid genome consisting of pairs of homologous chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in a typical human somatic cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 23 chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: 44 autosomes with no sex chromosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: 48 chromosomes: 23 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: 92 chromosomes

explanation.summary: Humans have 46 chromosomes: 22 homologous autosome pairs plus one pair of sex chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humans have diploid genomes with 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of homologous autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Each person inherits a set of 23 chromosomes from the mother and a homologous set of 23 from the father.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 is the haploid number contributed by a single gamete, not the total in a somatic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Somatic cells contain sex chromosomes in addition to 44 autosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Humans have 22 autosome pairs plus one sex chromosome pair, totaling 46, not 48.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 92 chromatids are present after DNA replication, but the cell still has 46 chromosomes because chromosome number is set by centromere number.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: During the S phase of the cell cycle, a cell replicates its entire genome. Immediately afterward, each chromosome consists of two identical DNA molecules held together until just before division. What are these two identical DNA molecules called, and what structure connects them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles connected at the nucleolus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromatin fibers connected at the major groove

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes connected at the telomere

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleosomes connected by the linker histone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sister chromatids connected at the centromere

explanation.summary: Replication yields two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
explanation.whyCorrect: After replication, each chromosome consists of two identical DNA molecules called sister chromatids. They are connected at a point called the centromere, which serves as the attachment site for the mitotic spindle that pulls the chromatids apart during division.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alleles are different versions of a gene, not the replicated DNA molecules, and the nucleolus does not join them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromatin fibers are a packaging level, and the major groove is a helical surface feature, not a junction between replicated DNA molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homologous chromosomes are the maternal and paternal copies of a chromosome; they are not the two identical products of replication, and they are not joined at the telomere.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleosomes are DNA-histone packaging units, not the replicated chromosome copies.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to sort the nitrogenous bases of DNA by ring structure. Which pair of bases consists of purines, the bases built from two fused rings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenine and guanine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adenine and thymine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytosine and thymine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytosine and uracil

choices.label: E
choices.text: Guanine and cytosine

explanation.summary: Adenine and guanine are the two-ring purines; cytosine and thymine are the one-ring pyrimidines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrogenous bases with two rings, adenine and guanine, are referred to as purines. Bases with just one ring, cytosine and thymine, are referred to as pyrimidines.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Adenine is a purine, but thymine is a single-ring pyrimidine; this is a base pair, not a purine pair.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytosine and thymine are both single-ring pyrimidines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytosine and uracil are both pyrimidines, and uracil is found only in RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guanine is a purine, but cytosine is a pyrimidine; this is a base pair, not a purine pair.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A laboratory isolates a small molecule consisting of thymine covalently attached to a deoxyribose sugar. No phosphate group is present. Which term correctly describes this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nitrogenous base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nucleoside

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleotide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polynucleotide

explanation.summary: A base attached to a pentose sugar is a nucleoside; adding a phosphate makes it a nucleotide.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term nucleoside refers to a nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar. When a phosphate group is added, it becomes a nucleotide. Thymine bonded to deoxyribose without a phosphate is therefore a nucleoside.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate carries three phosphate groups; this molecule carries none.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The nitrogenous base alone is thymine; here it is already attached to a sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nucleotide requires a phosphate group in addition to the base and sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A polynucleotide is a chain of nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds, not a single base-sugar unit.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A student comparing the nucleotide composition of DNA and RNA notes that one pyrimidine base is present in RNA but never incorporated into DNA. Which base is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytosine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guanine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uracil

explanation.summary: Uracil is a pyrimidine found only in RNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA incorporates four primary nucleotides: adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine. The pyrimidine base uracil is found only in RNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenine is a purine present in both DNA and RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytosine is a pyrimidine present in both DNA and RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanine is a purine present in both DNA and RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymine is the pyrimidine used in DNA, not the one restricted to RNA.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A student is drawing the sugar-phosphate backbone of a single DNA strand and must show exactly where the phosphodiester bond connects adjacent nucleotides. Which carbons of the two deoxyribose sugars does this bond link?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 1' carbon of one nucleotide and the base of the next

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 2' carbon of one nucleotide and the 3' carbon of the next

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 2' carbon of one nucleotide and the 5' carbon of the next

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 5' carbon of one nucleotide and the 3' carbon of the next

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 5' carbon of one nucleotide and the 5' carbon of the next

explanation.summary: Phosphodiester bonds join the 5' carbon of one nucleotide to the 3' carbon of the adjacent nucleotide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nucleotides are linked by covalent phosphodiester bonds between the 5' carbon of one nucleotide and the 3' carbon of the previous nucleotide within a strand. The phosphate on the 5' carbon bonds to the hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the neighboring sugar, which is what creates the 5' and 3' ends of each strand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 1' carbon is where the nitrogenous base attaches to the sugar; it is not part of the backbone bond.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 2' carbon of deoxyribose carries only a hydrogen and does not participate in the backbone linkage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 2' carbon of deoxyribose lacks a hydroxyl group and cannot form the phosphodiester linkage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 5'-to-5' linkage would not produce the directional 5' and 3' ends of a polynucleotide strand.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A molecular biologist isolates a 100-base-pair segment of naturally occurring double-stranded DNA. Based on the standard geometry of the helix, approximately how many complete helical turns does this segment contain, and how long is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 turn and about 34 nm long

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10 turns and about 3.4 nm long

choices.label: C
choices.text: 10 turns and about 34 nm long

choices.label: D
choices.text: 34 turns and about 10 nm long

choices.label: E
choices.text: 100 turns and about 34 nm long

explanation.summary: With 0.34 nm per base pair and about 10 base pairs per turn, 100 bp spans roughly 10 turns and 34 nm.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is 0.34 nm (3.4 angstrom) between each nucleotide pair, and a single turn of the naturally occurring right-handed helix requires about 10 base pairs, or 3.4 nm (34 angstrom). A 100-base-pair segment therefore contains about 10 turns and measures about 100 x 0.34 nm = 34 nm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One turn corresponds to only about 10 base pairs (3.4 nm), not to 100 base pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 3.4 nm is the length of a single turn of about 10 base pairs, not the length of 100 base pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the numbers; 34 is the length in nanometers, not the turn count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Each turn requires about 10 base pairs, so 100 base pairs give about 10 turns, not 100.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A researcher notes that intact double-stranded DNA helices carry an overall negative charge. Which structural feature is responsible for this charge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The exposed phosphate groups of the sugar backbone

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hydrogen bonds between complementary bases

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hydroxyl group at the 3' end of each strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lysine residues of associated histone tails

choices.label: E
choices.text: The nitrogenous bases stacked on the inside of the helix

explanation.summary: Exposed phosphates on the sugar backbone give DNA its net negative charge.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the helix the paired nitrogenous bases sit on the inside while the sugar-phosphate backbone forms the outside. The exposed phosphates of the sugar backbones of each strand give DNA helices an overall negative charge, which is why positively charged histones bind them.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrogen bonds hold the strands together but do not confer a net charge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single terminal hydroxyl group does not account for the charge along the entire molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysine residues on histones are positively charged; they neutralize rather than create the negative charge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The bases are tucked inside the helix and are not the source of the net negative charge.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A student observes that the two complementary strands of a long DNA molecule stay tightly associated at physiologic temperature, even though each individual bond joining the strands is relatively weak. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Covalent phosphodiester bonds also cross-link the two strands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each base pair contributes one exceptionally strong hydrogen bond

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histone octamers covalently clamp the two strands together

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ionic bonds form between phosphates on opposite strands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many weak hydrogen bonds acting together create a firm adhesion

explanation.summary: Individually weak hydrogen bonds gain strength in numbers to hold complementary strands together.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individual hydrogen bonds are relatively weak, but a large number of hydrogen bonds working together creates a tight adhesion between complementary DNA strands. The principle is individually weak, but strength in numbers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phosphodiester bonds run along the backbone within a single strand; they do not link the two strands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Base pairs form two (A-T) or three (G-C) hydrogen bonds, each of which is weak on its own.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histones bind DNA by electrostatic attraction, not covalent bonds, and they do not link the two strands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphate groups on both strands are negatively charged and would repel, not attract, one another.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A geneticist notes that different regions of a chromosome vary markedly in their G-C versus A-T content. Beyond the temperature required to separate the strands, which of the following is also influenced by this base composition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Condensation of DNA at centromeres and telomeres

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diameter of the double helix in those regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Handedness of the helical twist in those regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Identity of the pentose sugar in the backbone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Number of grooves present along the helix

explanation.summary: G-C and A-T concentration affect DNA condensing at centromeres and telomeres and the rate of transcription.
explanation.whyCorrect: G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds while A-T pairs have two, so G-C-rich stretches are more strongly bonded. Beyond raising the melting temperature, the G-C and A-T concentration also affects the condensing of DNA (centromeres and telomeres) as well as the rate of transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Helix diameter is not influenced by the number of hydrogen bonds in a region.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naturally occurring DNA is right-handed regardless of base composition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sugar in DNA is always deoxyribose; base composition has no bearing on sugar identity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The natural configuration always produces one major and one minor groove; base content does not change that count.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A history-of-medicine lecture describes how Watson and Crick were able to describe the double-helical structure of DNA. Their model depended on data produced by Rosalind Franklin and her team using which technique?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA sequencing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electron microscopy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotype preparation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pea plant crossbreeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-ray crystallography

explanation.summary: Watson and Crick used Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography research to describe DNA structure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Watson and Crick described the structure of DNA using the X-ray crystallography research of Rosalind Franklin and her team, which dramatically advanced the understanding of gene regulation and expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA sequencing reads base order and was not the basis of the double-helix model.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Electron microscopy was not the technique credited to Franklin's team in determining the helical structure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A karyotype depicts a full set of chromosomes for diagnosis; it does not reveal molecular helix structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pea plant experiments were Gregor Mendel's work characterizing dominant and recessive inheritance patterns, not the structural data used by Watson and Crick.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A nucleosome core particle is purified from chromatin and its protein content is analyzed. Which histone composition is expected in the core around which DNA winds twice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four copies of H1 and four copies of H3

choices.label: B
choices.text: One copy each of H1, H2A, H2B, and H3

choices.label: C
choices.text: One copy each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two copies each of H1, H2A, H3, and H4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4

explanation.summary: The nucleosome core is an octamer of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA winds twice around a core of eight histone protein subunits, consisting of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, to create a nucleosome. H1 is the ninth histone that later secures the DNA to form a chromatosome; it is not part of the core.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 is not part of the core, and the core needs H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, not just H3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H1 is not a core histone, and the core contains two copies of each subunit, not one; H4 is also missing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The core has two copies of each of the four histones (eight total), not one copy of each.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H1 is the linker histone, not a core component, and H2B is required in the core.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: Enzymes that acetylate or methylate histone tails act on specific amino acid residues that are especially abundant in the tails of H3 and H4. Which residues are these?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cysteine and methionine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate and aspartate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysine and arginine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylalanine and tryptophan

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serine and threonine

explanation.summary: Histone tails, especially H3 and H4, are rich in lysine and arginine, the residues that get methylated or acetylated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histones contain an abundance of positively charged amino acids, lysine and arginine, that bind tightly to the negatively charged phosphate groups of DNA. The tails of H3 and H4 contain many Lys and Arg residues, which can be methylated or acetylated to change how tightly the nucleosome is condensed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sulfur-containing residues are not the abundant, modifiable residues of histone tails.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate and aspartate are negatively charged and would repel DNA rather than bind it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bulky aromatic amino acids do not play a role in attracting DNA to histones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine and threonine are not the positively charged residues that dominate histone tails.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: Once DNA is secured to histone proteins, the string of beads coils further into a tube-like structure about 30 nm in diameter. What is this structure called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromatid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromatosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Major groove

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metaphase chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solenoid fiber

explanation.summary: The coiled string of nucleosomes forms the 30-nm solenoid, also called the chromatin fiber.
explanation.whyCorrect: Now that the DNA is secured to the histone proteins, the string of beads begins coiling and generates a tube-like structure referred to as a solenoid fiber (30-nm diameter), which can now be called a chromatin fiber.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chromatid forms only after the chromatin fiber loops and supercoils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chromatosome is a single nucleosome secured by H1, one bead on the string, not the coiled fiber.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The major groove is a surface feature of the double helix, not a packaging level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A metaphase chromosome is the final, most condensed structure after looping and supercoiling.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A student is asked to order the structures formed as a DNA double helix is progressively packaged into a chromosome visible during mitosis. Which sequence is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Looped chromatin, nucleosome, solenoid fiber, metaphase chromosome, supercoiled chromatid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleosome, chromatid, solenoid fiber, looped chromatin, metaphase chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nucleosome, looped chromatin, solenoid fiber, supercoiled chromatid, metaphase chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleosome, solenoid fiber, looped chromatin, supercoiled chromatid, metaphase chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solenoid fiber, nucleosome, looped chromatin, supercoiled chromatid, metaphase chromosome

explanation.summary: DNA packages as nucleosome, then solenoid (chromatin fiber), then loops, then supercoiled chromatid, then metaphase chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA first winds around histone octamers to form nucleosomes. The string of beads coils into a solenoid (chromatin) fiber, which then generates loops that are further condensed by supercoiling to create a chromatid. Two sister chromatids joined together form the condensed X-shaped metaphase chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Looped chromatin requires a pre-existing fiber, and the metaphase chromosome is the final product after chromatids form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The chromatid is the product of looping and supercoiling; it cannot precede the solenoid fiber.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The solenoid fiber forms before loops; loops are generated from the chromatin fiber.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleosomes must form before the string of beads can coil into a solenoid fiber.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A gene is transcribed at very high levels in a particular cell type. Analysis of the chromatin at this gene locus in those cells would most likely show which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA covalently cross-linked to the histone octamer core

choices.label: B
choices.text: Highly condensed heterochromatin with a high level of CpG methylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inaccessible DNA wrapped by unmodified, positively charged histone tails

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loosely condensed euchromatin with acetylated histone tails

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supercoiled chromatid structure typical of metaphase

explanation.summary: Actively transcribed genes reside in open euchromatin, which is loosely condensed and acetylated.
explanation.whyCorrect: When chromatin is less condensed it is referred to as euchromatin; in this state polymerases can be recruited to facilitate transcription. Acetylation of histone tails decreases the positive charge of histones, decondensing and opening the chromatin so the DNA is accessible and the gene is active.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA and histones interact through charge attraction, not covalent cross-links; such bonds would block transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heterochromatin with high methylation is inaccessible to polymerases and transcriptionally inactive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unmodified positively charged tails hold DNA tightly, making the gene inaccessible and inactive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supercoiled metaphase chromosomes are highly condensed structures formed for division, not for transcription.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes histone modifications at two different genes. Both genes show methylated histone tails, yet one gene is strongly transcribed while the other is silenced. Which statement best reconciles these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA methylation, rather than histone methylation, fully determines both outcomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histone methylation always silences a gene, so the transcribed gene must be an artifact

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histone methylation removes histone positive charge in exactly the same way acetylation does

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylated histones at the active gene have been converted directly into acetylated histones

choices.label: E
choices.text: The effect of histone methylation on expression depends on the level of methylation

explanation.summary: Unlike DNA methylation, histone methylation can either increase or decrease expression depending on its level.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histones can also be methylated. Unlike DNA methylation, where gene expression is decreased, in histone methylation gene expression may either increase or decrease depending on the level of methylation. Two methylated loci can therefore behave oppositely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The question describes histone modifications; DNA methylation was not what was measured and does not explain a methylated histone at an active gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histone methylation does not always silence genes; that consistent repression describes DNA methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is acetylation that decreases the overall positive charge of histones; histone methylation is described by its level-dependent effect, not by charge removal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyl and acetyl groups are distinct modifications; one is not converted into the other.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: Studies of cooperative chromatin folding examine which histone tails contribute most to the folding process and to maintaining contact between the histones and the DNA. Which set of histone tails is most important?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H1 only

choices.label: B
choices.text: H2A and H2B only

choices.label: C
choices.text: H2A, H2B, and H1

choices.label: D
choices.text: H3 and H2A only

choices.label: E
choices.text: H3, H4, and H1

explanation.summary: The tails of H3, H4, and H1 contribute the most to cooperative chromatin folding and DNA contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: All histone subunits, including H1, have an N-terminal or C-terminal tail. Studies show that the tails of H3, H4, and H1 contribute the most to the cooperative chromatin folding process and to maintaining contact between the histones and the DNA. The H3 and H4 tails are rich in lysine and arginine, which can be methylated or acetylated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 secures DNA to the core, but H3 and H4 tails also contribute strongly; H1 alone is incomplete.
