whyWrongByChoice.B: H2A and H2B are core histones but their tails are not the ones credited with the greatest contribution to folding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 is included, but H2A and H2B are not the key contributors; H3 and H4 are.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H3 is correct, but H2A is not among the major contributors, and H4 and H1 are omitted.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A cell in the G2 phase of the cell cycle has completed replication of its genome but has not yet divided. Which of the following correctly describes its chromosome and chromatid content?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids

choices.label: D
choices.text: 92 chromosomes and 184 chromatids

choices.label: E
choices.text: 92 chromosomes and 92 chromatids

explanation.summary: After replication a cell has 92 chromatids but still 46 chromosomes, because chromosome number is set by centromere number.
explanation.whyCorrect: Before cellular division each chromosome consists of two identical DNA molecules, the sister chromatids. At this point the cell contains double the genetic material, 92 chromatids, but is still said to have 46 chromosomes because the number of chromosomes in a cell is determined by the number of centromeres.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 is the haploid number contributed by one parent, not the count in a replicated somatic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Before replication a cell has 46 chromosomes with 46 chromatids, but after S phase each chromosome has two chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The genome doubles only once during S phase; there are not 184 chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sister chromatids joined at a single centromere count as one chromosome, so 92 chromatids still equal 46 chromosomes.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: Two individuals carry identical alleles at a particular gene locus, yet they display different phenotypes because the degree of chromatin condensation at that locus differs between them. This phenomenon is best described as an example of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic variation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epigenetic regulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genomic instability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mendelian dominance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sister chromatid cohesion

explanation.summary: Epigenetics studies phenotypes that emerge from gene regulation rather than from the alleles themselves.
explanation.whyCorrect: The regulation between euchromatin and heterochromatin states is a significant aspect of epigenetic regulation. Epigenetics studies heritable and nonheritable phenotypes that emerge from gene regulation, not from specific alleles themselves. Identical alleles with different chromatin states yielding different phenotypes fits this definition exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The individuals carry the same alleles, so allelic variation cannot explain the difference.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genomic instability refers to damage or changes in DNA structure, not differing chromatin condensation of intact identical alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mendelian dominance describes how different alleles interact; here the alleles are identical.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sister chromatid cohesion concerns holding replicated DNA molecules together before division, not phenotype regulation.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A developmental biologist studies a mouse embryo in which DNA methylation is experimentally blocked. Based on the known roles of DNA methylation, which of the following processes would be expected to be disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attachment of the mitotic spindle to the centromere

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of phosphodiester bonds in the backbone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genomic imprinting

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pairing of adenine with thymine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis of deoxyribose from ribose

explanation.summary: DNA methylation is required for normal genomic imprinting, embryonic development, and chromatin regulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA methylation is an epigenetic modification shown to be important for the normal regulation of chromatin structure, genome stability, transcription, embryonic development, and genomic imprinting. Blocking methylation would therefore disrupt imprinting. Aberrant DNA methylation has also been linked to neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's, depression, and Rett syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spindle attachment is a function of the centromere, not a methylation-dependent process described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phosphodiester bond formation is part of the covalent backbone and does not depend on methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Base pairing is governed by hydrogen bonding between complementary bases, independent of methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The identity of the pentose sugar is fixed in the nucleotide and unrelated to DNA methylation.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for a rare disorder characterized by features of accelerated aging. The disease is caused by a mutation that disrupts nuclear structure and thereby inhibits chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation. Which protein is mutated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cohesin

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histone H1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histone H4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lamin

explanation.summary: Progeria results from mutated lamin proteins of the nuclear envelope, disrupting chromatin organization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progeria is a rare disease that presents with features of accelerated aging. Mutated lamin proteins, a major component of the nuclear envelope, disrupt nuclear structure, which inhibits chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cohesins hold sister chromatids together after replication; they are not envelope components.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase replicates DNA and is not described as the mutated protein in progeria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 secures DNA to the nucleosome core; it is not a nuclear envelope protein and is not the cause of progeria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H4 is a core histone of the nucleosome, not a structural component of the nuclear envelope.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A clinician orders a test that produces an image of a patient's full set of chromosomes arranged in numbered pairs so that chromosomal abnormalities can be diagnosed. What is this depiction called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromatid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solenoid

explanation.summary: A karyotype is a depiction of a full set of chromosomes used for diagnostic purposes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within the nucleus, individual DNA molecules are referred to as chromosomes, and together a full set represents the organism's genome. A human karyotype is a depiction of that full set of chromosomes and can be used for diagnostic purposes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chromatid is one of the two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The genome is the full set of chromosomes itself, the library of genetic information, not the diagnostic image of them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nucleosome is DNA wound around a histone octamer, a packaging unit far smaller than a chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A solenoid is the 30-nm coiled chromatin fiber, an intermediate packaging structure.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A patient's maternal and paternal copies of chromosome 7 contain the same set of genes, yet at one gene locus the two copies carry different DNA sequences. What are these differing versions of the gene called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Centromeres

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chromatosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histone tails

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sister chromatids

explanation.summary: Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes but may carry different versions, called alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humans have diploid genomes consisting of pairs of homologous chromosomes. Homologous means the respective chromosomes contain the same set of genes, but they are not identical because they can contain different versions of a gene, called alleles.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The centromere is the point joining sister chromatids and the spindle attachment site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chromatosome is a nucleosome secured by H1, a packaging structure rather than a gene variant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histone tails are protein extensions that are methylated or acetylated; they are not gene versions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA molecules produced by replication, not differing gene versions.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: During S phase a cell duplicates each of its chromosomes. The two newly synthesized DNA molecules remain physically attached to one another until just before the cell divides. Which proteins are responsible for holding the sister chromatids together during this period?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cohesins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histone H1 linkers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lamins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitotic spindle fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcription factors

explanation.summary: Cohesins hold newly replicated sister chromatids together until just prior to cell division.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the S phase of the cell cycle, newly synthesized chromosomes remain attached to one another via proteins called cohesins. The two DNA molecules remain attached via cohesins until just prior to cellular division, and these cohesion proteins are then degraded as the cell proceeds through the cell cycle and mitosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H1 secures DNA around the histone core to form chromatosomes; it does not join two chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lamins are components of the nuclear envelope, not proteins linking sister chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mitotic spindle attaches at the centromere to pull sister chromatids apart, the opposite of holding them together.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transcription factors regulate gene expression and play no role in chromatid cohesion.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: Imaging of an interphase nucleus shows that each chromosome occupies its own discrete region rather than intermixing randomly with the others, and that zones where two chromosomes overlap contain increased amounts of transcription machinery. What is the primary purpose of maintaining chromosomes in these distinct territories?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To allow efficient assortment of chromosomes into daughter cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: To hold sister chromatids together during S phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: To keep all chromosomes transcriptionally silent until mitosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: To preserve the right-handed twist of each double helix

choices.label: E
choices.text: To prevent methyl groups from spreading between chromosomes

explanation.summary: Chromosomes occupy specific nuclear territories to allow efficient assortment into each daughter cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: For efficient assortment of chromosomes into each daughter cell, the chromosomes are maintained in specific territories within the nucleus. The overlapping regions between territories are associated with increased levels of transcription machinery, but the organizing purpose of the territories themselves is orderly assortment at division.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sister chromatids are held together by cohesins, not by nuclear territory organization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interphase chromosomes are not uniformly silent; the overlapping territory regions are enriched in transcription machinery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helix handedness is an intrinsic molecular property unrelated to the spatial position of chromosomes in the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA methylation is targeted to specific sequences; territories are not described as barriers to methylation.

questions.topicName: DNA Structure

questions.stem: A researcher grows cells so that their DNA contains a heavy nitrogen isotope, then allows the cells to complete a single round of DNA replication in medium containing only light nitrogen. When the daughter double helices are analyzed, each contains one original heavy strand and one newly synthesized light strand. Which model of DNA replication does this result demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bidirectional conservative replication

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conservative replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dispersive replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random-strand replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: Semiconservative replication

explanation.summary: DNA replication follows a semiconservative model in which each daughter helix keeps one parent strand and one new strand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because each strand of the original helix serves as a template for a new complementary strand, every daughter chromosome contains one original parent strand and one newly synthesized daughter strand. A result showing one heavy and one light strand per daughter helix is the hallmark of semiconservative replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bidirectional refers to fork movement from the origin, not to how parent and daughter strands are partitioned; the partitioning shown here is still semiconservative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A conservative model would keep the two parent strands together and produce one entirely new daughter helix, not a hybrid of one old and one new strand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A dispersive model would scatter old and new segments along both strands, so no strand would be entirely heavy or entirely light.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no random-strand model; strand inheritance in replication is defined and predictable, not random.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: During initiation of DNA replication, helicase and its helper proteins preferentially begin separating the parent strands at regions of the helix that are rich in adenine-thymine base pairs rather than guanine-cytosine base pairs. Which of the following best explains why A-T rich regions are easier to separate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-T pairs are held together by two hydrogen bonds, whereas G-C pairs have three

choices.label: B
choices.text: A-T pairs are joined by covalent phosphodiester bonds that helicase cleaves quickly

choices.label: C
choices.text: A-T pairs are located only at the origin of replication, so helicase cannot reach G-C pairs

choices.label: D
choices.text: A-T pairs lack hydrogen bonds entirely and therefore fall apart on their own

choices.label: E
choices.text: G-C pairs are stabilized by single-stranded binding proteins that block helicase

explanation.summary: A-T base pairs are held by two hydrogen bonds while G-C base pairs are held by three, making A-T rich DNA easier to unwind.
explanation.whyCorrect: Helicase severs the hydrogen bonds between paired bases to separate the strands. Because A-T pairs have only two hydrogen bonds compared with three for G-C pairs, less energy is needed to open A-T rich regions, so helicase and its helper proteins favor them.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrogen bonds, not phosphodiester bonds, hold complementary strands together; phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within a single strand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A-T pairs are distributed throughout the genome, not confined to the origin; the ease of separation reflects hydrogen bond number, not location.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A-T pairs are held by hydrogen bonds; they simply have fewer of them, but they do not lack them altogether.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Single-stranded binding proteins bind exposed single strands after separation to prevent reannealing; they are not responsible for stabilizing intact G-C pairs against helicase.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: In an in vitro system, purified DNA polymerase is added to a single-stranded DNA template with abundant free nucleotides, yet no new DNA is synthesized. Synthesis begins only after a second enzyme is added that generates a short segment with a free 3'-hydroxyl group. Which enzyme was added, and what does it produce?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flap endonuclease, which produces a trimmed 3' flap

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase, which produces a replication bubble

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase, which produces a phosphodiester bond

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primase, which produces an RNA primer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase, which produces a single-stranded nick

explanation.summary: DNA polymerase cannot start on a bare template and requires a primer with a free 3'-OH, which primase supplies as a short RNA segment.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides to an existing polynucleotide that has a 3'-OH; they cannot initiate synthesis on a naked template. Primase lays down a short RNA primer that provides this 3'-OH, allowing DNA polymerase to bind and begin elongating the new strand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims a displaced flap during Okazaki fragment processing; it does not generate a starting primer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase separates the strands to form the replication bubble but does not provide the 3'-OH primer that polymerase requires.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligase seals gaps between existing fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds; it does not create the initial primer needed to start synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase nicks and reseals DNA to relieve supercoiling; the transient nick does not serve as a starting primer for polymerase.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: As helicase unwinds the double helix at the replication fork, the two exposed parent strands are complementary and tend to snap back together into a duplex, which would block the replicative enzymes. Which of the following proteins directly prevents this reannealing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA ligase at the lagging strand

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA primase of the Pol alpha complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Single-stranded binding proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The PCNA sliding clamp protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase ahead of the fork

explanation.summary: Single-stranded binding proteins coat the exposed nucleotides of separated parent strands to keep them from reannealing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once helicase separates the strands, single-stranded binding proteins bind the exposed nitrogenous bases, providing a physical barrier that prevents the complementary strands from reassociating and stops them from interacting with free nucleotides. They are readily displaced by DNA polymerase and primase so synthesis is not blocked.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA ligase seals gaps between Okazaki fragments and has no role in keeping separated parent strands apart.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Primase synthesizes RNA primers; it does not prevent the parent strands from reannealing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PCNA sliding clamp keeps polymerase anchored to the template to boost processivity, not to prevent strand reannealing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling tension downstream of the fork; it does not coat single strands to prevent reannealing.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: As helicase unwinds DNA, excessive supercoiling builds up ahead of the replication fork. An ATP-dependent enzyme relieves this tension by grabbing two portions of the same supercoiled helix, introducing a double-stranded break at one location, and passing the other segment through the break before resealing it. Which enzyme is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flap endonuclease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topoisomerase I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase II

explanation.summary: Topoisomerase II is ATP-dependent and relieves supercoiling by creating a double-stranded break and passing another segment of helix through it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type II topoisomerases exist as homodimeric or heterotetrameric ATP-dependent enzymes. They grab two portions of the same supercoiled helix, introduce a double-stranded break at one location, and pass the other portion through that break before resealing, which relaxes the supercoil.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims displaced flaps during Okazaki fragment processing and does not act on supercoiling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase separates strands by breaking hydrogen bonds and is the source of the supercoiling tension, not the enzyme that relieves it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primase synthesizes RNA primers and has no role in relaxing supercoils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topoisomerase I is a monomeric, ATP-independent enzyme that makes only a transient single-stranded break, allowing the helix to rotate around the intact strand.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A student is tracing how DNA polymerase moves during synthesis of a new daughter strand. Because DNA strands are complementary and antiparallel, in order to build the new strand in the 5' to 3' direction the polymerase must travel along the template strand in which direction?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Always toward the nearest origin of replication regardless of strand polarity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both 5' to 3' and 3' to 5' simultaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: In whichever direction the RNA primer points, independent of polarity

explanation.summary: Because strands are antiparallel, synthesizing the new strand 5' to 3' requires the polymerase to read the template 3' to 5'.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end, so new strands are always synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction. Since the two strands run antiparallel, the polymerase must move along the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction to accomplish this.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Moving 5' to 3' along the template would require building the new strand 3' to 5', which DNA polymerase cannot do.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polymerase direction is set by strand polarity and the 5'-to-3' rule, not by proximity to an origin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single polymerase reads the template in one fixed direction; it cannot move both ways at once.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Directionality is dictated by the antiparallel, 5'-to-3' chemistry of synthesis, not by the orientation of the primer alone.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: At each replication fork, one new strand is made continuously while the other is assembled from many short segments called Okazaki fragments, each requiring its own RNA primer. Which fundamental property of DNA is the underlying reason the lagging strand must be synthesized in this semi-discontinuous manner?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 3' to 5' polymerization style of DNA Pol epsilon

choices.label: B
choices.text: The complementary, antiparallel nature of the DNA molecule

choices.label: C
choices.text: The poor processivity and rapid dissociation of DNA Pol delta from templates

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of multiple origins of replication on the chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The RNA primase activity of a subunit of DNA Pol alpha

explanation.summary: The antiparallel nature of DNA means only one strand can be copied continuously, forcing the other to be made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because DNA polymerases synthesize only in the 5' to 3' direction and the two strands are antiparallel, at any given fork only one strand (the leading strand) can be made continuously. The other template is exposed in the wrong orientation, so its new strand must be built in short Okazaki fragments as more template becomes available.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA polymerases synthesize in the 5' to 3' direction, not 3' to 5'; this option misstates polymerase chemistry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA Pol delta actually has high processivity because it associates with a sliding clamp, so poor processivity is not the reason.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple origins speed up replication of long chromosomes but do not explain why one strand is made discontinuously.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RNA primase subunit permits semi-discontinuous synthesis by laying primers, but it is not the underlying cause of the discontinuity.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: DNA Pol delta and Pol epsilon are the primary replicative polymerases in eukaryotes and remain bound to the template long enough to copy long stretches of DNA accurately. This high processivity is most directly explained by their association with which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flap endonuclease trimming the displaced 5' DNA flap

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single-stranded binding proteins coating the exposed template

choices.label: C
choices.text: The PCNA sliding clamp, which forms a ring around the DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The RNA primase subunit of the DNA Pol alpha complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase acting as a swivel just ahead of the fork

explanation.summary: The proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) sliding clamp encircles the DNA and keeps Pol delta and Pol epsilon attached, giving them high processivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Processivity describes how long a polymerase stays bound to the template. Pol delta and Pol epsilon achieve high processivity by associating with the PCNA sliding clamp, which forms a ring around the DNA and literally keeps the polymerase attached during replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims displaced flaps during fragment processing and has no role in polymerase processivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Single-stranded binding proteins prevent reannealing of separated strands and are displaced by the polymerase; they do not confer processivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The primase subunit of Pol alpha initiates synthesis with RNA primers but does not anchor Pol delta or Pol epsilon to the template.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork and does not tether the polymerase to DNA.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Eukaryotic DNA replication begins with a unique multi-subunit polymerase. One of its subunits has RNA primase activity and lays the primer needed to start synthesis on the leading strand and for each Okazaki fragment, but the enzyme detaches after adding only about 20 nucleotides. Which polymerase is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA ligase

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA Pol alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA Pol delta

choices.label: D
choices.text: DNA Pol epsilon

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase I

explanation.summary: DNA Pol alpha is the multi-subunit initiating polymerase; its primase subunit lays the primer, but it has low processivity and stays bound for only about 20 nucleotides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Replication starts with DNA Pol alpha, a unique multi-subunit enzyme. One subunit has RNA primase activity and generates the primer that allows initiation on the leading strand and for each Okazaki fragment. Pol alpha has low processivity and stays attached to the template for only about 20 nucleotides before Pol delta and Pol epsilon take over.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA ligase seals gaps between fragments and does not initiate synthesis or synthesize primers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA Pol delta is recruited after initiation to complete the Okazaki fragments and has high processivity, not primase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA Pol epsilon completes the leading strand with high processivity and does not carry the primase subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase I relaxes supercoils and is not a polymerase and does not lay primers.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: In eukaryotes, as DNA Pol delta synthesizes an Okazaki fragment it does not stop when it reaches the previous RNA primer; instead it displaces the primer and a short 5' segment of the previous fragment, creating a single-stranded flap. Which enzyme removes this flap so the fragments can be joined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA ligase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flap endonuclease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helicase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single-stranded binding protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase II

explanation.summary: Strand-displacement synthesis by Pol delta creates a flap that a special flap endonuclease trims before ligase seals the gap.
explanation.whyCorrect: When Pol delta displaces the RNA primer and a short 5' segment of the previous Okazaki fragment, it produces a flap that requires resection. A special flap endonuclease trims this flap, which then allows ligase to seal the gap between the fragments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA ligase seals the gap only after the flap has been trimmed; it does not cut the flap itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helicase unwinds the parent duplex at the fork and does not act on displaced flaps during fragment processing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Single-stranded binding proteins prevent reannealing of parent strands and do not remove flaps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase II relieves supercoiling by cutting and passing helix segments and does not trim lagging strand flaps.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: After the RNA primers on the lagging strand are removed and the flaps are trimmed, adjacent Okazaki fragments remain as separate segments with nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone between them. Which enzyme joins these fragments into a continuous strand, and by forming what type of bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA ligase, by forming phosphodiester bonds

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA polymerase, by forming hydrogen bonds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helicase, by forming phosphodiester bonds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primase, by forming phosphodiester bonds

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase, by forming hydrogen bonds

explanation.summary: DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds in the backbone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ligase creates phosphodiester bonds between adjacent Okazaki fragments to seal the remaining gaps, converting the discontinuous lagging strand segments into one continuous daughter strand. This is the final joining step of lagging strand synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to build strands; it does not seal the nick between fragments, and hydrogen bonds link complementary bases rather than joining backbone segments.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helicase separates strands and plays no role in joining fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primase makes RNA primers and does not seal gaps between DNA fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling by nicking and resealing; it does not ligate separate Okazaki fragments, and base-pair hydrogen bonds are not what join the backbone.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: During synthesis, DNA Pol epsilon occasionally inserts a nucleotide that does not correctly pair with the template. Before continuing polymerization, the enzyme detects the mismatch, removes the incorrectly paired nucleotide, and then inserts the correct one. Which intrinsic polymerase activity is responsible for this correction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3' to 5' exonuclease activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5' to 3' polymerase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic RNA primase activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sliding clamp anchoring activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strand-unwinding helicase activity

explanation.summary: The 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity of Pol delta and Pol epsilon removes a mismatched nucleotide before synthesis continues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both primary replicative polymerases have proofreading capability provided by 3' to 5' exonuclease activity. When a mispairing is identified, this activity removes the incorrectly paired nucleotide from the 3' end so the correct nucleotide can be inserted, giving these polymerases very high fidelity and an estimated mutation rate below one in one hundred million base pairs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 5' to 3' polymerase activity adds nucleotides to build the strand; it is the activity that can introduce the error, not correct it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RNA primase activity generates primers and does not remove mismatched nucleotides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sliding clamp increases processivity by anchoring the polymerase but does not itself excise mismatched nucleotides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Helicase activity unwinds the duplex and is not part of proofreading.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: During the S phase of the cell cycle, replication of a eukaryotic chromosome begins when a specific DNA sequence is bound by initiator proteins, which begin to separate the strands at that spot and recruit helicase. The DNA sequence being recognized is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advancing replication fork

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newly made Okazaki fragment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Open replication bubble

choices.label: D
choices.text: Origin of replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primase-laid RNA primer

explanation.summary: Duplex opening occurs at the origin of replication (ori site), which is recognized by initiator proteins that recruit helicase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The site where duplex opening occurs is the origin of replication, or ori site. Initiator proteins recognize this sequence, begin separating the DNA there, and recruit the helicase that then dissociates the hydrogen bonds between paired bases to open the double helix.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A replication fork is the moving junction at each end of the bubble where helicase continues to separate the strands; it is a structure that forms after initiation, not the sequence recognized by initiator proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An Okazaki fragment is a short segment of newly synthesized lagging strand DNA, not a sequence in the parent DNA that starts replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The replication bubble is the portion of the parent strands that has already been separated; it is the product of opening at the ori site, not the sequence that is recognized.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RNA primer is a short RNA segment laid down by primase to give polymerase a 3'-OH; it is made after the strands are already separated.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A researcher compares replication of a small bacterial chromosome with replication of a human chromosome that contains roughly 250 million base pairs. She observes that the human chromosome initiates replication at many separate sites simultaneously. Which of the following best explains why this arrangement is necessary?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single origin would make copying such a long molecule impractically slow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each origin is needed to supply a separate proofreading exonuclease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eukaryotic DNA polymerases have too little processivity to copy long stretches

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helicase cannot open G-C rich regions without additional origins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linear chromosomes cannot form a replication bubble at a single site

explanation.summary: Long linear eukaryotic chromosomes use multiple ori sites because a single origin would take an impractically long time to replicate the molecule.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eukaryotes possess extremely long, linear chromosomes; a single human chromosome can contain up to approximately 250 million base pairs. Relying on one origin of replication would make the process take an incredibly long time and be impractical for the survival of a living organism, so replication of large eukaryotic DNA typically uses multiple ori sites per chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Proofreading is an intrinsic 3' to 5' exonuclease activity of the polymerase itself and is not supplied by origins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The primary replicative polymerases Pol delta and Pol epsilon have high processivity because of the PCNA sliding clamp; the need for multiple origins is about time, not polymerase processivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helicase favors A-T rich regions because they are easier to separate, but it is fully capable of opening G-C pairs; additional origins are not required for that.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A linear chromosome can certainly form a bubble at a single site; the problem is that a single bubble would be far too slow to replicate hundreds of millions of base pairs.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A biochemist compares the two classes of topoisomerase that relieve tension ahead of a replication fork. Topoisomerase I differs from topoisomerase II in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It functions as a heterotetramer rather than as a monomer

choices.label: B
choices.text: It grabs two portions of the helix rather than acting at one location

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces supercoils ahead of the fork rather than relaxing them

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes a transient single-stranded break rather than a double-stranded break

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires ATP hydrolysis, whereas topoisomerase II does not

explanation.summary: Topoisomerase I is a monomeric, ATP-independent enzyme that makes a transient single-stranded break, whereas topoisomerase II is ATP-dependent and makes a double-stranded break.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topoisomerase I is a monomeric enzyme that makes transient single-stranded breaks in the double helix; the break lets the helix rotate around the intact strand before it is resealed, relaxing the supercoil. Type II topoisomerases instead grab two portions of the same supercoiled helix, introduce a double-stranded break at one location, and pass the other portion through that break before resealing. Both classes relieve supercoiling, but their mechanisms differ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topoisomerase I is monomeric; it is the type II enzymes that exist as homodimeric or heterotetrameric complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grabbing two portions of the same supercoiled helix is the hallmark of topoisomerase II; topoisomerase I acts at just one location.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both classes of topoisomerase undo supercoiling by introducing breaks and resealing the helix; neither introduces additional supercoils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is backward: topoisomerase I functions independently of ATP, while type II topoisomerases are ATP-dependent.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A student observes that each time DNA polymerase adds a new nucleotide to the growing daughter strand, a pyrophosphate is released. Which of the following is the source of the energy that drives formation of the new phosphodiester bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cleavage of the RNA primer by flap endonuclease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen bonding between the incoming nucleotide and the template base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrolysis of ATP bound within the polymerase active site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxation of supercoils by topoisomerase ahead of the fork

choices.label: E
choices.text: The triphosphate tail of the incoming free nucleotide

explanation.summary: DNA polymerases harness the stored energy in a free nucleotide's triphosphate tail to form the new phosphodiester bond, releasing pyrophosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Polymerization is the consecutive attachment of free nucleotides according to the template. DNA polymerases facilitate this by harnessing the stored energy in the free nucleotide's triphosphate tail, creating a new phosphodiester bond between the incoming matching nucleotide and the growing polynucleotide while pyrophosphate is released.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims displaced flaps during Okazaki fragment processing; it does not provide energy for polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases guide which nucleotide is selected, but they do not supply the energy for backbone bond formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ATP hydrolysis powers type II topoisomerase, not the phosphodiester bond formation carried out by DNA polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topoisomerase relieves topological stress ahead of the fork; supercoil relaxation is not coupled to nucleotide addition.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A cultured cell line is treated with a compound that completely inactivates all topoisomerase activity while helicase continues to unwind DNA at active replication forks. Which of the following is the most likely consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mismatched nucleotides accumulate at the 3' end of daughter strands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Okazaki fragments remain separated by nicks in the backbone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Over-winding ahead of the fork impedes replication and damages DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parent strands reanneal behind the helicase within the bubble

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA primers can no longer be laid on the lagging strand template

explanation.summary: Without topoisomerase, the supercoiling that helicase creates downstream of the fork becomes excessive, impeding replication and damaging the DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: As helicase unwinds the molecule, it creates stress in the helix downstream of its activity that manifests as supercoiling, the over-winding of the helix. If the degree of supercoiling becomes too excessive, it can impede DNA replication and damage the DNA. Topoisomerase normally alleviates this topological stress by unwinding the helix ahead of the replication fork, so its loss leaves the tension unrelieved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Removal of mismatched nucleotides is performed by the 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading of Pol delta and Pol epsilon, which is independent of topoisomerase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sealing nicks between Okazaki fragments is the job of ligase; topoisomerase loss does not directly affect ligation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reannealing of the separated parent strands is prevented by single-stranded binding proteins, which are unaffected by loss of topoisomerase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primer synthesis depends on primase (the primase subunit of Pol alpha), not on topoisomerase.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: At a replication fork, the bases of one parent template strand are exposed in the 3' to 5' direction as helicase advances. Which of the following correctly describes synthesis of the daughter strand on this template?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is copied by DNA Pol alpha alone without any further polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is copied continuously and requires only a single RNA primer

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is copied in short fragments, each needing its own RNA primer

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is copied in the 3' to 5' direction to match helicase movement

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is copied only after the entire replication bubble has opened

explanation.summary: The template exposed 3' to 5' is the leading strand template, which is copied continuously behind the helicase with only one RNA primer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each replication fork involves one parent strand whose bases are continuously exposed in a 3' to 5' direction, termed the leading strand. Along this template, DNA polymerase travels 3' to 5' directly behind the helicase, continuously synthesizing new DNA in the 5' to 3' direction, and only one RNA primer is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pol alpha has low processivity and stays bound for only about 20 nucleotides; Pol delta and Pol epsilon are recruited to complete the strand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Synthesis in short primer-dependent fragments (Okazaki fragments) describes the lagging strand, whose template is exposed in the 5' to 3' direction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: New strands are always synthesized 5' to 3'; the polymerase moves along the template 3' to 5', which on the leading strand is the same direction the helicase is moving.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synthesis begins as soon as the primer is laid and does not wait for the bubble to open fully; the fork keeps advancing during synthesis.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Single-stranded binding proteins coat the exposed parent strands at a replication fork and physically block the bases from interacting with free nucleotides or other single-stranded polynucleotides. Despite this barrier, synthesis of the daughter strands proceeds without hindrance. Which of the following best explains why SSBs do not block synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SSBs are cleaved from the strand by flap endonuclease before synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: SSBs are readily displaced by DNA polymerase and primase as they advance

choices.label: C
choices.text: SSBs bind only the leading strand template and never the lagging strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: SSBs bind only the sugar-phosphate backbone, leaving the bases free to pair

choices.label: E
choices.text: SSBs dissociate spontaneously once topoisomerase relaxes the helix

explanation.summary: The replication machinery, DNA polymerase and primase, easily displaces SSBs so they do not interfere with formation of the new strand.
explanation.whyCorrect: SSBs bind to the exposed nitrogenous bases of the separated parent strands, providing a physical barrier that prevents reannealing and blocks interaction with free nucleotides. However, the replication machinery comprised of DNA polymerase and primase are both able to easily displace SSBs, so the proteins do not interfere with the formation of a new DNA strand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims the displaced flap during Okazaki fragment processing and does not remove SSBs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SSBs coat both separated parent strands at the fork; they are not restricted to the leading strand template.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SSBs bind the exposed nitrogenous bases themselves, which is exactly why they block interaction with free nucleotides until displaced.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SSB removal is not triggered by topoisomerase, which acts on supercoiling ahead of the fork; SSBs are displaced by the advancing polymerase and primase.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Following duplex opening at a single ori site, helicases continue to separate the parental strands and the replication bubble enlarges. Which of the following best describes how replication proceeds from this one origin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new origin must be recognized before either fork can advance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both ends of the bubble become forks, each copying both strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helicase stops once the bubble forms and polymerase unwinds the rest

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only one parent strand is copied until the bubble reaches full size

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis proceeds in one direction only, away from the origin

explanation.summary: From an origin, replication proceeds at both ends of the bubble on both strands simultaneously, with each end of the bubble forming a replication fork.
explanation.whyCorrect: From the origin of replication, DNA replication proceeds at both ends of the replication bubble on both strands simultaneously. Each end of the replication bubble becomes a replication fork as the helicases separating the two parental strands continue to work, so each fork carries one leading strand and one lagging strand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The forks advance from the existing origin; additional origins speed replication of long chromosomes but are not prerequisites for fork movement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helicase creates the initial bubble and then continues to separate the helix at the edge of the replication forks; polymerase does not unwind DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both parent strands serve as templates simultaneously at each fork; copying is not delayed on one strand until the bubble is fully open.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Replication is not unidirectional from an origin; it proceeds at both ends of the bubble at the same time.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A student traces the movement of DNA polymerase on each template at a single replication fork. On the leading strand template, the polymerase follows directly behind the advancing helicase. On the lagging strand template, in which direction does DNA polymerase synthesize each new segment relative to the direction in which the helicase is opening the duplex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alternately toward and away from the helicase depending on the primer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perpendicular to the helicase, across the fork

choices.label: C
choices.text: The opposite direction from the helicase, in short fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same direction as the helicase, but only after ligase joins fragments

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same direction as the helicase, continuously

explanation.summary: Because polymerase can only build 5' to 3', lagging strand synthesis runs opposite to the direction the helicase opens the duplex and is done in short Okazaki fragments.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 5' to 3' directionality of DNA polymerase means synthesis of the lagging strand occurs in the opposite direction as the helicase opens the duplex. The lagging strand template is exposed 5' to 3', so the polymerase must move away from the fork, and synthesis occurs in a semi-discontinuous manner: after enough nucleotides are exposed, a new primer is laid and a new Okazaki fragment is built back toward the previous one.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direction of lagging strand synthesis is fixed by the 5' to 3' rule; it is always away from the fork, not alternating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Polymerase always moves along the length of the template strand it is copying; there is no perpendicular movement across the fork.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligase seals the gaps between completed Okazaki fragments; it does not change the direction in which polymerase moves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Continuous synthesis in the same direction as the helicase describes the leading strand, not the lagging strand.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Failures during lagging strand synthesis are a meaningful source of genome instability, in part because of the sheer number of separate starts the replication machinery must make. Approximately how many Okazaki fragments must be initiated during replication of a single human genome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 to 3 million

choices.label: B
choices.text: 20 to 30 million

choices.label: C
choices.text: 20 to 30 thousand

choices.label: D
choices.text: 200 to 300 million

choices.label: E
choices.text: 200 to 300 thousand

explanation.summary: Replicating a human genome requires initiating roughly 20 to 30 million Okazaki fragments.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the replication of a human genome, the replication machinery must initiate 20 to 30 million Okazaki fragments, each requiring its own RNA primer, extension, primer removal, and ligation. This large number of separate events is why failures in lagging strand processing can lead to an increase in genome instability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few million is still an order of magnitude below the 20 to 30 million fragments required.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tens of thousands is far too few; the lagging strand of every chromosome is built from many short fragments, totaling tens of millions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hundreds of millions overestimates the count by about tenfold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hundreds of thousands underestimates the count by about a hundredfold.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Eukaryotic cells possess three DNA polymerases that participate in chromosomal replication: DNA Pol alpha, Pol delta, and Pol epsilon. Which of the following activities is shared by all three of these enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5' to 3' polymerase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flap endonuclease activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: High processivity via the PCNA sliding clamp

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA primase activity

explanation.summary: Every DNA polymerase possesses 5' to 3' polymerase activity; the other activities are specific to particular polymerases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every DNA polymerase possesses 5' to 3' polymerase activity, which is what allows each of them to add nucleotides and assemble new daughter strands. Pol alpha uses it to lay the first roughly 20 nucleotides, while Pol delta and Pol epsilon use it to complete the leading strand and the Okazaki fragments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading capability belongs to the primary replicative polymerases Pol delta and Pol epsilon, not Pol alpha.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flap trimming is performed by a special flap endonuclease, not by any of the DNA polymerases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High processivity from association with the PCNA sliding clamp is a feature of Pol delta and Pol epsilon; Pol alpha has low processivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only Pol alpha has a subunit with RNA primase activity; it is the only polymerase that lays down its own primer.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: During replication, DNA Pol epsilon incorporates an incorrect nucleotide that escapes detection by its 3' to 5' exonuclease activity, and polymerization continues past the error. Which of the following mechanisms provides the cell's next opportunity to correct this mispairing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flap endonuclease resection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair systems

choices.label: C
choices.text: RNA primase activity of Pol alpha

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strand displacement synthesis by Pol delta

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase II strand passage

explanation.summary: Mismatch repair mechanisms correct errors in nucleotide pairing that were not caught by DNA polymerase proofreading.
explanation.whyCorrect: The high fidelity of Pol delta and Pol epsilon comes from a combination of their intrinsic ability to select correct nucleotides, their 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading, and the involvement of mismatch repair systems. On top of proofreading, cells have mismatch repair mechanisms that are able to correct errors in nucleotide pairings that were not caught by DNA polymerase proofreading, acting as proofreaders of the proofreaders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flap endonuclease trims the displaced flap so ligase can seal Okazaki fragments; it does not survey the strand for mispairing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primase generates RNA primers to start synthesis; it has no role in detecting or correcting mispaired nucleotides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Strand displacement synthesis by Pol delta displaces the RNA primer of the previous Okazaki fragment; it is not an error-correction pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase II relieves supercoiling by passing one segment of helix through a double-stranded break; it does not repair mismatches.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with recurrent pulmonary infections and pancreatic insufficiency is diagnosed with cystic fibrosis. His parents ask how a serious illness could arise from a change in DNA. Which of the following best describes the type of genetic change that underlies cystic fibrosis and several other disorders, including Tay-Sachs disease and thalassemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A change in a single base pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of all origins of replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duplication of a whole chromosome arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of helicase to separate the strands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of an entire chromosome

explanation.summary: A single base pair mutation is sufficient to cause diseases such as cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs disease, thalassemia, hemolytic anemia, and neurofibromatosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although Pol delta and Pol epsilon are extremely accurate, a single base pair mutation is the cause of multiple diseases and disorders. Common examples of diseases caused by a single base change include cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs disease, thalassemia, hemolytic anemia, and neurofibromatosis, which is why even one nucleotide incorrectly paired at a critical point in a gene can introduce a pathologic mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Origins of replication are required to begin replication of every chromosome; their absence is not the basis of these single base change diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These disorders result from a single base change, not from large-scale duplication of chromosomal material.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helicase failure would prevent strand separation and replication altogether; it does not describe the heritable single base change behind cystic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cystic fibrosis is an example of a disease caused by a single base change, not by loss of a whole chromosome.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: Pol delta and Pol epsilon achieve high fidelity in part through an exonuclease activity. Which of the following best defines an exonuclease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An enzyme that cleaves a displaced flap from the interior of a strand

choices.label: B
choices.text: An enzyme that forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent fragments

choices.label: C
choices.text: An enzyme that lays down short RNA segments on a template strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: An enzyme that removes nucleotides from the end of a nucleic acid strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: An enzyme that separates strands by breaking hydrogen bonds

explanation.summary: An exonuclease removes nucleotides from the end of a nucleic acid strand and can act in either the 3' to 5' or 5' to 3' direction.
explanation.whyCorrect: An exonuclease is an enzyme with the ability to remove nucleotides from the end of a nucleic acid strand. These enzymes can act in either a 3' to 5' or 5' to 3' direction, removing nucleotides from the respective ends of the molecule. The 3' to 5' exonuclease activity of Pol delta and Pol epsilon is what lets them remove an incorrectly paired nucleotide from the 3' end before proceeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutting a displaced flap describes the flap endonuclease, which cleaves within a strand rather than from its end.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forming phosphodiester bonds between fragments is the function of ligase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Laying down short RNA segments is the function of primase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Separating strands by breaking hydrogen bonds is the function of helicase.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A newly characterized DNA polymerase is found to pair each incoming nucleotide with the complementary template base with extremely high accuracy, but it dissociates from the template after adding only a small number of nucleotides. Which of the following best describes this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High fidelity, high processivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: High fidelity, low processivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: High processivity with no proofreading

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low fidelity, high processivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low fidelity, low processivity

explanation.summary: Fidelity describes accuracy of nucleotide pairing, while processivity describes how long a polymerase stays bound to the template; the two properties are independent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Processivity is used to describe how likely a DNA polymerase is to remain attached or bound to the template DNA strand, so an enzyme that detaches after only a few nucleotides has low processivity. DNA polymerases are said to have high fidelity if they are very accurate in pairing the appropriate new nucleotides to the complementary nucleotide on the template strand. This enzyme is therefore accurate but not processive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapid dissociation from the template is the definition of low, not high, processivity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An enzyme that dissociates after a few nucleotides cannot be described as highly processive, and nothing in the description indicates absent proofreading.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The enzyme is accurate (high fidelity) and detaches quickly (low processivity); this option reverses both properties.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extremely accurate base pairing is high fidelity, not low fidelity.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A template strand at a replication fork has the sequence 3'-TACGGA-5'. Given that nitrogenous base pairs within DNA are always adenine-thymine or guanine-cytosine and that the two strands are antiparallel, which of the following is the sequence of the newly synthesized daughter strand, written 5' to 3'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5'-AGGCAT-3'

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5'-ATGCCA-3'

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5'-ATGCCT-3'

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5'-TACGGA-3'

choices.label: E
choices.text: 5'-TCCGTA-3'

explanation.summary: Because base pairing is always A-T and G-C and the strands are antiparallel, the sequence of one strand perfectly corresponds to its partner: 3'-TACGGA-5' templates 5'-ATGCCT-3'.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within DNA, base pairs are always adenine-thymine or guanine-cytosine, so the sequence of one strand perfectly corresponds to the sequence of its paired strand. Reading the template 3' to 5' (T-A-C-G-G-A) and pairing each base gives A-T-G-C-C-T, and because the daughter strand is synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction opposite the template, it reads 5'-ATGCCT-3'.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the template strand itself written in 5' to 3' orientation, not the complementary daughter strand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The final base is wrong: the template's 5'-terminal A must pair with T, not A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This simply repeats the template's letters with the polarity labels reversed; it is not the complementary strand.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the correct complement written backward, giving the wrong 5' to 3' polarity for an antiparallel daughter strand.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: The initial separation of the two parent strands at the origin of replication, which exposes their nitrogenous bases to the replicative enzymes, is referred to by which of the following terms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplex opening

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polymerization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reannealing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strand displacement synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supercoiling

explanation.summary: The initial separation of the parent strands at the ori site is called duplex opening.
explanation.whyCorrect: For the parent strands to both serve as templates, they must be separated from each other, exposing their nitrogenous bases to the replicative enzymes. The initial separation of the parent strands is called duplex opening, occurs at the origin of replication, and is recognized and started by initiator proteins that recruit helicase.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Polymerization is the consecutive attachment of free nucleotides to build a new strand, which happens after the strands are separated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reannealing is the reassociation of separated parent strands, the opposite of opening, and is prevented by single-stranded binding proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Strand displacement synthesis is Pol delta's displacement of the previous RNA primer and a short 5' segment during Okazaki fragment processing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supercoiling is the over-winding of the helix downstream of helicase activity, not the initial separation of strands.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A single origin of replication on a eukaryotic chromosome has opened into a replication bubble with an active replication fork at each end. Considering both forks together, how many leading strands and how many lagging strands are being synthesized within this one bubble?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four leading strands and four lagging strands

choices.label: B
choices.text: One leading strand and one lagging strand

choices.label: C
choices.text: One leading strand and two lagging strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two leading strands and one lagging strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two leading strands and two lagging strands

explanation.summary: Each replication fork consists of one leading strand and one lagging strand, so a bubble with two forks contains two leading and two lagging strands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Replication proceeds at both ends of the replication bubble on both strands simultaneously, and each end becomes a replication fork. Each replication fork consists of one leading strand and one lagging strand. With two forks moving away from the origin in opposite directions, there are two leading strands and two lagging strands within the bubble; on each parent strand, the daughter is leading at one fork and lagging at the other.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Four of each would require four forks; a single origin produces only two.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One leading and one lagging strand describes a single fork, but a bubble opened from one origin has two forks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Every fork has exactly one leading strand, so two forks cannot share a single leading strand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Every fork has exactly one lagging strand, so two forks cannot share a single lagging strand.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: On the lagging strand template at a replication fork, DNA polymerase has just finished extending an Okazaki fragment. Which of the following must occur before synthesis of the next Okazaki fragment can begin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enough new template must be exposed for a new RNA primer to be laid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flap endonuclease must remove the completed fragment's primer first

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helicase must reverse direction to expose the 3' end of the template

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ligase must first join the completed fragment to the previous one

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase must introduce a double-stranded break at the fork

explanation.summary: On the lagging strand, a new RNA primer is laid only after enough new template nucleotides have been exposed by the advancing helicase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because lagging strand synthesis runs opposite to the direction the helicase opens the duplex, it must proceed in a semi-discontinuous manner. On the lagging strand, after enough nucleotides have been exposed, a new RNA primer is laid for a DNA polymerase to associate, and that polymerase then extends until it reaches the previous primer, creating the next Okazaki fragment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primer displacement and flap trimming happen as the following polymerase runs into the previous fragment; they do not have to precede the next primer being laid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helicase continues opening the duplex in the same direction; the next primer is placed on newly exposed template, not on template exposed by reversing the helicase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligation of fragments occurs after primer removal and flap trimming and is not a prerequisite for starting the next fragment further along the template.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork; a double-stranded break is not part of initiating an Okazaki fragment.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: On the lagging strand, a DNA polymerase begins extending from a newly laid RNA primer. Which of the following marks the point at which this stretch of polymerase activity ends, thereby defining the length of the Okazaki fragment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a mismatched nucleotide is detected by the exonuclease

choices.label: B
choices.text: When approximately 20 nucleotides have been added after the primer

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the polymerase encounters the previously laid RNA primer

choices.label: D
choices.text: When the polymerase reaches the origin of replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: When the sliding clamp dissociates from the polymerase

explanation.summary: Each stretch of lagging strand polymerase activity continues until the previous RNA primer is encountered, producing an Okazaki fragment.
explanation.whyCorrect: On the lagging strand, each new stretch of DNA polymerase activity continues until the previous RNA primer is encountered, creating a polynucleotide referred to as an Okazaki fragment. This is why the lagging strand is constructed from several small Okazaki fragments rather than one continuous strand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Detection of a mismatch triggers 3' to 5' exonuclease removal of that nucleotide and synthesis then continues; it does not terminate the fragment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Roughly 20 nucleotides is how long Pol alpha stays attached before Pol delta or Pol epsilon takes over; it does not define the end of an Okazaki fragment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Okazaki fragments are made continuously as the fork moves away from the origin; the polymerase does not return to the origin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The PCNA sliding clamp keeps the polymerase attached to give high processivity; its dissociation does not define fragment boundaries.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, DNA Pol delta extending an Okazaki fragment does not stop when it encounters the RNA primer of the previous fragment. Which of the following is the correct order of events from that point until the two fragments are joined into a continuous strand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flap cleavage, then ligation, then strand displacement synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flap cleavage, then strand displacement synthesis, then ligation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligation, then flap cleavage, then strand displacement synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strand displacement synthesis, then flap cleavage, then ligation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strand displacement synthesis, then ligation, then flap cleavage

explanation.summary: Eukaryotic primer removal proceeds as strand displacement synthesis by Pol delta, flap cleavage by flap endonuclease, and finally ligation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In eukaryotes, Pol delta displaces the RNA primer and a short segment of the 5' end of the previous Okazaki fragment (strand displacement synthesis), which creates a flap requiring resection. A special flap endonuclease then trims the flap (flap cleavage), which finally allows ligase to seal the gap between the fragments (ligation).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Strand displacement synthesis is the first event, since it is what generates the flap, so it cannot come last.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no flap to cleave until Pol delta has displaced the primer, so flap cleavage cannot precede strand displacement synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligase cannot act first; the displaced flap must be created and then trimmed before there is a clean gap to seal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ligation cannot occur while the flap is still present; the flap must be cleaved before the gap can be sealed.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A student reviewing DNA structure before studying replication is asked to describe the bond that links adjacent nucleotides within a single DNA strand. Which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A covalent bond between complementary bases across the helix

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hydrogen bond between the 3'-OH and the neighboring 5' phosphate

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hydrogen bond between the nitrogenous bases of adjacent nucleotides

choices.label: D
choices.text: A phosphodiester bond between the nitrogenous base and its phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: A phosphodiester bond joining the 3' and 5' positions of adjacent sugars

explanation.summary: Nucleotides within a strand are linked by phosphodiester bonds between the 3' and 5' positions of deoxyribose sugars, while the two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The individual nucleotides of each strand of DNA are linked together by phosphodiester bonds between the 3' and 5' positions of the deoxyribose sugars to form one strand. The two strands of polynucleotides are held together separately via hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases (A-T, G-C) in a complementary antiparallel orientation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complementary bases across the helix are joined by hydrogen bonds, which is why helicase can separate the strands without breaking covalent bonds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 3'-OH and 5' phosphate are joined by a covalent phosphodiester bond, not a hydrogen bond.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrogen bonds form between complementary bases on opposite strands, not between adjacent nucleotides within a strand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phosphodiester bond links sugar to sugar through the phosphate; it does not connect the nitrogenous base to the phosphate.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: In an experiment, helicase is abruptly inactivated shortly after replication bubbles have formed at all origins, while all other replication proteins remain functional. Which of the following would most directly result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Okazaki fragments are joined prematurely by ligase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parent strands reanneal within the existing bubbles despite bound SSBs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pol alpha continues laying primers on the still-closed duplex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replication forks stop advancing because no further template is exposed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supercoiling ahead of the fork increases as topoisomerase becomes overactive

explanation.summary: Helicase not only creates the initial bubble but continues to separate the helix at the edge of each replication fork, so without it no new template is exposed and the forks stall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Helicase creates the initial replication bubble and then continues to separate the helix at the edge of the replication forks. Each end of the bubble becomes a replication fork only as the helicases separating the two parental strands continue to work, and DNA polymerase travels behind the helicase on newly exposed template. If helicase stops, no additional bases are exposed and the forks cannot advance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ligase seals nicks only after primer removal and flap trimming; loss of helicase does not cause premature joining.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Single-stranded binding proteins are still bound and functional, so the already-separated strands would remain apart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primase lays primers on separated single-stranded template; it cannot prime a closed duplex, so primer synthesis would also cease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supercoiling is generated by helicase unwinding; stopping helicase removes the source of the stress rather than increasing it, and topoisomerase relaxes rather than creates supercoils.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A single incorrectly paired nucleotide at a critical point in a gene can introduce a pathologic mutation. Based on the flow of genetic information in the cell, which of the following best explains why such an error in the DNA sequence can produce disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The altered DNA blocks topoisomerase from relieving supercoils

choices.label: B
choices.text: The altered DNA cannot be bound by single-stranded binding proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: The altered DNA is directly translated into protein without an mRNA intermediate

choices.label: D
choices.text: The altered DNA is transcribed into mRNA and translated into a nonfunctional protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The altered DNA prevents helicase from binding at any origin of replication

explanation.summary: Per the Central Dogma, DNA is transcribed into mRNA and translated into protein, so a copying error in DNA can yield a nonfunctional enzyme and disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: As per the Central Dogma, DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which is then translated into proteins. During replication it is therefore crucial for the DNA sequence to be copied correctly, because the proper sequence is incredibly important in generating functional enzymes. DNA replication errors are linked to a variety of human diseases, including cancer, premature aging, and certain immunodeficiencies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling introduced by helicase and is not blocked by a single altered base pair within a gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Single-stranded binding proteins bind exposed bases regardless of sequence; a point change does not prevent their binding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genetic information does not flow directly from DNA to protein; DNA is first transcribed into mRNA, which is then translated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single base change within a gene does not abolish origin recognition or helicase binding; the harm comes from the altered gene product.

questions.topicName: DNA Replication

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is prescribed an antibiotic that treats his bacterial infection by disrupting the translation of mRNA into protein. After reading the drug information sheet, he worries the drug will also shut down protein synthesis in his own cells. Which of the following best explains why the antibiotic will not interfere with translation in humans?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells lack ribosomes entirely and instead translate their mRNA using the spliceosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human cells synthesize all of their proteins inside the nucleus, where the antibiotic cannot penetrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human mRNA is rapidly degraded by the antibiotic before it can ever be translated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prokaryotic ribosomes differ from human ribosomes, and the drug binds only the prokaryotic subunits

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 5' cap on human mRNA prevents any antibiotic from binding to the transcript or ribosome

explanation.summary: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomes are built from different subunits, so ribosome-targeting antibiotics are selective for bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prokaryotic ribosomes are made of 30S and 50S subunits that combine into a 70S ribosome, whereas human ribosomes use 40S and 60S subunits that combine into an 80S ribosome. Because the antibiotic binds only the subunits found in bacteria, it cannot affect human ribosomes or human protein synthesis.
