whyWrongByChoice.A: All human cells contain ribosomes; the spliceosome removes introns from pre-mRNA and does not translate mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eukaryotic translation occurs in the cytoplasm on free or RER-bound ribosomes, not in the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibiotic targets bacterial ribosomes and does not degrade human mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 5' cap aids export, protects against exonucleases, and initiates translation, but it does not block antibiotics; selectivity comes from ribosome differences.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A researcher studying the initiation of transcription in a human cell line wants to identify a proximal regulatory sequence that recruits transcription factors and RNA polymerase to begin transcription. Which of the following is such a proximal regulatory element?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AUG start codon

choices.label: B
choices.text: CAAT box

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pribnow box

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 5' UTR

explanation.summary: The CAAT and TATA boxes are proximal promoter elements that initiate eukaryotic transcription.
explanation.whyCorrect: CAAT and TATA boxes are proximal regulatory sequences located close to the gene that recruit transcription factors and RNA polymerase II to initiate transcription. The CAAT box lies roughly 70-80 nucleotides upstream of the start site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AUG is the start codon for translation, not a transcription regulatory sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An enhancer is a distal regulatory sequence that can act thousands of base pairs away, not a proximal one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Pribnow box is a prokaryotic promoter element, not a eukaryotic proximal sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 5' UTR is a segment of mRNA upstream of the start codon and does not initiate transcription.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: While mapping the regulatory landscape of a gene, an investigator identifies a DNA sequence located roughly 12,000 base pairs downstream of the gene that binds activating transcription factors and markedly increases the amount of the corresponding protein produced. Which of the following best describes this sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CAAT box

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyadenylation signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silencer

choices.label: E
choices.text: TATA box

explanation.summary: Enhancers are distal regulatory sequences that recruit activating transcription factors to upregulate expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enhancers are distal regulatory sequences that can lie thousands of base pairs upstream or downstream of a gene. They recruit activating transcription factors that promote recruitment of RNA polymerase II, upregulating expression of the target gene and its protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The CAAT box is a proximal promoter element roughly 70-80 nucleotides upstream, not a distal enhancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA) marks the site for poly(A) tail addition on pre-mRNA and does not increase transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A silencer is also distal, but it recruits repressor factors and downregulates expression rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TATA box is a proximal promoter element about 25-30 nucleotides upstream, not a distal element thousands of base pairs away.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A student observes that the mRNA sequence produced from a gene exactly matches the coding (sense) strand of the DNA, aside from one type of base. Which of the following statements about transcription is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RNA is synthesized in the 3' to 5' direction, with new bases added to its 5' end

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA polymerase II travels 5' to 3' along the template strand as it elongates RNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: RNA polymerase II uses the coding strand as its template and ignores the antisense strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mRNA is identical to the coding strand except that uracil replaces thymine

choices.label: E
choices.text: The template strand is also called the sense strand because it matches the mRNA

explanation.summary: The RNA transcript matches the coding (sense) strand with uracil in place of thymine, while the template (antisense) strand is read.
explanation.whyCorrect: RNA polymerase II reads the template (antisense) strand to produce a transcript that corresponds to the other strand of the helix, the coding (sense) strand, except that uracil is paired with adenine instead of thymidine. Thus the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand with U substituted for T.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The RNA transcript is built 5' to 3' by adding nucleotides to its 3' end.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RNA polymerase II moves 3' to 5' along the template strand while the RNA is elongated 5' to 3'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polymerase uses the template (antisense) strand as its template, not the coding strand.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The template strand is the antisense strand; the coding strand is the sense strand.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A cell line carries a mutation in the enzyme that adds the 7-methylguanosine cap to the 5' end of pre-mRNA, so newly made transcripts remain uncapped. Which of the following is the most likely direct consequence for these transcripts once they reach the cytoplasm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of the mRNA back into DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure to remove introns from the transcript

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased degradation by 5' exonucleases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Introduction of a premature stop codon

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the 3' poly(A) tail

explanation.summary: The 5' cap protects mRNA from 5' exonucleases; without it, the transcript is rapidly degraded.
explanation.whyCorrect: One key function of the 5' cap is to protect mRNA from degradation by 5' exonucleases in the cytoplasm that remove nucleotides from the ends of polynucleotides. An uncapped transcript loses this protection and is degraded more readily; the cap also normally aids nuclear export and translation initiation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reverse transcription of mRNA to DNA requires reverse transcriptase and is unrelated to loss of the cap.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intron removal is carried out by the spliceosome and is independent of the 5' cap.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Capping does not alter the coding sequence, so it cannot introduce a premature stop codon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The poly(A) tail is added at the 3' end by poly(A) polymerase and does not depend on 5' capping.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A patient's cells harbor a mutation that changes the pre-mRNA sequence 5'-AAUAAA-3' near the 3' end of a transcript. Which of the following steps of mRNA maturation is most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of the 5' 7-methylguanosine cap to the nascent transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charging of tRNA with its amino acid by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of the pre-mRNA and addition of the poly(A) tail

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recognition of the start codon by the scanning 40S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removal of introns by the spliceosome at the branch point adenine

explanation.summary: The 5'-AAUAAA-3' polyadenylation signal directs cleavage and poly(A) tail addition at the 3' end.
explanation.whyCorrect: The polyadenylation signal (5'-AAUAAA-3') near the 3' end of the pre-mRNA signals a nearby downstream cleavage site; after cleavage, poly(A) polymerase uses ATP to add 40-250 adenosine nucleotides. A mutation in this signal impairs cleavage and poly(A) tail addition, destabilizing the mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 5' cap is added at the opposite end of the transcript and is independent of the AAUAAA signal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: tRNA charging occurs in the cytoplasm and is unrelated to processing of the 3' end of pre-mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Start codon recognition occurs during translation initiation and does not depend on the polyadenylation signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splicing is directed by intron donor/acceptor sites and the branch point, not by the AAUAAA sequence.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A point mutation destroys the conserved GU dinucleotide at the 5' end of an intron in a pre-mRNA transcript. Which of the following is the most likely consequence for the mature transcript?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 5' cap fails to be added to the transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: The intron is retained

choices.label: C
choices.text: The poly(A) tail is not added to the 3' end

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transcript is reverse transcribed into DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcription terminates prematurely within the intron

explanation.summary: Each intron has a 5' donor site (5'-GU) recognized by the spliceosome; disrupting it prevents proper splicing and causes intron retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each intron has a 5' donor site containing 5'-GU and a 3' acceptor site containing AG-3'. The spliceosome first cleaves at the 5' splice site to form the lariat; if the GU donor site is mutated, the spliceosome cannot recognize and cut the site, so the intron is not removed and is retained in the transcript.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capping occurs at the 5' end of the whole transcript and is independent of individual intron splice sites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The poly(A) tail depends on the AAUAAA polyadenylation signal, not on an intron donor site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcription requires reverse transcriptase and does not result from a splice-site mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The donor-site mutation affects splicing of the finished transcript, not termination of transcription.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A single B-lymphocyte gene gives rise to two structurally related immunoglobulin proteins: a membrane-bound form and a secreted form. Both are encoded by the same gene, yet they differ in their final domains. Which of the following processes best explains how one gene produces these different but related proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A silent mutation in the coding exon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Addition of a longer poly(A) tail

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alternative splicing of the pre-mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcription of the mRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use of a prokaryotic 70S ribosome

explanation.summary: Alternative splicing lets a single gene generate a range of unique but structurally related proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Organisms use alternative splicing to produce a range of unique but structurally related proteins, such as a transmembrane versus a secreted immunoglobulin. The same gene can be alternatively spliced into different mRNA molecules that yield the different protein isoforms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A silent mutation does not change the amino acid sequence and cannot create two distinct protein forms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Poly(A) tail length affects mRNA stability, not which protein domains are produced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA and does not generate protein isoforms from one gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Human cells use 80S ribosomes; ribosome type does not create alternative isoforms from a gene.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: In a cell-free translation system, an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase mistakenly attaches arginine to a tRNA whose anticodon is specific for valine. The mischarged tRNA is then used in an otherwise normal ribosome. Which of the following is most likely to occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The arginine will be chemically converted into valine before incorporation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The arginine will be incorporated at positions where valine is called for

choices.label: C
choices.text: The arginine will be incorporated at random positions along the peptide

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ribosome will detect the mismatched arginine and prevent its incorporation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tRNA will spontaneously dissociate from the arginine before reaching the ribosome

explanation.summary: Ribosomes read the tRNA anticodon, not the attached amino acid, so a mischarged tRNA inserts the wrong amino acid at the codon it recognizes.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a tRNA is charged with an incorrect amino acid, it still enters the ribosome and incorporates that amino acid according to its anticodon. Because the tRNA's anticodon is specific to the valine codon, the arginine will be incorporated wherever valine is called for.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No cellular process spontaneously converts one amino acid into another after charging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: tRNAs are highly specific to the codon code via their anticodon, so incorporation is not random.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribosomes lack proofreading of amino acid identity; they rely on the accuracy of tRNA charging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A charged tRNA is unlikely to spontaneously dissociate from its attached amino acid.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: During initiation of eukaryotic translation, the small ribosomal subunit and a charged tRNA scan the mRNA to locate the start codon before the large subunit joins. Which of the following statements about this initiation step is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 60S subunit binds the mRNA first and scans for the start codon

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first amino acid is always methionine, and its charged tRNA enters at the A site

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first amino acid is always methionine, and its charged tRNA occupies the P site

choices.label: D
choices.text: The initiator tRNA is charged with leucine encoded by the AUG codon

choices.label: E
choices.text: Translation begins at the first UAA codon encountered from the 5' end

explanation.summary: Translation starts at AUG with methionine, and the initiator Met-tRNA uniquely enters at the P site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because there is only one start codon (AUG) in the genetic code, the first amino acid incorporated is always methionine, so met-tRNA is always used to initiate translation. Uniquely, this initiator tRNA enters the ribosome at the P site rather than the A site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The small 40S subunit recognizes the 5' cap and scans for the start codon; the 60S subunit joins afterward.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The initiator met-tRNA is the exception that enters at the P site, not the A site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AUG codes for methionine, not leucine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UAA is a stop codon; translation begins at the AUG start codon, not a stop codon.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: During the elongation phase of translation, a charged tRNA carrying the next amino acid must enter the ribosome so that a peptide bond can form. At which ribosomal site does an incoming charged tRNA normally enter, and what happens there?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The A site, where uncharged tRNAs exit after donating their amino acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The A site, which accepts the incoming charged tRNA matching the next codon

choices.label: C
choices.text: The E site, which holds the tRNA carrying the growing peptide chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: The E site, which is the entry point for all incoming charged tRNAs

choices.label: E
choices.text: The P site, which ejects uncharged tRNAs from the ribosome

explanation.summary: The A (aminoacyl) site is where charged tRNAs enter; the P site holds the growing peptide, and the E site ejects uncharged tRNAs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ribosome has three sites. The A site is where charged tRNAs enter the ribosome, matching the next codon. The P site holds the tRNA with the growing peptide chain, and the E site is where uncharged tRNAs are ejected after their amino acid has been incorporated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uncharged tRNAs exit from the E site, not the A site; the A site accepts incoming charged tRNAs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The E site holds uncharged tRNAs just before ejection, not the tRNA carrying the growing peptide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The E site is the exit site; incoming charged tRNAs enter at the A site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The P site holds the tRNA bearing the growing peptide chain; ejection of uncharged tRNA occurs at the E site.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: SARS-CoV-2, a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus, replicates its genome inside a human cell without ever converting its RNA into DNA. Which of the following enzymes, representing an exception to the central dogma, does this virus use to copy its genome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Host mitochondrial DNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Host nuclear RNA polymerase II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retroviral reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase

explanation.summary: Positive-sense ssRNA viruses like SARS-CoV-2 use an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to make RNA from an RNA template.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses, but not eukaryotes, have an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that uses RNA as a template to make more RNA. SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, uses this enzyme to replicate, as do all positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. This is one of the two exceptions to the unidirectional central dogma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNAs during translation and does not replicate viral genomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA and is used in DNA replication, not RNA-to-RNA copying.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RNA polymerase II transcribes DNA into pre-mRNA and does not copy RNA into RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template and is used by retroviruses like HIV, not by SARS-CoV-2 for genome replication.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A molecular biologist is studying the earliest events in the transcription of a protein-coding gene in a human cell. Which of the following best describes what occurs during the initiation phase of transcription?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Poly(A) polymerase adds adenosine nucleotides to the 3' end of the transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA polymerase moves along the DNA helix adding nucleotides to the transcript

choices.label: C
choices.text: The polymerase disengages from the DNA and releases the completed RNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spliceosome removes introns from the newly formed transcript

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transcription machinery identifies the gene and attaches to the DNA

explanation.summary: Transcription occurs in three phases; initiation is when the transcription machinery identifies the gene and attaches to DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transcription takes place in three phases: initiation, elongation, and termination. First, the complex of proteins that conducts transcription (the transcription machinery) must identify the gene and attach to the DNA, a process called initiation. Only after this does the machinery move along the helix elongating an RNA transcript, and finally disengage and release the RNA at termination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Poly(A) tail addition is a 3' RNA-processing modification, not the initiation of transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Movement along the DNA helix while elongating the RNA transcript is the elongation phase, not initiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disengagement of the machinery and release of the RNA is termination, the final phase of transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intron removal by the spliceosome is part of RNA processing that occurs after the transcript is made, not a phase of transcription initiation.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: The human genome is approximately 3 billion nucleotides long, and roughly 98.5% of it is noncoding. Which of the following best explains how the transcription machinery locates the beginning of a gene within this sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhancers located thousands of base pairs away bind RNA polymerase directly without transcription factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exon sequences are chemically distinct from intron sequences and are recognized directly by RNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promoter sequences recruit transcription factors that bind RNA polymerase to the DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 5' cap marks the first nucleotide of each gene in the DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The start codon AUG in the DNA recruits RNA polymerase to the gene

explanation.summary: Promoters are specific DNA sequences that recruit transcription factors, which in turn recruit and bind an RNA polymerase to the DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because approximately 98.5% of the 3-billion-nucleotide human genome is noncoding, cells rely on specific DNA sequences called promoters to mark where a gene begins. Promoters recruit proteins called transcription factors, and transcription factors recruit and bind one of the three RNA polymerases (RNAP I, II, or III) to DNA. For protein-coding genes, RNAP II binds a promoter sequence specifically recognized by RNAP II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enhancers recruit activating transcription factors that promote RNA polymerase II recruitment; they do not bind the polymerase directly, and they are distal elements, not the gene-locating promoter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RNA polymerase does not recognize exons directly; it is recruited by transcription factors bound to promoters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 5' cap is added to the pre-mRNA transcript, not to the DNA, and does not mark genes in the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AUG is the start codon for translation on mRNA; it is not the signal that recruits RNA polymerase to a gene.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A researcher isolates the enzyme responsible for transcribing a protein-coding gene into pre-mRNA in a human hepatocyte. Which of the following enzymes was most likely isolated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: C
choices.text: RNA polymerase I

choices.label: D
choices.text: RNA polymerase II

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA polymerase III

explanation.summary: Transcription of protein-coding genes in eukaryotes is carried out by RNA polymerase II.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transcription factors recruit and bind one of three RNA polymerases (RNAP I, RNAP II, and RNAP III) to DNA. Transcription of protein-coding genes is facilitated by RNAP II, which binds to a promoter sequence in the genome specifically recognized by RNAP II and produces the pre-mRNA transcript.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA during replication; it does not produce pre-mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase uses RNA as a template to make DNA, the reverse of transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RNAP I is one of the three eukaryotic RNA polymerases, but it is not the polymerase that transcribes protein-coding genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNAP III is one of the three eukaryotic RNA polymerases, but protein-coding genes are transcribed by RNAP II.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A geneticist maps a promoter element of a human gene and finds it located between 25 and 30 nucleotides before the first transcribed nucleotide of the gene. Using the standard numbering convention relative to the transcription start site, which of the following best describes this element and its position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CAAT box, at approximately +25 to +30

choices.label: B
choices.text: CAAT box, at approximately -70 to -80

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhancer, at approximately -25 to -30

choices.label: D
choices.text: TATA box, at approximately +25 to +30

choices.label: E
choices.text: TATA box, at approximately -25 to -30

explanation.summary: The TATA box sits about 25-30 nucleotides upstream of the start site, and upstream positions are numbered -N.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first transcribed nucleotide of a gene is the +1 site or transcription start site (TSS). Nucleotides after the start site are downstream and numbered +N; nucleotides before it are upstream and numbered -N (there is no 0 site). The TATA box lies 25-30 nucleotides upstream of the start site, i.e., at approximately -25 to -30, while the CAAT box lies around 70-80 nucleotides upstream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The CAAT box is located around -70 to -80, and positive numbers denote downstream positions, not upstream ones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The CAAT box is indeed at about -70 to -80, but the element described is 25-30 nucleotides upstream, which is the TATA box.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enhancers are distal regulatory sequences that can lie thousands of base pairs from the gene, not a proximal element at -25 to -30.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positions upstream of the +1 site are numbered negatively; +25 to +30 would be downstream of the start site.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A researcher engineers a reporter gene that contains an intact CAAT box and TATA box but deliberately removes all DNA sequences located more than 1,000 base pairs upstream and downstream of the gene. When the construct is introduced into human cells, transcription by RNA polymerase II is initiated but proceeds at a very low level. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efficient initiation and elongation require interaction with enhancer elements

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA polymerase II requires a silencer to be present for elongation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The CAAT box cannot function without an adjacent Pribnow box

choices.label: D
choices.text: The TATA box is only active when located downstream of the start site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcription factors cannot bind a promoter lacking a 5' cap

explanation.summary: Proximal promoter sequences are necessary but not sufficient; all RNAP II-dependent genes also need enhancer interaction for efficient initiation and elongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although proximal promoter sequences such as the CAAT and TATA boxes are necessary for initiation of transcription, they are not sufficient. All RNAP II-dependent genes also require interaction with enhancer elements for efficient initiation and elongation. Enhancers are distal regulatory sequences that can occur thousands of base pairs upstream or downstream of a gene, so deleting all distant sequences removes the enhancers and leaves only inefficient basal transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Silencers recruit repressor factors that inhibit transcription; they are not required for elongation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Pribnow box is a prokaryotic promoter element and is not required for CAAT box function in eukaryotes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The TATA box normally functions 25-30 nucleotides upstream of the start site, not downstream.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 5' cap is a modification of the pre-mRNA transcript, not a feature of the DNA promoter that transcription factors bind.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A distal DNA sequence located several thousand base pairs upstream of a gene is found to recruit repressor factors. Deletion of this sequence in cultured cells results in a marked increase in the amount of the gene's mRNA and protein. Which of the following best describes the deleted sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CAAT box

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyadenylation signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silencer

choices.label: E
choices.text: TATA box

explanation.summary: Silencers are distal regulatory sequences that recruit repressor factors and downregulate gene expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Distal regulatory sequences, which can occur thousands of base pairs upstream or downstream from a gene, act as either enhancers or silencers. Silencer sequences operate like enhancers but instead recruit repressor factors that inhibit transcription, downregulating expression of the gene and the resultant protein. Removing a silencer therefore relieves repression and increases mRNA and protein levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The CAAT box is a proximal promoter element roughly 70-80 nucleotides upstream, not a distal repressor-binding sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An enhancer is distal, but it recruits activating transcription factors that upregulate expression; deleting it would decrease, not increase, expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA) is a sequence in the pre-mRNA that directs 3' cleavage and poly(A) addition, not a DNA element that recruits repressors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TATA box is a proximal promoter element about 25-30 nucleotides upstream that helps initiate transcription; it does not recruit repressors.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A molecular biologist isolates the RNA molecule immediately produced by RNA polymerase II in the nucleus of a human cell, before any modification has occurred. Which of the following best describes this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A complementary DNA copy of the coding strand of the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterogeneous nuclear RNA that requires processing before export

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mature mRNA that is ready for immediate export to the cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ribosomal RNA that will assemble with proteins into a subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfer RNA that carries an amino acid on its acceptor stem

explanation.summary: The immediate product of eukaryotic transcription is heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), or pre-mRNA, which must be processed before export.
explanation.whyCorrect: In eukaryotes, the RNA transcript is not immediately ready to be translated. The immediate product of transcription, referred to as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) or pre-mRNA, requires modification (5' capping, 3' poly(A) tail addition, and intron splicing) before it is ready to be exported from the nucleus into the cytoplasm where it is translated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNA polymerase II produces an RNA transcript, not a DNA copy; DNA from RNA would require reverse transcriptase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The unmodified transcript is not mature mRNA; it becomes mRNA only after RNA processing in the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: rRNA forms the ribosomal subunits; the immediate product of RNAP II transcription of a protein-coding gene is pre-mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: tRNA carries amino acids into the ribosome during translation; it is not the immediate product of transcribing a protein-coding gene by RNAP II.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: Using a technique that visualizes nascent RNA, an investigator observes that a 7-methylguanosine cap has already been added to the 5' end of a transcript while RNA polymerase II is still elongating the 3' end of the same transcript. Which of the following best describes this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sign that the spliceosome has already removed all introns

choices.label: B
choices.text: An artifact, because capping can only occur after transcription has terminated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidence that the transcript is a prokaryotic mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence that the transcript is being reverse transcribed into DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal RNA processing, which occurs co-transcriptionally

explanation.summary: RNA processing in eukaryotes occurs co-transcriptionally, so modifications can be added while the transcript is still being produced.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three important alterations to pre-mRNA (5' capping, addition of a 3' poly(A) tail, and intron splicing) occur co-transcriptionally, meaning they can be facilitated as the RNA transcript is still being produced. Observing a 5' cap on a transcript that is still being elongated is therefore expected, not an error.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The presence of a cap indicates only that capping has occurred; it says nothing about whether intron splicing has been completed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RNA processing does not wait for termination; it occurs co-transcriptionally while the transcript is still being made.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 5' cap, RNAP II, and co-transcriptional processing are features of eukaryotic pre-mRNA, not prokaryotic mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcription uses RNA as a template to make DNA and has nothing to do with the presence of a 5' cap during elongation.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A biochemist characterizes the structure at the 5' end of a mature eukaryotic mRNA. Which of the following best describes the chemical structure of the 5' cap?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 7-methylguanosine joined to the 3' hydroxyl of the first transcribed nucleotide

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 7-methylguanosine joined to the transcript through a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge

choices.label: C
choices.text: A guanosine linked to the first nucleotide by a conventional 3'-5' phosphodiester bond

choices.label: D
choices.text: A methylated adenine linked to the transcript by a 5'-2' phosphodiester bond

choices.label: E
choices.text: A string of 40-250 adenosine nucleotides joined by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds

explanation.summary: The 5' cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5' end of the primary transcript via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 5' cap is a distinct structure consisting of a 7-methylguanosine linked to the 5' end of the primary transcript (RNA chain) through a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge, rather than the usual 3'-5' linkage found within the RNA chain. This cap is recognized by nuclear pores for export, protects the mRNA from 5' exonucleases, and serves as an initiating factor for translation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cap is joined to the 5' end of the transcript, not to a 3' hydroxyl, and the linkage is a triphosphate bridge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cap nucleotide is 7-methylguanosine, and it is joined by an unusual 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge rather than a conventional 3'-5' phosphodiester bond.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 5'-2' phosphodiester bond to an adenine describes the lariat linkage formed at the intron branch point during splicing, not the cap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A string of 40-250 adenosine nucleotides describes the poly(A) tail added to the 3' end, not the 5' cap.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A cell biologist studies the synthesis of two proteins in a human cell: an enzyme that functions inside the peroxisome and a digestive enzyme that is trafficked to the lysosome. Which of the following correctly identifies the ribosomes that translate each protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both enzymes by free ribosomes circulating in the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both enzymes by ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peroxisomal enzyme by 70S ribosomes; lysosomal enzyme by 80S ribosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peroxisomal enzyme by free ribosomes; lysosomal enzyme by RER-bound ribosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peroxisomal enzyme by RER-bound ribosomes; lysosomal enzyme by free ribosomes

explanation.summary: Proteins destined for the cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria, or peroxisome are made on free ribosomes; secreted, RER/Golgi, lysosomal, and plasma membrane proteins are made on RER-bound ribosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Where translation occurs depends on where a protein will ultimately function. Proteins that will function in the cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria, or peroxisome are translated by freely circulating ribosomes and released to their destination. Proteins destined to be secreted, retained in the RER or Golgi, trafficked to the lysosome, or bound to the plasma membrane are instead translated by ribosomes bound to the RER, so the peptide ends up in the RER lumen for packaging and transport.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lysosomal digestive enzymes require the bound ribosomal pathway so they do not end up circulating freely in the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peroxisomal proteins are translated by free ribosomes, not RER-bound ribosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 70S ribosomes are prokaryotic; all human ribosomes are 80S, and free and bound ribosomes have the exact same structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the assignments: peroxisomal proteins use free ribosomes, and lysosomal enzymes use RER-bound ribosomes.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A cell line is engineered to lack functional poly(A)-binding proteins (PABP). Transcripts in these cells are correctly cleaved and receive a poly(A) tail of normal length, yet their half-life is markedly reduced. Which of the following best explains the decreased mRNA stability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exonucleases degrade the unshielded 3' end of the mRNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Poly(A) polymerase can no longer use ATP as a substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 5' cap cannot be recognized by nuclear pores

choices.label: D
choices.text: The polyadenylation signal is no longer recognized

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spliceosome cannot assemble on the transcript

explanation.summary: PABP binds the poly(A) tail and shields the RNA from exonucleases that degrade the 3' end.
explanation.whyCorrect: The poly(A) tail helps stabilize mRNA molecules. Poly(A)-binding proteins (PABP) associate with the poly(A) tail, shielding the RNA from exonucleases that facilitate degradation of the 3' end of the pre-mRNA. Without PABP, the tail is present but unprotected, so exonucleases degrade the 3' end and the mRNA half-life falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Poly(A) polymerase uses ATP to build the tail, and the stem states the tail is of normal length, so this step is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nuclear pore recognition is a function of the 5' cap and is independent of PABP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem states cleavage and tail addition occur normally, so the AAUAAA signal is still recognized.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spliceosome assembly depends on snRNPs recognizing the intron splice sites and branch point, not on PABP.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: During 3' end processing of a pre-mRNA, cleavage occurs at a site located 10-35 nucleotides downstream of the AAUAAA sequence and upstream of a GU-rich element. Which of the following best describes the fate of the RNA fragment located downstream of this cleavage site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is degraded in the nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is exported to the cytoplasm and translated as a separate short peptide

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is folded into a lariat and recycled by the spliceosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is ligated back onto the transcript after the poly(A) tail is added

choices.label: E
choices.text: It receives a poly(A) tail and is retained as the 3' untranslated region

explanation.summary: After cleavage downstream of AAUAAA, the GU-rich/U-rich downstream fragment is degraded in the nucleus while the upstream piece receives the poly(A) tail.
explanation.whyCorrect: The polyadenylation signal (5'-AAUAAA-3') signals a nearby downstream cleavage site, about 10-35 nucleotides away, with a GU-rich or U-rich element roughly 50 nucleotides further downstream. Following cleavage, poly(A) polymerase uses ATP to add 40-250 adenosine nucleotides to the new 3' end of the upstream portion, while the downstream fragment containing the GU-rich or U-rich element is degraded in the nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The downstream fragment is not exported or translated; it is degraded within the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lariat formation is a feature of intron removal by the spliceosome, not of 3' end cleavage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cleaved downstream fragment is not re-ligated; the poly(A) tail is added directly at the cleavage site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The poly(A) tail is added to the new 3' end of the upstream portion of the transcript; the 3' UTR is the region between the stop codon and the poly(A) site, not the discarded fragment.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: During the first step of intron splicing, the spliceosome cleaves the 5' splice site of an intron, and the freed 5' end of the intron becomes covalently attached to an internal nucleotide, producing a looped intermediate. Which of the following best describes the bond and the nucleotide involved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 3'-5' phosphodiester bond to a cytosine at the branch point

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 5'-2' phosphodiester bond to a uracil at the 3' splice site

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 5'-2' phosphodiester bond to an adenine at the branch point

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 5'-3' phosphodiester bond to a guanine at the 3' acceptor site

choices.label: E
choices.text: A covalent ester bond to the 3' hydroxyl of the upstream exon

explanation.summary: The lariat forms when the intron's free 5' end makes a special 5'-2' phosphodiester bond with the internal branch point adenine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each intron has a 5' donor site (5'-GU), a 3' acceptor site (AG-3'), and an internal adenine base referred to as the branch point. The spliceosome first severs the donor site's 5' phosphodiester bond and establishes a new special 5'-2' phosphodiester bond between the now-free end of the intron and the internal branch point. This creates the characteristic lariat structure of removed introns.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The branch point nucleotide is an adenine, and the bond is a 5'-2' linkage rather than a conventional 3'-5' bond.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The branch point is an adenine located within the intron, not a uracil at the 3' splice site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lariat bond is 5'-2', not 5'-3', and it is made to the internal branch point adenine, not to the AG at the 3' acceptor site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The upstream exon's free 3' hydroxyl is later joined to the downstream exon in step 2; it does not form the lariat.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: An investigator purifies the protein complex that removes introns from pre-mRNA in the nucleus. Analysis shows that the complex is built from several species of small RNA molecules associated with proteins. Which of the following best describes the components of this complex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: General transcription factors bound to the CAAT box

choices.label: B
choices.text: Poly(A)-binding proteins bound to the 3' tail

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ribosomal RNAs assembled with proteins into small 40S and large 60S subunits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small transfer RNAs charged with amino acids

explanation.summary: The spliceosome is composed of several species of small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs).
explanation.whyCorrect: The protein complex that facilitates splicing, referred to as the spliceosome, is composed of several species of small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs). The primary transcript combines with snRNPs (such as U1 at the 5' splice site and U2 at the branch point) and other proteins to form the spliceosome, which removes introns and joins exons.

whyWrongByChoice.A: General transcription factors assemble at the promoter to initiate transcription; they do not form the spliceosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Poly(A)-binding proteins protect the poly(A) tail from exonucleases; they do not remove introns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: rRNAs plus proteins form the ribosomal subunits that conduct translation, not the spliceosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Charged tRNAs carry amino acids into the ribosome during translation; they are not spliceosome components.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A point mutation alters the conserved AG dinucleotide at the 3' end of an intron in a pre-mRNA. In cells carrying this mutation, the spliceosome still cleaves the 5' splice site and a lariat intermediate is formed. Which of the following steps is most directly prevented by this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of the 7-methylguanosine cap to the 5' end of the transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of the donor site's 5' phosphodiester bond at the GU dinucleotide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the 5'-2' bond between the intron and the branch point adenine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Joining of the upstream exon's free 3' end to the downstream exon's 5' end

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recognition of the AAUAAA sequence by the cleavage and polyadenylation machinery

explanation.summary: The 3' acceptor site (AG-3') is where the second splicing step occurs, joining the upstream exon to the downstream exon and releasing the lariat.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each intron has a 5' donor site (5'-GU) and a 3' acceptor site (AG-3'). After the first step (cleavage at the 5' splice site and lariat formation at the branch point), the spliceosome facilitates the formation of a phosphodiester bond between the upstream exon's free 3' end and the downstream exon's 5' end at the 3' splice site, releasing the lariat. A mutation of the AG acceptor site disrupts this second step, so the exons cannot be precisely joined.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capping occurs at the 5' end of the whole transcript and is independent of intron splice sites.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleavage of the donor site's 5' bond is the first step and depends on the 5'-GU donor site, which the stem says still occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lariat-forming 5'-2' bond involves the intron's 5' end and the branch point adenine; the stem states the lariat intermediate is formed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AAUAAA recognition governs 3' end cleavage and polyadenylation, not intron splicing.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with an autoimmune disease is found to carry a variant in the CTLA4 gene. Sequencing shows that the variant lies outside the coding exons, within a transcription factor binding site in the promoter, and that CTLA4 mRNA levels in her lymphocytes are reduced. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this variant contributes to disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alters transcription initiation and the level of gene expression

choices.label: B
choices.text: It causes the CTLA4 transcript to be reverse transcribed into DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It changes an amino acid in the CTLA4 protein sequence

choices.label: D
choices.text: It changes the anticodon of the tRNA used during translation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It introduces a premature stop codon into the CTLA4 mRNA

explanation.summary: Regulatory variants in non-coding DNA, such as transcription factor binding sites within promoters, can alter mRNA levels and cause disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is not only DNA errors within coding genes that cause disease; problems with the central dogma process itself can as well. Gene expression (mRNA levels) can be modified by mutations in both coding and non-coding DNA, including transcription factors or the binding sites within promoters. Regulatory variants affecting transcription initiation, splicing, RNA stability, and translational efficiency play roles in autoimmune disease (CTLA4), malaria (DARC), various cancers (SMYD3), and many other conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcription is an enzymatic process of certain viruses and cells and is not caused by a promoter variant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The variant lies outside the coding exons, so it does not alter the amino acid sequence of the protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A variant in the CTLA4 promoter does not affect tRNA anticodons, which are encoded by separate tRNA genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A premature stop codon requires a change within the coding sequence; a promoter variant does not create one.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A point mutation in an exon changes the mRNA codon 5'-UGG-3' to 5'-UGA-3'. Which of the following is the most likely consequence for the protein product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No change, because both the UGG and UGA codons specify tryptophan

choices.label: B
choices.text: Premature termination of translation, producing a truncated protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retention of the intron containing the mutation, adding extra residues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Substitution of cysteine for tryptophan at that position in the chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substitution of methionine, causing translation to reinitiate downstream

explanation.summary: UGG encodes tryptophan, whereas UGA is one of the three stop codons; the mutation causes premature termination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The genetic code uses three-nucleotide codons to encode specific amino acids. In the standard genetic code, UGG is the sole codon for tryptophan, while UGA (along with UAA and UAG) is a stop codon. When the ribosome encounters a stop codon, a release factor rather than a charged tRNA enters the A site, the peptide is hydrolyzed from its tRNA, and the ribosome disassembles, so a premature stop codon yields a truncated protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: UGG and UGA are not synonymous; UGA is a stop codon (mnemonic: U Go Away).
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mutation is within an exon and affects a codon, not an intron donor or acceptor site, so it does not cause intron retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cysteine is encoded by UGU and UGC; UGA does not encode cysteine but signals termination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methionine is encoded by AUG, the start codon; UGA does not encode methionine.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Although hepatitis B is not a retrovirus, its replication cycle uses an enzyme that represents an exception to the unidirectional flow of the central dogma. Which of the following best describes the activity of this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Uses DNA as a template to synthesize DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Uses DNA as a template to synthesize pre-mRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uses mRNA as a template to assemble amino acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uses RNA as a template to synthesize DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uses RNA as a template to synthesize more RNA

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase uses RNA as a template to transcribe it back into DNA and is used by retroviruses, some non-retroviruses such as hepatitis B, and eukaryotic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are two exceptions to the central dogma being unidirectional, both using RNA as a template to make additional nucleic acids. The reverse transcriptase enzyme uses RNA as a template and then transcribes it back into a DNA strand. Most retroviruses (like HIV), some non-retroviruses (like hepatitis B), and eukaryotic cells utilize this reverse transcription process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA-templated DNA synthesis is DNA replication by DNA polymerase, not an exception to the central dogma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA-templated synthesis of pre-mRNA is ordinary transcription by RNA polymerase II, which follows the central dogma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Using mRNA to assemble amino acids is translation by the ribosome, the normal final step of the central dogma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA-templated RNA synthesis is the activity of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, used by positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, not the enzyme described for hepatitis B.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A mutation alters a specific arm of a tRNA molecule such that aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase can no longer reliably attach the correct amino acid, even though the anticodon loop and the 3' acceptor stem are intact. Which of the following regions of the tRNA is most likely mutated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3'-CCA acceptor end

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anticodon loop

choices.label: C
choices.text: D-arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: T-arm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable loop

explanation.summary: The D-arm of tRNA is used by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase to ensure correct charging.
explanation.whyCorrect: All tRNAs fold into a relatively rigid three-dimensional L-shaped structure with multiple functional sites. The 3' acceptor stem carries the specific amino acid, the anticodon loop aligns with a specific codon in the mRNA, the D-arm is used by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase to ensure correct charging, and the T-arm helps the tRNA enter the ribosome. A defect in the D-arm would therefore impair accurate charging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 3' acceptor stem is where the amino acid is attached; the stem states it is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The anticodon loop aligns with the mRNA codon during translation; the stem states it is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The T-arm helps the tRNA enter the ribosome rather than serving as the synthetase recognition site for charging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The variable loop is a structural region of the tRNA and is not described as the site used by the synthetase for charging.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A biochemist studies how an amino acid becomes attached to its cognate tRNA before translation begins. Which of the following best describes this charging reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydrogen bond forms between the amino acid and the D-arm without energy input

choices.label: B
choices.text: A peptide bond is formed between the amino acid and the anticodon using GTP

choices.label: C
choices.text: A phosphodiester bond links the amino acid to the 5' end of the tRNA using ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: An ester bond is formed at the 3' acceptor stem by a synthetase using ATP

choices.label: E
choices.text: An ester bond is formed at the anticodon loop by the ribosome using GTP

explanation.summary: tRNA charging is the ATP-dependent formation of a covalent ester bond between the amino acid and the tRNA's 3' acceptor stem, catalyzed by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a tRNA establishes a covalent ester bond with an amino acid, the tRNA is said to be charged. An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase catalyzes the charging process using the energy of ATP, attaching the amino acid to the 3' acceptor stem. There is a unique aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase for each of the 20 amino acids to ensure accurate charging with cognate tRNAs (ATP: tRNA Activation).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Charging forms a covalent ester bond and requires ATP; it is not a passive hydrogen-bonding interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peptide bonds are formed between amino acids by the ribosome during elongation, not between an amino acid and a tRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The amino acid is attached by an ester bond at the 3' acceptor stem, not by a phosphodiester bond at the 5' end.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Charging is catalyzed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase using ATP, not by the ribosome using GTP, and it occurs at the acceptor stem rather than the anticodon loop.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A viral mRNA lacks a 5' cap yet is efficiently translated by human ribosomes. Which of the following best explains how the 40S subunit is able to attach to this mRNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds directly to the poly(A) tail at the 3' end

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds the stop codon and scans toward the 5' end

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is recruited by the spliceosome bound to the transcript

choices.label: D
choices.text: It recognizes an internal ribosomal entry site on the mRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: It recognizes the AAUAAA sequence in the 3' UTR

explanation.summary: The 40S subunit attaches to mRNA by recognizing either the 5' cap or an internal ribosomal entry site.
explanation.whyCorrect: To initiate translation, a 40S subunit and a charged tRNA, with the assistance of initiation factors, slide down from the mRNA's 5' end to locate the start codon (5'-AUG-3'). The 40S subunit recognizes the 5' cap, or an internal ribosomal entry site, to attach to the mRNA. An uncapped mRNA with an internal ribosomal entry site can therefore still recruit the 40S subunit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The poly(A) tail stabilizes the mRNA and is bound by PABP; it is not the attachment site for the 40S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 40S subunit scans from the 5' end toward the start codon; it does not bind the stop codon, which is recognized by a release factor at termination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spliceosome removes introns in the nucleus and does not recruit ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AAUAAA is the polyadenylation signal that directs 3' cleavage, not a ribosome attachment site.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: In a cell-free translation system, a non-hydrolyzable GTP analog is added while ATP remains available. tRNAs are successfully charged with their amino acids, but the polypeptide chain fails to grow beyond the initiator methionine. Which of the following steps is most directly blocked?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of the poly(A) tail to the mRNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charging of tRNA by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Entry of the next charged tRNA into the A site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of the 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge of the cap

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removal of introns by the spliceosome

explanation.summary: GTP powers tRNA entry into the A site and translocation during elongation, whereas ATP powers tRNA charging.
explanation.whyCorrect: During elongation, an appropriately charged tRNA enters the A site with the assistance of an elongation factor by consuming the energy from one GTP molecule; the ribosome then catalyzes a peptide bond and shifts one codon down the mRNA in the 3' direction. A non-hydrolyzable GTP analog blocks this GTP-dependent entry (and translocation), so no amino acid can be added after methionine. Charging is unaffected because it uses ATP (ATP: tRNA Activation; GTP: tRNA Gripping and Going).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Poly(A) polymerase uses ATP, not GTP, and poly(A) addition is a nuclear RNA-processing step, not part of elongation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Charging uses ATP, which remains available, and the stem states charging is successful.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cap is added during RNA processing in the nucleus and is not the elongation step blocked by a GTP analog.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intron splicing is a nuclear processing step and is not the GTP-dependent step that stalls the growing peptide.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: During translation of an mRNA, the ribosome advances until the codon 5'-UAA-3' occupies the A site. Which of the following molecules enters the A site at this point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A charged tRNA carrying methionine

choices.label: B
choices.text: A release factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: A signal recognition particle

choices.label: D
choices.text: An uncharged tRNA from the E site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Poly(A) polymerase

explanation.summary: When a stop codon (UAA, UGA, or UAG) reaches the A site, a release factor rather than a charged tRNA enters and terminates translation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elongation continues cyclically until the ribosome encounters a stop codon (5'-UAA-3', 5'-UGA-3', or 5'-UAG-3'). Instead of a charged tRNA, a release factor enters the ribosome's A site (requiring one GTP, just like tRNA entry) and facilitates hydrolysis between the final amino acid and its tRNA in the P site, leading to disassembly of the ribosome and release of the newly synthesized peptide. All nucleotides downstream of the stop codon form the 3' UTR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methionine-charged tRNA is used at initiation (AUG) and enters the P site; no tRNA matches a stop codon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The signal recognition particle recognizes a signal sequence on a nascent peptide and directs the ribosome to the RER; it does not enter the A site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uncharged tRNAs are ejected from the E site after their amino acid is incorporated; they do not enter the A site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Poly(A) polymerase adds the poly(A) tail to pre-mRNA in the nucleus and has no role at the ribosome.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A fibroblast line produces a lysosomal digestive enzyme with a normal N-terminal targeting sequence, yet the enzyme accumulates in the cytoplasm rather than reaching the lysosome. Translation of the enzyme is never paused, and the ribosomes synthesizing it are not found bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Which of the following is most likely defective in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 60S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 7-methylguanosine cap

choices.label: C
choices.text: The aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase for methionine

choices.label: D
choices.text: The poly(A)-binding protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The signal recognition particle

explanation.summary: The signal recognition particle recognizes the signal sequence, pauses translation, and binds the ribosome to a pore in the RER.
explanation.whyCorrect: All peptides that require processing or transport through the RER contain a signal sequence that is recognized in the cytoplasm by a signal recognition particle (SRP), which associates with the peptide bound to the ribosome. SRPs pause translation and help bind ribosomes to pores in the RER; translation then resumes through the pore so the finished peptide resides in the RER lumen. Without SRP, a lysosomal enzyme with an intact signal sequence is never paused or directed to the RER and ends up circulating freely in the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A defective 60S subunit would impair translation itself; the enzyme is fully synthesized, just mislocalized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 5' cap aids export, protects from exonucleases, and initiates translation; it does not direct ribosomes to the RER.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A defective methionine synthetase would block initiation of all proteins, not specifically the targeting of RER-bound proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PABP protects the poly(A) tail from exonucleases and affects mRNA stability, not ribosome targeting to the RER.

questions.topicName: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is enrolled in a research study. Sequencing of a gene reveals a single-nucleotide change in the third position of one codon, yet the amino acid sequence of the encoded protein is completely unchanged and her phenotype is normal. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The change substituted an amino acid with very different chemical properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutated codon still specifies the same amino acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutation created a new splice acceptor site within the exon

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation introduced a premature stop codon that was later repaired

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutation shifted the reading frame back into the correct position

explanation.summary: A silent (synonymous) mutation changes a nucleotide but not the amino acid because of codon redundancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The genetic code has 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, so multiple codons can specify the same amino acid. When a point mutation produces a codon that still codes for the original amino acid, it is a silent or synonymous mutation with no effect on protein structure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Substituting an amino acid with different properties describes a non-conservative missense mutation, which would change the sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Creating a splice site would alter mRNA processing and the final protein, contrary to the unchanged sequence described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A premature stop codon is a nonsense mutation and would truncate the protein, changing the product rather than leaving it identical.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single point mutation does not delete or insert nucleotides, so the reading frame is not shifted.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: DZ, a 10-year-old boy, is evaluated in the cystic fibrosis clinic. His attending explains that his disease is due to a point mutation in the CFTR gene that produces a premature termination codon (UAG) within the coding sequence. Which of the following is the most likely direct consequence of this mutation on the CFTR protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insertion of an extra amino acid without a change in reading frame

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overexpression of a normal protein at abnormally high levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of a full-length protein with a single altered amino acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retention of an intron in the mature mRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis of a truncated, non-functional protein

explanation.summary: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon that terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: A premature termination codon (UAA, UGA, or UAG) causes the ribosome to stop translation before the full protein is made. Most truncated proteins lack the active portion and are non-functional; in cystic fibrosis this yields a dysfunctional CFTR protein and thick, sticky mucus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inserting an amino acid without a frameshift describes an in-frame insertion, not a premature stop codon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Overexpression of a normal product describes a gain-of-function mutation, the opposite of premature termination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single altered amino acid in a full-length protein describes a missense mutation, not a nonsense mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intron retention results from a splice donor site mutation, not from a nonsense point mutation.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A newborn with sickle cell disease has a point mutation in the beta-globin gene in which a codon for glutamate (an acidic, negatively charged amino acid) is changed to a codon for valine (a nonpolar amino acid). Which of the following best classifies this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservative missense point mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frameshift insertion or deletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-conservative missense mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonsense (stop-gain) mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent (synonymous) point mutation

explanation.summary: A missense change to an amino acid with very different chemical properties is a non-conservative missense mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mutated codon encodes a different amino acid, making it a missense (nonsynonymous) mutation. Because valine (nonpolar) has very different properties than the original glutamate (acidic, charged), it is classified as non-conservative and often has a greater effect on protein function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A conservative missense mutation substitutes an amino acid with similar properties (same charge or acidity), not a charged residue for a nonpolar one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A frameshift requires insertion or deletion of nucleotides, not a single base substitution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nonsense mutation introduces a stop codon; here a functional amino acid is still incorporated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged; here the amino acid is replaced.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A researcher inserts a single extra nucleotide into the coding region of a gene, downstream of the start codon. When the mutant gene is translated, the amino acid sequence beyond the insertion is entirely different from the normal protein. Which of the following best describes this type of mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conservative missense mutation affecting one codon

choices.label: B
choices.text: A frameshift mutation that alters every downstream codon

choices.label: C
choices.text: A silent mutation with no downstream effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: A splice acceptor mutation causing exon skipping

choices.label: E
choices.text: An in-frame insertion that adds a single amino acid

explanation.summary: Inserting a non-triplet number of nucleotides shifts the reading frame, altering all downstream codons.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a single nucleotide (a non-triplet segment) is inserted into the coding region, a frameshift mutation occurs. Every downstream codon is read in a new frame, so the entire sequence past the insertion is altered and a premature stop codon may appear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A missense mutation changes only a single codon, not the entire downstream sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A silent mutation changes a base but not the amino acid, and it does not affect downstream codons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exon skipping results from a splice acceptor site mutation, not from inserting a nucleotide in the coding region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adding a single amino acid in-frame requires an insertion of three nucleotides, which would not shift the frame.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A gene is found to have a small deletion within its coding region. Compared with the normal protein, the encoded protein is missing one amino acid but the rest of its downstream sequence is unchanged. Which of the following best explains why a frameshift did not occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deletion converted the codon to one for the same amino acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The deletion created a new stop codon that halted translation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The deletion involved a multiple of three nucleotides

choices.label: D
choices.text: The deletion occurred in the splice donor site

choices.label: E
choices.text: The deletion was located in a noncoding region

explanation.summary: Deleting a multiple of three nucleotides removes whole codons and preserves the reading frame, avoiding a frameshift.
explanation.whyCorrect: Any deletion or insertion that is a multiple of three keeps the downstream sequence in the same reading frame, so only a few amino acids are removed or added while the ribosome stays in frame. This is why a three-nucleotide deletion (as in CFTR delta-F508) removes a single amino acid without frameshifting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Converting a codon to one for the same amino acid describes a silent point mutation, not a three-nucleotide deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A new stop codon would truncate the protein, not simply remove one amino acid with an otherwise normal downstream sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A splice donor site deletion would disrupt intron removal, not cleanly delete one amino acid in frame.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stem states the deletion is within the coding region, and a noncoding location would not remove an amino acid from the protein.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A patient has a mutation that alters the 5'-GU start sequence at the boundary of an intron in a gene. Analysis of the mature mRNA shows that the intron adjacent to the mutation is incorrectly included in the final transcript. This start sequence corresponds to which splicing element, and what is the expected result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Branch point; two adjacent exons are fused

choices.label: B
choices.text: Splice acceptor site; a cryptic exon is created within the intron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Splice acceptor site; the adjacent exon is skipped

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splice donor site; the adjacent intron is retained

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splice donor site; the reading frame is unaffected and no change occurs

explanation.summary: The 5'-GU intron start is the splice donor site; disrupting it leads to intron retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Introns are typically flanked by 5'-GU (splice donor) and AG-3' (splice acceptor) sequences. If the donor (start) sequence is altered, the spliceosome fails to remove that intron correctly and the entire intron is incorrectly included in the mature mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 5'-GU sequence is the donor site, not the branch point, and the described outcome is intron retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryptic exon insertion requires creation of new splice sequences within an intron, not simple loss of a donor site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exon skipping results from disruption of the AG-3' acceptor site, not the 5'-GU donor site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retaining an intron changes the mRNA sequence, so translation and the protein are affected, not unchanged.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: In a different patient, a mutation destroys the AG-3' end sequence of an intron. The spliceosome scans past the destroyed site to the next available end sequence. Which of the following outcomes is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A silent mutation with no effect on the mRNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single amino acid substitution in the protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: An entire exon is removed from the final mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: An intron is retained in the final mRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overexpression of the normal gene product

explanation.summary: Loss of the AG-3' splice acceptor site causes the spliceosome to skip to the next end sequence, removing an exon.
explanation.whyCorrect: The AG-3' end sequence is the splice acceptor site. If it is altered, the spliceosome scans for the next end sequence in the pre-mRNA, which results in an entire exon being removed from the final mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A splice site mutation changes mRNA processing, so it is not silent with no effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single amino acid substitution is a missense point mutation, unrelated to loss of a splice acceptor site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intron retention follows loss of the 5'-GU donor (start) site, not the AG-3' acceptor site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Overexpression describes a gain-of-function regulatory change, not a splicing defect.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl presents with cafe-au-lait spots, a large head, and several bones affected by fibrous dysplasia and skin patches following developmental lines; her parents and siblings are unaffected. Genetic testing shows the causative mutation is present in affected tissues but absent from her blood leukocytes and germ cells. Which of the following best describes this type of mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frameshift mutation inherited from an affected parent

choices.label: B
choices.text: A germline mutation present in every cell of the body

choices.label: C
choices.text: A silent mutation with no clinical consequence

choices.label: D
choices.text: A somatic mutation limited to a subset of tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: A splice site mutation affecting all tissues equally

explanation.summary: A mutation present only in some tissues and not in germ cells is a somatic mutation, exemplified by McCune-Albright syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Somatic mutations occur in non-reproductive tissue and are not passed to offspring. When they occur early in development they can cause a widespread but patchy phenotype, as in McCune-Albright syndrome affecting bone, skin, and endocrine tissues. The mutation is seen only in the individual and not inherited.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The family history is negative and the mutation is not in germ cells, so it was not inherited from a parent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A germline mutation would be present in every cell, including blood and germ cells, which contradicts the testing results.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A silent mutation has no clinical consequence, but this patient has a defined disease phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation is described as present in only a subset of tissues, not affecting all tissues equally.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has multiple cafe-au-lait spots and benign tumors growing along nerves in the skin and brain due to a mutation in the NF-1 gene. His father is similarly affected. The mutation is detectable in every cell type tested, including his sperm. Which of the following best characterizes this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A germline mutation present in all cells and heritable

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mutation present only in tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mutation that arose after birth and is not passed to offspring

choices.label: D
choices.text: A silent mutation that does not affect the phenotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: A somatic mutation confined to neural tissue

explanation.summary: A mutation present in every cell, including germ cells, and passed through a family is a germline mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Germline mutations occur in the tissue that produces sex cells (ova or sperm), so they are passed to offspring and are present in every cell of the affected individual. Neurofibromatosis type 1, caused by an NF-1 gene mutation, is a classic inherited (germline) disorder with cafe-au-lait spots and nerve-associated tumors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The mutation is present in every cell type tested, not only in tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mutation is inherited from his father and present in sperm, so it is heritable rather than acquired after birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A silent mutation does not change the phenotype, yet this patient clearly has disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A somatic mutation would be confined to certain tissues and not found in germ cells, but this mutation is in every cell.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A child with a neurodevelopmental disorder is found to have a deletion of one copy of a set of genes at 7q11.23, leaving one normal functional allele of each gene. The remaining single allele produces only about 50% of the normal amount of gene product, which is insufficient for a normal phenotype.
