Which of the following best describes this mechanism of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservative missense mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dominant-negative effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gain-of-function

choices.label: D
choices.text: Haploinsufficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent mutation

explanation.summary: When 50% of gene product from a single working allele is not enough for a normal phenotype, the mechanism is haploinsufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Haploinsufficiency occurs when one functional copy of a gene, producing about 50% of the normal product, cannot generate a normal phenotype. This underlies Williams syndrome, caused by haploinsufficiency of genes at 7q11.23. In such cases the loss-of-function acts as a dominant condition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A conservative missense mutation is a single amino acid substitution, not a deletion causing reduced gene dosage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In a dominant-negative effect the abnormal product actively interferes with the normal protein; here one allele is simply deleted and no interfering product is made.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gain-of-function involves inappropriate or excessive activity of a product, not a deficiency from losing one allele.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A silent mutation has no phenotypic effect, whereas this patient has a disorder.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A patient is heterozygous for a mutation in a gene encoding a protein that assembles into a multi-subunit complex. Although one allele is normal, the abnormal subunit not only fails to function but also binds and disrupts the normal subunits, so overall protein function is well below the 50% expected. Which of the following best describes this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dominant-negative effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gain-of-function producing a beneficial trait

choices.label: C
choices.text: Haploinsufficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silent mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Simple recessive loss-of-function with a normal phenotype

explanation.summary: When an abnormal product interferes with the normal protein in a heterozygote, driving function below 50%, it is a dominant-negative effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dominant-negative (double-negative) effect occurs when the abnormal gene product not only fails to function but actively interferes with the normal form produced by the other allele. Even though at least 50% functionality would be expected, function ends up much lower because the mutant protein disrupts the normal one, acting as if both alleles are defective.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The mutation reduces function rather than conferring a new beneficial trait, so it is not a gain-of-function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In haploinsufficiency the normal allele simply cannot make enough product; the mutant product does not actively interfere with the normal protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A silent mutation causes no change in protein or function, contradicting the reduced function described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A simple recessive loss-of-function in a heterozygote usually yields a normal phenotype, but here function drops well below 50%.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A tumor is found to carry a mutation that causes a gene's normal product to be expressed at abnormally high levels and at the wrong time in the cell cycle, driving unchecked proliferation. Which of the following best classifies this type of mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gain-of-function mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haploinsufficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss-of-function mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Null mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent mutation

explanation.summary: A mutation causing inappropriate, excessive, or mistimed expression (or a new abnormal activity) of a gene product is a gain-of-function mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: A gain-of-function mutation causes the normal gene product to be expressed inappropriately, such as at abnormally high levels, at the wrong time, or in the wrong location, or gives the protein a new abnormal function. Excessive, mistimed expression that drives proliferation fits this definition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Haploinsufficiency is a deficiency in which 50% of product is not enough, not an increase in expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A loss-of-function mutation reduces gene activity, the opposite of the increased expression described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A null mutation causes the complete absence of a functional product, not overexpression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A silent mutation causes no change in the product or its expression.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A research seminar reviews estimates that each of the 30-50 trillion cells in the human body sustains roughly 70,000 sites of DNA damage per day, yet the vast majority of these never become permanent changes in the genome. Which of the following best describes the relationship between these sites of damage and mutations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every site of damage is a mutation that is transmitted to daughter cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sites of damage are lesions, and only those not properly repaired become mutations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sites of damage are limited to strand breaks and never alter individual bases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sites of damage become mutations only when they occur in germline tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sites of damage occur only in noncoding regions and therefore have no effect

explanation.summary: A DNA lesion is any site of damage within a polynucleotide; lesions that are not properly repaired become mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA is fragile, and every cell incurs around 70,000 DNA lesions per day. A lesion is a broad term for any site of damage within a polynucleotide, which may result in a strand break, base modification, base deletion, or base insertion. Only lesions that are not properly repaired persist as mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most lesions are repaired; a lesion is a site of damage, not automatically a heritable mutation passed to daughter cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lesions include base modification, base deletion, and base insertion in addition to strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lesions become mutations when they escape repair regardless of tissue; somatic mutations occur in non-germline tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lesions occur anywhere in the genome, and even a single altered base in a single gene can have profound consequences.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a sharply demarcated patch of abnormally pigmented skin on her left flank that has been present since infancy. Sequencing of a biopsy from the patch reveals a mutation that is absent from adjacent normal skin and from her blood. Which of the following best explains why the mutant phenotype is confined to a single region of the body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mutation arose in the germ line and was silenced in all other tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutation destroyed a splice site that is used only in flank skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutation is silent and produces a phenotype only where the gene is transcribed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation occurred in one dividing cell whose daughter cells stayed close together

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutation was inherited from one parent and lost from most cells after birth

explanation.summary: Somatic mutations arise in a single dividing cell, and its daughter cells stay close together, producing a localized phenotypically mutated region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Somatic mutations occur in a single cell as it divides to produce daughter cells. These cells tend to stay close to one another and result in a phenotypically mutated region of the body. Because the mutation is limited to somatic cells, it is seen only in that region of the individual and is not found in blood or unaffected skin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A germline mutation would be present in every cell of the individual, including blood, not confined to one patch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The localized pattern reflects clonal spread from one mutated cell, not tissue-specific use of a splice site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A silent mutation has no effect on protein structure and would not produce a visible phenotype anywhere.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An inherited mutation is present in every cell from conception; it is not selectively lost from most cells after birth.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Two unrelated children carry the same somatic mutation. The first has fibrous dysplasia of multiple bones, cafe au lait skin patches, and endocrine abnormalities consistent with McCune-Albright syndrome, whereas the second has only a single small cafe au lait patch. Which of the following best explains the difference in the extent of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first child inherited two mutant alleles whereas the second inherited one

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first child's mutation created a cryptic exon whereas the second child's did not

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first child's mutation is germline whereas the second child's is somatic

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first child's mutation is non-conservative whereas the second child's is conservative

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first child's mutation occurred earlier in development than the second child's

explanation.summary: The earlier in development a somatic mutation occurs, the larger the spread of the mutant phenotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a somatic mutation occurs early enough in development, the spread of the mutant phenotype can be much larger because more descendant cells carry it. McCune-Albright syndrome is the brick's example: a mutation very early in development causes widespread expression of the phenotype in bone, skin, and several endocrine tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Somatic mutations arise in the individual's own tissue and are not inherited as alleles from parents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Creation of a cryptic exon describes a splicing outcome, not the developmental timing that determines extent of involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem states both children carry a somatic mutation; a germline mutation would be in every cell and could be inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conservative versus non-conservative describes the amino acid change, not how widely the mutant cell population spread.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is found to carry a new disease-causing mutation that is not present in either of his parents. He asks whether his future children could inherit the condition. For the mutation to be passed to his offspring, it must be present in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone and endocrine tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating blood leukocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skin cells at the site of the phenotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic cells of the affected organ

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tissue that produces sperm

explanation.summary: Only mutations in the germ line, the tissue that produces ova or sperm, are passed to offspring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Germline mutations occur in the germ line, the special tissue uniquely designed to produce sex cells (ova or sperm). Germline mutations are passed to the offspring and can result in genetically inherited diseases. Somatic mutations, by contrast, occur in tissue that is not passed on and are only seen in the individual.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone and endocrine tissues are somatic; they are affected in McCune-Albright syndrome, which is not inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood leukocytes are somatic cells; a mutation there is not transmitted to children.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skin cells are somatic tissue, and a mutation confined to them is not inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic tissue is by definition not passed on to offspring, so a mutation limited to an affected organ is not inherited.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A bioinformatics program scans a newly sequenced stretch of DNA and flags a region that contains a potential start codon and a potential stop codon based on sequence features alone. No mRNA or protein corresponding to this region has ever been detected. Which of the following best describes this region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A coding sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mature mRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: A retained intron

choices.label: D
choices.text: A splice acceptor site

choices.label: E
choices.text: An open reading frame

explanation.summary: An open reading frame is a potential protein-coding region identified from sequence features, without evidence that it is actually transcribed and translated.
explanation.whyCorrect: An ORF is a sequence identified as a region of DNA that could code for a protein, but other evidence of it being transcribed and translated into a functional protein does not exist. Per Table 1, an ORF is identified based on specific sequence features, may or may not code for a protein, may have potential start and stop codons, and may or may not be transcribed into mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CDS has been confirmed to code for a protein by experimental RNA and protein data, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No mRNA has been detected for this region, so it cannot be a mature mRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A retained intron is a splicing error in mRNA, not a computationally predicted coding region in DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A splice acceptor site is the AG-3' sequence at the end of an intron, not a potential protein-coding region.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A region of DNA was originally annotated as an open reading frame. It is later reclassified as a coding sequence (CDS). Which of the following findings most likely justified the reclassification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A point mutation within the region was shown to be silent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computer analysis identified a possible start codon within the region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Experimental RNA and protein data confirmed it codes for a protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: The region was found to have six possible reading frames

choices.label: E
choices.text: The region was found to lie between intronic GU and AG sequences

explanation.summary: A CDS differs from an ORF in having been confirmed by experimental evidence to code for a protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main difference between a coding sequence and an open reading frame is that the CDS has been confirmed to code for a protein, with RNA and protein data to support it. Table 1 lists CDS identification as based on experimental evidence or annotation, with the direct role of the protein identified and the sequence found in the transcribed mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Demonstrating a silent mutation says nothing about whether the region is actually transcribed and translated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Identification based on sequence features such as a possible start codon is how an ORF is defined, not what upgrades it to a CDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Any segment of DNA has six possible reading frames; this is not evidence of protein coding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GU and AG sequences flank introns and mark splice sites; they do not establish that a region is translated into protein.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A student examines a double-stranded segment of DNA and asks how many distinct reading frames a ribosome could theoretically use to translate sequence derived from that segment. Which of the following is the correct total?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One

choices.label: B
choices.text: Six

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sixty-four

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two

explanation.summary: Any segment of DNA has six possible reading frames: three on the (+)-strand and three on the (-)-strand.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term reading frames refers to the six possible reading frames that a ribosome could use, three possible frames on the (+)-strand and three possible frames on the (-)-strand, as shown in Figure 1 (+1, +2, +3, -1, -2, -3).

whyWrongByChoice.A: One is the single frame the ribosome must stay in once it starts translating, not the total number available.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sixty-four is the number of possible codons in the genetic code, not the number of reading frames.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Three is the number of frames on a single strand, but a double-stranded segment has three on each strand.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two would correspond to the number of strands, not the number of reading frames.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: An mRNA with the sequence 5'-CUCAGCGUUACCAU-3' is normally translated as Leu-Ser-Val-Thr. In a mutant cell, the ribosome begins translating this same unchanged sequence one nucleotide downstream of the normal starting point. Which of the following best describes the resulting product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leu-Ser-Ala-Thr, because a single codon is altered

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leu-Ser-Val, because translation stops one codon early

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leu-Ser-Val-Thr, because the genetic code is redundant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ser-Ala-Leu-Pro, because a different reading frame is used

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ser-Val-Thr, because only the first amino acid is lost

explanation.summary: Starting translation one nucleotide off puts the ribosome in a different reading frame, so every codon and amino acid changes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 shows the same mRNA read in three frames: frame 1 gives Leu-Ser-Val-Thr, frame 2 (UCA GCG UUA CCA) gives Ser-Ala-Leu-Pro, and frame 3 gives Gln-Arg-Tyr-His. Once the ribosome chooses one of the six reading frames it must continue to use only that frame to generate the correct protein, so beginning one nucleotide downstream reads entirely different codons.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single altered codon would describe a point mutation, but here every codon boundary has moved.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sequence is unchanged and contains no stop codon in the new frame; the product is a different peptide, not a truncated one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Redundancy means multiple codons encode the same amino acid, but shifting the frame changes which codons are read, so the sequence is not preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shifting by one nucleotide does not simply drop the first amino acid; it regroups all nucleotides into new codons.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has markedly reduced levels of a plasma enzyme. Sequencing shows that the coding region of the gene and all of its splice sites are normal, and the small amount of enzyme that is produced has a normal amino acid sequence and normal activity. A single-nucleotide variant is identified in a noncoding region of the gene. Which of the following best explains the reduced enzyme level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The variant altered expression of the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: The variant caused a conservative missense change

choices.label: C
choices.text: The variant introduced a premature stop codon within the coding sequence

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant shifted the reading frame of all downstream codons

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant substituted an amino acid at the enzyme's active site

explanation.summary: Mutations in noncoding regions can have no effect, alter gene expression, or induce alternative splice sites.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mutations in noncoding regions can have no effect, can alter gene expression, or can induce alternative splice sites. Because the coding region and splice sites are normal and the protein that is made has a normal sequence and activity, the reduced amount of enzyme is best explained by altered expression of the gene.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A conservative missense change is a coding-region substitution that alters an amino acid, but the sequence is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A premature stop codon is a coding-region change that would truncate the protein; here the protein sequence and coding region are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A frameshift alters every downstream codon and would change the protein sequence, which is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An active-site substitution would reduce activity of the enzyme, but the enzyme produced has normal activity.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Sequencing of a patient's gene reveals a single-nucleotide change that converts a lysine codon (AAG) into an arginine codon (AGG). Both lysine and arginine are basic amino acids. Which of the following best classifies this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservative missense mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frameshift mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-conservative missense mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonsense mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent mutation

explanation.summary: A missense change to an amino acid that shares the original's structural properties, such as the same charge, is a conservative missense mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 3 shows AAG (Lys) mutated to AGG (Arg), both basic amino acids. Because the mutated codon encodes a different amino acid it is a missense mutation, and because the new amino acid shares structural properties of the original (same charge or acidity) it is deemed conservative. Conservative missense mutations are generally expected to have milder consequences.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A frameshift requires insertion or deletion of a non-triplet number of nucleotides, not a single-base substitution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A non-conservative missense mutation substitutes an amino acid with very different properties, such as AAG (Lys, basic) to ACG (Thr, polar).
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nonsense mutation introduces a stop codon, as in AAG to UAG; AGG still codes for an amino acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged, as in AAG to AAA (still lysine); here the amino acid changes.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Two patients have missense mutations at the same position of the same enzyme. In patient 1, an acidic residue is replaced by another acidic residue of similar size. In patient 2, the same acidic residue is replaced by a large nonpolar residue. Which of the following best explains why patient 1 is expected to have milder consequences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A substitution between similar amino acids is not transcribed into mRNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: A substitution between similar amino acids is read by the ribosome as a stop codon

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substitution between similar amino acids restores the original codon sequence

choices.label: D
choices.text: A substitution that preserves charge and size is less likely to alter protein folding

choices.label: E
choices.text: A substitution that preserves charge keeps the mutation out of the reading frame

explanation.summary: Conservative missense mutations are milder because they are less likely to dramatically alter protein folding, and protein shape equals protein function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conservative missense mutations substitute an amino acid with similar structural properties (same charge or acidity), so they are less likely to dramatically alter protein folding or structure and generally have little effect on functionality. The brick stresses that protein shape equals protein function. A non-conservative change (different charge, acidity, or size) often has a greater effect, though not always.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both mutant genes are transcribed and translated; the difference lies in how the new amino acid affects folding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stop codons arise from nonsense mutations; a missense change still specifies an amino acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patient 1 still has a changed codon encoding a different amino acid; the original codon is not restored.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both patients have single-base substitutions, which do not alter the reading frame at all.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A researcher generates several different single-nucleotide substitutions in the same gene and measures the function of the encoded protein for each. Which of the following types of mutation is generally expected to have the most significant impact on protein function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservative missense mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-conservative missense mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonsense mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silent mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substitution that creates a new splice donor site within an intron

explanation.summary: Among point mutations, the nonsense mutation has the most significant impact because it truncates the protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the point mutation that causes the most significant impact on protein function is a nonsense mutation, which introduces a stop codon where there should be an amino acid and terminates translation prematurely. Most truncated proteins are non-functional and are often missing the active portion of the protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A conservative missense mutation preserves amino acid properties and generally has mild consequences.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A non-conservative missense mutation often has a greater effect than a conservative one, but the protein is still full length; nonsense mutations are the most severe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A silent mutation codes for the same amino acid and has no effect on protein structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A new intronic splice site can alter the mRNA, but the brick identifies the nonsense mutation as the point mutation with the greatest impact on protein function.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A genetic testing report describes a patient's variant as nonsynonymous. Which of the following single-nucleotide changes is consistent with this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A change in the 5'-GU sequence at the start of an intron

choices.label: B
choices.text: A change in the AG-3' sequence at the end of an intron

choices.label: C
choices.text: A leucine codon CUC changed to CUU, which also encodes leucine

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lysine codon AAG changed to AAA, which also encodes lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: A lysine codon AAG changed to UAG, a stop codon

explanation.summary: Nonsynonymous mutations are nonsense and missense mutations, both of which change the amino acid sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonsense and missense (both conservative and non-conservative) mutations are referred to as nonsynonymous mutations because they alter the amino acid sequence. AAG to UAG replaces lysine with a stop codon (Figure 3), a nonsense mutation, and is therefore nonsynonymous.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A change in the intronic 5'-GU splice donor site is a splice site mutation, a separate category from point mutations within codons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A change in the intronic AG-3' splice acceptor site is a splice site mutation, not a nonsynonymous codon change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CUC to CUU still encodes leucine, so it is a synonymous mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AAG to AAA still encodes lysine, so it is a silent or synonymous mutation that does not alter the amino acid sequence.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A population study identifies a single-nucleotide substitution in a coding region that changes one amino acid in an enzyme. Individuals carrying the variant show improved survival in a particular environment. Which of the following best characterizes this variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dominant-negative mutation, because it interferes with the normal enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: A nonsense mutation, because it truncates the enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: A nonsynonymous mutation, because it changed a trait in a helpful way

choices.label: D
choices.text: A null mutation, because it eliminates the functional gene product

choices.label: E
choices.text: A synonymous mutation, because the protein product is unchanged

explanation.summary: Nonsynonymous mutations change the protein and can be helpful as well as harmful, affecting traits that help an organism adapt and evolve.
explanation.whyCorrect: A substitution that changes an amino acid is a missense mutation and therefore nonsynonymous. Nonsynonymous mutations result in protein changes that affect the functionality of the protein in some way, helpful or harmful. The brick notes they can be beneficial because they can affect the organism's traits, helping it adapt and evolve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dominant-negative effect involves an abnormal product interfering with the normal protein, a harmful mechanism, not an adaptive benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A nonsense mutation introduces a stop codon and truncates the protein; here a single amino acid was substituted.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A null mutation causes complete absence of a functional gene product, which would not improve survival through enzyme function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synonymous mutation does not alter the amino acid sequence, but this variant changed one amino acid.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A patient has a gene with three exons. A mutation destroys the AG-3' sequence at the end of intron 2, and a second change creates a new AG sequence a short distance inside exon 3. Analysis of the mature mRNA shows that exons 1 and 2 are intact and joined to exon 3, but the first portion of exon 3 is missing. Which of the following best describes this splicing outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete exon skipping

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insertion of a cryptic exon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intron retention

choices.label: D
choices.text: Partial exon skipping

choices.label: E
choices.text: Partial intron inclusion

explanation.summary: When a splice end sequence is destroyed and a new one is created nearby, a partial deletion of an exon can result.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that if an end sequence (AG, the splicing acceptor site) is destroyed while a new one is created, a partial deletion or insertion is possible. Here the spliceosome uses the new AG inside exon 3, so the portion of exon 3 upstream of that site is removed along with the intron. Figure 4 labels this outcome partial exon skipping.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete exon skipping would remove all of exon 3 when the spliceosome scans to the next end sequence; here only the first portion is lost.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A cryptic exon requires both a new AG and a new GU created within an intron, adding sequence rather than removing part of an exon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intron retention follows loss of the GU start sequence (donor site), and the intron would remain in the mRNA; here intron 2 is removed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Partial intron inclusion would add intronic sequence to the mRNA, not remove exonic sequence.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Sequencing of a patient's gene identifies two nucleotide changes within the same intron: one creates a new AG sequence and, further downstream, another creates a new GU sequence. The mature mRNA contains an additional segment between the two exons that normally flank this intron. Which of the following best describes this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creation of an entirely novel exon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Partial deletion of the downstream exon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Removal of the upstream exon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retention of the entire intron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skipping of the downstream exon

explanation.summary: Creating both a new end sequence (AG) and a new start sequence (GU) within an intron generates a novel, cryptic exon.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that if both a new end sequence and start sequence are created within an intron, this can create an entirely novel exon. Figure 4 illustrates this as insertion of a cryptic exon: a new AG and GU within the intron define an extra exon that is spliced into the mature mRNA between the original exons.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Partial exon deletion occurs when an acceptor site is destroyed and a new one created within an exon; here the new sites are intronic and add sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No original exon is removed; the mRNA gained a segment between the two flanking exons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intron retention results from loss of the original GU donor site and would include the whole intron, not a defined segment bounded by new splice sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exon skipping follows loss of an AG acceptor site and removes sequence from the mRNA rather than adding it.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A molecular biologist inspects the sequence of a pre-mRNA to locate the boundaries that spliceosomes use to identify an intron. Which of the following pairs of sequences is most likely found at the 5' start and the 3' end of the intron, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AAG and AGG

choices.label: B
choices.text: AG and GU

choices.label: C
choices.text: AUG and UAG

choices.label: D
choices.text: GU and AG

choices.label: E
choices.text: UAA and UGA

explanation.summary: Introns are usually flanked by 5'-GU (splice donor) and AG-3' (splice acceptor) sequences that spliceosomes use for identification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Introns are flanked by specific sequences, usually 5'-GU ... AG-3', that serve as splicing sites for spliceosomes. The GU start sequence is the splicing donor site and the AG end sequence is the splicing acceptor site; altering either produces intron retention or exon skipping, respectively.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AAG and AGG are lysine and arginine codons from Figure 3, not intron boundary sequences.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the order; GU marks the intron start and AG marks the intron end.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AUG is the start codon and UAG is a stop codon, which define a coding sequence, not intron boundaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UAA and UGA are stop codons that terminate translation; they are not splice site sequences.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Two mutant alleles of the same gene are created in the laboratory. Mutant 1 has a 4-nucleotide insertion, and mutant 2 has a 6-nucleotide insertion; both insertions lie within the coding region downstream of the start codon. Which of the following best predicts the effect on the encoded proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both alleles produce silent changes, because insertions do not alter existing codons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both alleles shift the reading frame, because any insertion alters downstream codons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither allele shifts the reading frame, because both insertions exceed three nucleotides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only mutant 1 shifts the reading frame; mutant 2 adds amino acids and stays in frame

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only mutant 2 shifts the reading frame; mutant 1 adds amino acids and stays in frame

explanation.summary: Only insertions or deletions that are not a multiple of three shift the reading frame; multiples of three add or remove a few amino acids and stay in frame.
explanation.whyCorrect: When any non-triplet DNA segment is inserted or deleted within the coding region, a frameshift usually occurs and every downstream codon can be significantly altered; a 4-nucleotide insertion is non-triplet. If the insertion involves a multiple of three nucleotides, as with 6 nucleotides, a few amino acids are added but the sequence gets back in frame, so a frameshift is avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insertions change the mRNA and protein; a silent mutation is a substitution that preserves the amino acid, which is not the case for either allele.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An insertion that is a multiple of three does not shift the frame; only the 4-nucleotide insertion does.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Frame preservation depends on being a multiple of three, not on exceeding three; 4 nucleotides is not a multiple of three.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the outcomes; 6 is a multiple of three and stays in frame, whereas 4 is not.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: Two unrelated adults are found to carry the identical single-nucleotide substitution at the same position of the same gene. One has severe disease requiring hospitalization, whereas the other has only mild symptoms. Which of the following best explains the difference in clinical severity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The overall genetic background differs between the two individuals

choices.label: B
choices.text: The substitution created a stop codon in only one individual

choices.label: C
choices.text: The substitution is silent in one individual and missense in the other

choices.label: D
choices.text: The substitution lies in the coding region in only one individual

choices.label: E
choices.text: The substitution shifted the reading frame in only one individual

explanation.summary: The clinical consequences of a point mutation depend on the gene affected, the location within the gene, and the individual's overall genetic background.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the clinical consequences of point mutations vary widely, from mild to severe, depending on the specific gene affected, the location of the mutation within the gene, and the overall genetic background of the individual. Because these two people share the same substitution at the same position of the same gene, the remaining variable is their genetic background.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The same substitution yields the same codon in both people; it cannot be a stop codon in only one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An identical nucleotide change at the same codon produces the same type of codon change in both individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The same position in the same gene is either coding or noncoding for both individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single-nucleotide substitution does not shift the reading frame in either individual.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is diagnosed with Tay-Sachs disease. The attending notes that, like cystic fibrosis and sickle-cell anemia, the disorder is commonly caused by the same general category of genetic alteration. Which of the following best describes that category?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A change in a single nucleotide

choices.label: B
choices.text: A somatic mutation arising very early in development

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creation of a novel exon within an intron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deletion of an entire gene from the genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Haploinsufficiency of a cluster of genes at 7q11.23

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anemia, and Tay-Sachs are common diseases caused by point mutations, which alter a single nucleotide.
explanation.whyCorrect: A point mutation is an alteration in a single nucleotide. Although point mutations involve only one nucleotide, they can significantly affect phenotype and lead to disease; the brick lists cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anemia, and Tay-Sachs as common diseases caused by a point mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An early somatic mutation is the mechanism of McCune-Albright syndrome, which is not inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Creation of a novel exon is a splice site mutation outcome, not the category the brick cites for these diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deletion of an entire gene is one cause of a null mutation, not the point mutation category shared by these three diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haploinsufficiency of genes at 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A missense mutation in a signaling protein is found to increase the protein's half-life, so the protein persists and remains active far longer than normal. It is expressed at the normal time and in the normal cell type, and its remaining sequence is unchanged. Which of the following best classifies this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dominant-negative mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gain-of-function mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Haploinsufficiency effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Null (amorphic) mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synonymous silent mutation

explanation.summary: Gain-of-function missense mutations can increase the efficiency or half-life of a protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick summarizes that gain-of-function missense mutations occur less often and either increase the efficiency of the protein or the half-life of the protein, or change its regulatory sequences. A missense change that makes the protein persist and act longer than normal is therefore a gain-of-function mutation, even though timing and location of expression are unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dominant-negative effect requires the abnormal product to interfere with the normal protein's function; here the protein is more active, not obstructive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haploinsufficiency is a deficiency in which 50% of gene product is not enough, not an increase in protein activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A null mutation causes complete absence of a functional gene product, the opposite of a longer-lived active protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synonymous mutation does not change the amino acid sequence; this is a missense change that altered protein stability.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A healthy 28-year-old woman undergoes carrier testing. One allele of a gene carries a point mutation that introduces a stop codon only a few codons after the start codon, and no protein product from that allele is detectable. Her other allele is normal, and she produces about 50% of the normal amount of the protein. Which of the following best classifies the mutation on the affected allele?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservative missense mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dominant-negative mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gain-of-function mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Null mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent mutation

explanation.summary: A null mutation is a loss-of-function mutation that causes complete absence of a functional gene product from that allele, leaving 50% of normal product in a heterozygote.
explanation.whyCorrect: A null mutation is a loss-of-function mutation that causes the complete absence of a functional gene product from one allele, so only 50% of the normal amount is produced and the individual is heterozygous at the locus. The brick lists a single base point mutation introducing a stop codon near the beginning of a gene's start codon, such that no protein product is ever made, as one cause of a null mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A conservative missense mutation yields a full-length protein with a similar amino acid substituted, not absence of product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dominant-negative mutation produces an abnormal protein that interferes with the normal one; this allele produces no protein to interfere.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A gain-of-function mutation causes inappropriate or excessive expression or a new function; here the allele makes no product at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A silent mutation does not change the protein at all, but this allele produces no detectable protein.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A couple, both healthy, have a child with an inherited enzyme deficiency. Each parent is found to be heterozygous for the same loss-of-function allele, and the child is homozygous for it. Which of the following best explains why the parents have a normal phenotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each parent's single normal allele produces more than twice the normal product

choices.label: B
choices.text: One normal allele supplies enough functional product to prevent disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: The abnormal product in each parent actively interferes with the normal protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parents' mutant allele is expressed only in the germ line

choices.label: E
choices.text: The parents' mutation is somatic and therefore confined to a few tissues

explanation.summary: A heterozygous carrier of a loss-of-function allele is healthy when 50% of the functional gene product is sufficient, so the condition behaves as recessive.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a person is a heterozygous carrier of a loss-of-function mutation, having one functional allele producing the correct gene product is generally sufficient to perform the required function, so the individual has a normal phenotype. When 50% of a functional gene product is sufficient, the individual is a carrier and the loss-of-function mutation acts as a recessive inherited condition; only the homozygous child lacks a functional allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes the single normal allele as producing 50% of the normal amount, which is enough; it does not overproduce.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Active interference by the abnormal product describes the dominant-negative effect, which would make heterozygotes symptomatic rather than healthy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Germline mutations are present in every cell of the individual, not expressed solely in the germ line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The allele was transmitted to the child, so it is germline and present in every cell of each parent, not a somatic mutation.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A researcher compares the mRNA codon sequences of several mutant alleles with the normal sequence. Which of the following single-nucleotide changes would be classified as a nonsense mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AAG to AGG

choices.label: B
choices.text: ACC to ACG

choices.label: C
choices.text: CAG to UAG

choices.label: D
choices.text: CAU to CAC

choices.label: E
choices.text: CUC to CUU

explanation.summary: A nonsense mutation converts an amino acid codon into one of the stop codons UAA, UGA, or UAG.
explanation.whyCorrect: A nonsense mutation introduces a stop codon where there should be an amino acid, terminating translation prematurely. The stop codons are UAA, UGA, and UAG; changing the glutamine codon CAG to UAG creates a premature termination codon and yields a truncated protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AAG (lysine) to AGG (arginine) is a conservative missense mutation, as shown in Figure 3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACC and ACG both encode threonine, so this is a silent mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CAU and CAC both encode histidine, so this is a silent mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CUC and CUU both encode leucine, so this is a silent (synonymous) mutation.

questions.topicName: DNA Point Mutations

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in for a photosensitive rash over sun-exposed skin, intermittent cerebellar ataxia, and diarrhea. Urine amino acid analysis shows markedly elevated excretion of several amino acids, and the child improves with a niacin supplement. A defect in a renal transporter for neutral amino acids is suspected. Which of the following amino acids would be most expected to be increased in this patient's urine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspartate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tryptophan

explanation.summary: Hartnup disease impairs reabsorption of neutral (uncharged) amino acids, so they are lost in the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The renal transporter defect in Hartnup disease causes loss of neutral amino acids, producing hyperaminoaciduria. Tryptophan is a neutral amino acid, and its depletion reduces NAD+ synthesis, producing a pellagra-like picture (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia) that responds to niacin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arginine is basic and positively charged, so it is not handled by the neutral amino acid transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspartate is acidic and negatively charged at blood pH, not neutral, so it is not preferentially wasted here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamate carries a negatively charged carboxylic acid side chain, so it is not among the neutral amino acids lost by this transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysine has a basic, positively charged amine side chain and is not a neutral amino acid.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: During the Bohr effect, a drop in tissue pH protonates a specific histidine residue in hemoglobin, stabilizing a lower-affinity conformation that favors oxygen unloading. Once protonated and positively charged, this histidine most logically forms a stabilizing ionic salt bridge with which of the following amino acids?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspartate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histidine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylalanine

explanation.summary: A positively charged residue forms a salt bridge with a negatively charged partner.
explanation.whyCorrect: When histidine is protonated it becomes positively charged. An ionic salt bridge requires an oppositely charged partner, and the only amino acids with negatively charged side chains are aspartate and glutamate. Aspartate is therefore the correct partner.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arginine is also positively charged and would electrostatically repel the protonated histidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A second histidine would carry the same positive charge and could not form a stabilizing ionic bond.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysine is positively charged, so it would repel the protonated (positive) histidine rather than form a salt bridge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylalanine has a nonpolar, uncharged side chain and cannot participate in an ionic salt bridge.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A signaling protein normally promotes cell division only after a hormone triggers its phosphorylation. In a certain cancer, a mutation replaces the modifiable residue with a different amino acid that mimics the phosphate group, causing constitutive activation independent of the hormone. Which single amino acid substitution best explains this constitutive, unregulated growth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A leucine is replaced by an arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lysine is replaced by a serine

choices.label: C
choices.text: A serine is replaced by a lysine

choices.label: D
choices.text: A threonine is replaced by an aspartate

choices.label: E
choices.text: An aspartate is replaced by a threonine

explanation.summary: A phosphomimetic swaps a phosphorylatable hydroxyl residue for a negatively charged residue that imitates the phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The original residue must be serine, threonine, or tyrosine because only these hydroxyl-bearing residues are phosphorylated. Replacing threonine with aspartate introduces a permanent negative charge that mimics the phosphate group, locking the protein in its active state independent of the hormone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither leucine nor arginine can be phosphorylated, and arginine is positively charged, not phosphomimetic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This removes the phosphorylatable serine rather than mimicking phosphorylation, so it would not drive constitutive activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serine can be phosphorylated, but lysine adds a positive charge, which does not mimic the negative phosphate group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspartate is not a phosphorylation target and threonine does not carry a negative charge, so this reverses the needed logic.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables presents with bleeding, inflamed gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, easy bruising, and poorly healing wounds. His fibroblasts contain a normally folded prolyl hydroxylase enzyme, yet collagen in his tissues lacks structural integrity. Which of the following best explains the defective collagen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A missense mutation that misfolds and denatures prolyl hydroxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficiency of vitamin B12 needed for peptide bond formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficiency of vitamin C, a required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess ubiquitination targeting collagen for proteasomal degradation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of N-linked glycosylation of collagen asparagine residues

explanation.summary: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency, which deprives prolyl hydroxylase of its required cofactor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolyl hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) to hydroxylate proline to hydroxyproline, a modification that stabilizes collagen. In scurvy the enzyme is present and properly folded but simply lacks the cofactor, so collagen loses structural integrity and produces bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, and poor wound healing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vignette states the enzyme is normally folded; the problem is a missing nonprotein cofactor, not a denatured enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 is not the cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, and peptide bonds are formed during translation, not by this enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is failed hydroxylation, not excessive ubiquitin-tagged degradation of collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Collagen's key modification here is proline hydroxylation; N-linked glycosylation of asparagine is not the failed step in scurvy.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A cell biologist is studying N-linked glycosylation, in which a carbohydrate chain is covalently attached to a nitrogen atom of a specific amino acid side chain. Which amino acid is the target for N-linked glycosylation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asparagine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Threonine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine

explanation.summary: N-linked glycosylation attaches sugar to the nitrogen of asparagine.
explanation.whyCorrect: N-linked glycosylation requires a nitrogen atom for the carbohydrate linkage, and asparagine is the only amino acid targeted for this modification. This routing modification is medically relevant because its disruption underlies I-cell disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysine's amine is the target for ubiquitination, not for N-linked glycosylation of proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serine bears a hydroxyl group and is a target for O-linked glycosylation, not N-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Threonine has a hydroxyl side chain used in O-linked glycosylation, not the nitrogen-based N-linkage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tyrosine's hydroxyl group supports O-linked glycosylation, not N-linked attachment.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A damaged cytosolic protein is tagged for degradation when a small 76-amino-acid protein is covalently attached, and additional copies are then added to one another to form a polymeric tag. To which amino acid side chain is this tag initially attached?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspartate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cysteine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serine

explanation.summary: Ubiquitin is attached to the epsilon-amino group of a lysine side chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ubiquitin, a conserved 76-amino-acid protein, is covalently linked to the epsilon-amino group within a lysine side chain, and subsequent ubiquitin molecules are added to form a polyubiquitin chain that traffics the protein to the proteasome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspartate is a negatively charged residue and is not the site of ubiquitin conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cysteine's thiol forms disulfide bonds; it is not the residue that anchors ubiquitin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proline can be hydroxylated in collagen but is not the anchor for ubiquitination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine's hydroxyl group is a target for phosphorylation and O-linked glycosylation, not ubiquitin attachment.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A patient with multiple myeloma, a cancer of antibody-producing B cells, is treated with bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor. These malignant cells rapidly ubiquitinate and degrade the mediators of programmed cell death. Which of the following best explains how proteasome inhibition helps kill these cancer cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks degradation of pro-apoptotic proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It chelates the calcium cofactor required for the coagulation cascade

choices.label: C
choices.text: It denatures the primary structure of antibodies by hydrolyzing peptide bonds

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits phosphorylation of serine residues needed for cell division

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents lysosomal acidification, halting autophagy of mitochondria

explanation.summary: Inhibiting the proteasome restores pro-apoptotic proteins that the cancer cells were destroying.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ubiquitin-proteasome pathway degrades polyubiquitin-tagged cytosolic proteins. Myeloma cells escape apoptosis by degrading pro-apoptotic proteins, so inhibiting the proteasome allows those proteins to accumulate, restoring apoptosis and enhancing cancer cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium chelation to block coagulation is the action of agents like EDTA, not a proteasome inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptide-bond hydrolysis of antibodies is not the mechanism; the drug prevents degradation of intracellular proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug blocks proteasomal degradation; it does not inhibit serine phosphorylation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bortezomib acts on the proteasome, not on lysosomal acidification or autophagy of organelles.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A researcher wants to selectively destroy the primary structure of a protein without relying on disruption of weaker stabilizing forces. Which of the following agents or conditions is required to accomplish this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A change in pH

choices.label: B
choices.text: A detergent

choices.label: C
choices.text: A protease enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated heat

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mechanical agitation

explanation.summary: Primary structure is held by covalent peptide bonds, which only an enzyme can hydrolyze.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary structure is stabilized by covalent peptide bonds. Unlike the weaker forces that maintain higher-order structure, these bonds are not easily broken and require a protease, a hydrolytic enzyme, to cleave them with water.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Changes in pH neutralize charged side chains and disrupt ionic salt bridges, affecting higher-order structure but not covalent peptide bonds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Detergents disrupt hydrophobic interactions and denature proteins without breaking the covalent primary structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heat compromises weaker interactions such as hydrogen bonds while the covalent peptide backbone persists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mechanical stress disrupts weak forces and promotes misfolding but does not cleave peptide bonds.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A student is reviewing the forces that stabilize each level of protein structure. The two predominant elements of secondary structure, the alpha-helix and the beta-pleated sheet, are held together primarily by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Covalent peptide bonds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disulfide bonds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen bonds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ionic salt bridges

choices.label: E
choices.text: Van der Waals interactions

explanation.summary: Secondary structure (alpha-helix, beta-sheet) is stabilized by hydrogen bonds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet are stabilized by hydrogen bonds, which are specialized dipole-dipole interactions occurring when hydrogen is attached to an electronegative atom such as oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Covalent peptide bonds stabilize primary structure, not the folding of secondary elements.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disulfide bonds form between oxidized cysteines and help stabilize tertiary structure, not secondary structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ionic salt bridges between charged side chains contribute to tertiary structure, not the backbone hydrogen bonding of secondary structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Van der Waals interactions arise from transient dipoles among side chains and stabilize tertiary structure.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: Before running a coagulation-independent laboratory analysis, blood is collected into a vacutainer tube pre-loaded with EDTA. Despite the glass and plastic surfaces that normally activate clotting, the sample does not coagulate. Which of the following best explains why EDTA prevents coagulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It chelates Ca++, an inorganic cofactor required by coagulation proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It covalently attaches a heme prosthetic group to fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It denatures the primary structure of clotting factors by hydrolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It donates NADH as a coenzyme to reverse the coagulation cascade

choices.label: E
choices.text: It phosphorylates serine residues on clotting factors to inhibit them

explanation.summary: EDTA sequesters calcium, a cofactor multiple coagulation proteins require.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple proteins in the coagulation cascade require the cofactor Ca++. EDTA is a metal chelator that binds and coordinates positively charged metals like Ca++, sequestering them away from the clotting proteins so the cascade cannot proceed. The proteins themselves remain intact but lack their required cofactor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EDTA sequesters calcium rather than adding a heme prosthetic group to any protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EDTA does not hydrolyze peptide bonds or denature the primary structure of clotting factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADH is an intracellular coenzyme and is unrelated to EDTA's chelating mechanism in the tube.
whyWrongByChoice.E: EDTA chelates metal ions; it does not phosphorylate residues.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: An examiner asks a student to classify the non-protein components proteins require for function. Heme, which is covalently linked within a hemoglobin subunit and whose removal disrupts the protein's structure and function, is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoenzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coenzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inorganic cofactor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prosthetic group

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substrate

explanation.summary: A cofactor covalently linked to a protein is a prosthetic group.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prosthetic group is a cofactor that is covalently linked to the protein structure, with heme given as the classic example. Unlike loosely bound cofactors, removal of a prosthetic group often disrupts structure and function and cannot simply be restored by adding it back.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An apoenzyme is the protein portion lacking its cofactor, not the covalently bound helper itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A coenzyme is an organic cofactor such as NADH or FADH2 and is not defined by covalent attachment to the protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inorganic cofactors such as metal ions are typically loosely associated and readily removable, unlike a covalently attached heme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A substrate is the molecule an enzyme acts upon, not a bound non-protein helper.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A key step in influenza infection is the ability of a latent viral fusion protein to undergo a conformational change that promotes viral spread. This change occurs after the extracellular virus is internalized by the cell and the fusion protein is exposed to a slightly acidic environment. Which of the following best describes a vital aspect of this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A histidine on the fusion protein becomes deprotonated and negatively charged within the lysosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: A histidine on the fusion protein becomes deprotonated and negatively charged within the proteasome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A histidine on the fusion protein becomes protonated and positively charged within the lysosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: A histidine on the fusion protein becomes protonated and positively charged within the proteasome

choices.label: E
choices.text: A serine on the fusion protein becomes phosphorylated within the proteasome

explanation.summary: An internalized protein is routed to the acidic lysosome, where histidine becomes protonated and positively charged.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extracellular material that is internalized is routed to the lysosome, which has an acidic interior (pH 4.5-5.0). Because histidine has a side-chain pKa near physiological pH, this acidic environment protonates it, giving it a positive charge that drives the fusion protein's conformational change.

whyWrongByChoice.A: In an acidic environment histidine gains a proton and becomes positively charged, not deprotonated and negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The proteasome is the wrong compartment, and acidic conditions would protonate rather than deprotonate histidine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The proteasome degrades cytosolic proteins and is not the acidic compartment that receives internalized extracellular virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine phosphorylation is a signaling modification and does not describe the acid-driven conformational change of the fusion protein.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to explain why the 20 proteogenic amino acids display such diverse chemistry despite sharing a common architecture built around a central alpha-carbon. Which structural feature is responsible for distinguishing one amino acid from another?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The alpha-amino group attached to the alpha-carbon

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alpha-carboxylic acid group attached to the alpha-carbon

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hydrogen atom attached to the alpha-carbon

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of alpha-carbons within the amino acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variable R-side chain attached to the alpha-carbon

explanation.summary: The R-side chain is the only variable component of an alpha-amino acid and provides its distinctive chemistry.
explanation.whyCorrect: All alpha-amino acids contain a central alpha-carbon bearing four groups: a hydrogen, an amine, a carboxylic acid, and an R-side chain. R is a generic shorthand for the variable side chain, which may contain carbon, hydrogen, and/or heteroatoms such as oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur. The R-side chains distinguish amino acids and provide the diverse chemistry required for biological reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The alpha-amino group is a shared, invariant component present in all 20 proteogenic amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The alpha-carboxylic acid group is common to every alpha-amino acid and participates in peptide bond formation rather than conferring identity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Every alpha-amino acid carries a hydrogen on the alpha-carbon, so it cannot distinguish one amino acid from another.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Each alpha-amino acid has a single central alpha-carbon; the count does not vary among the 20.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a markedly elevated plasma homocysteine level on screening labs. A student notes that although homocysteine has a central alpha-carbon bearing a hydrogen, an amine, a carboxylic acid, and a side chain, it is not among the 20 amino acids in a standard protein table. Which of the following best describes homocysteine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dipeptide formed from two cysteine residues joined by a peptide bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: A medically relevant alpha-amino acid not incorporated into proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: A post-translationally hydroxylated form of the amino acid methionine

choices.label: D
choices.text: A proteogenic alpha-amino acid targeted for phosphorylation by protein kinases

choices.label: E
choices.text: A proteogenic alpha-amino acid carrying a positively charged basic side chain

explanation.summary: Homocysteine is a non-proteogenic alpha-amino acid with health relevance.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are medically relevant alpha-amino acids within the human body that are not incorporated into proteins. Homocysteine is the example given of such a non-proteogenic alpha-amino acid: it has the general alpha-amino acid architecture but is not one of the 20 proteogenic amino acids used to build proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homocysteine is a single alpha-amino acid, not a peptide-linked pair of cysteines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxylation as taught here produces hydroxyproline within collagen; homocysteine is a free non-proteogenic amino acid, not a hydroxylated methionine residue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homocysteine is not incorporated into proteins; the phosphorylation targets are serine, threonine, and tyrosine within proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homocysteine is not proteogenic, and the positively charged proteogenic residues are lysine, arginine, and histidine.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: During translation, two alpha-amino acids are joined to extend a growing polypeptide. Which of the following best describes the chemistry of the linkage formed between them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The alpha-amino group of one amino acid bonds to the alpha-amino group of the next, releasing water

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alpha-amino group of one amino acid bonds to the alpha-carboxylic acid group of the next, releasing water

choices.label: C
choices.text: The alpha-carbon of one amino acid bonds directly to the alpha-carbon of the next, releasing water

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alpha-carboxylic acid group of one amino acid bonds to the R-side chain of the next, consuming water

choices.label: E
choices.text: The R-side chain of one amino acid bonds to the R-side chain of the next, consuming water

explanation.summary: A peptide bond is a dehydration reaction that links the alpha-amino group of one amino acid to the alpha-carboxylic acid group of another.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteins are polymers of alpha-amino acids linked through specialized amide bonds known as peptides. Peptide formation is a dehydration reaction in which water is formed, allowing the new covalent linkage. The bond forms by linking the alpha-amino group from one amino acid to the alpha-carboxylic acid group of the other, which creates directionality with a free amino end (N-terminus) and a free carboxyl end (C-terminus).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Joining two amino groups would not form an amide linkage; the peptide bond requires an amine and a carboxylic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The alpha-carbons are not directly bonded; they are connected through the amide (peptide) linkage between the amine and carboxylic acid groups.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The backbone linkage does not involve the R-side chain, and water is a product, not a reactant, of peptide formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The R-side chains are not joined in the peptide backbone, and peptide formation releases rather than consumes water.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A purified enzyme loses all activity after dialysis against a buffer that removes small ions. When Mg++ is added back to the dialyzed preparation, full activity returns immediately. Which of the following best characterizes the role of Mg++ for this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A loosely associated inorganic cofactor that can be removed and resupplied

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prosthetic group covalently linked within the enzyme's folded structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: A permanent structural component whose removal irreversibly denatures the enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: A substrate that is consumed during each round of the catalytic cycle

choices.label: E
choices.text: An organic coenzyme derived from a water-soluble B vitamin precursor

explanation.summary: Metal ions such as Zn++, Mg++, and Ca++ are inorganic cofactors that can be removed to prevent activity or supplemented to restore it.
explanation.whyCorrect: A cofactor is an inorganic (lacking carbon) or organic molecule required by a protein for activity; even a fully folded protein lacks activity if its cofactor is absent. Routine inorganic cofactors are metal ions like Zn++, Mg++, and Ca++, which can easily be removed by agents to prevent protein activity or supplemented to restore or augment function. The immediate return of activity on adding Mg++ back fits this reversible, loosely associated inorganic cofactor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A prosthetic group is covalently linked to the protein, and its removal often disrupts structure so that simply adding it back does not restore activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of a covalently attached prosthetic group can denature a protein, but this ion was removed and restored with full recovery of function, so no permanent damage occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts upon; Mg++ here is a required helper for activity, not a consumed reactant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coenzymes are organic (carbon-containing) cofactors such as NADH and FADH2; Mg++ is an inorganic metal ion.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A dietary protein rich in a particular amino acid is ingested. In the acidic environment of the stomach, the side chain of this amino acid is protonated and carries no charge, yet the same side chain is nearly always negatively charged once the amino acid enters the blood or a cell. Which of the following amino acids has this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspartate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tryptophan

explanation.summary: Glutamate and aspartate carboxylic acid side chains are protonated and uncharged in the stomach but charged in blood and cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only glutamate and aspartate have negatively charged side chains, which are carboxylic acids. These can be protonated and uncharged in the stomach but are nearly always charged within the blood or within a cell. Aspartate is therefore the amino acid described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arginine, like lysine, stays protonated and positively charged in the stomach, blood, and cells; it never becomes negatively charged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysine has an amine side chain that is protonated and positively charged in the stomach and remains positively charged in the blood and cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serine has a neutral alcohol-containing side chain that is not charged in either the stomach or the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tryptophan has a nonpolar, neutral side chain and does not carry charge at any of these locations.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: Blood pH is normally maintained at approximately 7.35-7.45. Of the three amino acids with positively charged amine side chains, one is uniquely able to readily gain or lose a proton at this pH range and therefore acts as an effective physiological buffer. Which amino acid is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histidine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine

explanation.summary: Histidine's side-chain pKa lies near physiological pH, letting it buffer by readily gaining or losing a proton.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysine, arginine, and histidine have positively charged amine side chains and are all protonated in the stomach. Lysine and arginine side chain chemistry keeps them protonated and positively charged within the blood and cells. In contrast, histidine has a side-chain pKa near physiological pH, allowing it to readily gain or lose a proton and function as an effective buffer at bodily pH of around 7.35-7.45.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arginine, like lysine, stays protonated and positively charged at physiological pH and is not an effective buffer there.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate has a negatively charged carboxylic acid side chain, not an amine, and is nearly always charged in blood and cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysine remains protonated and positively charged in blood and cells, so it does not readily exchange protons at pH 7.4.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tyrosine has a neutral alcohol-containing side chain and is not one of the positively charged amino acids.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: The 20 proteogenic amino acids can be grouped by the chemical nature of the R-group into nonpolar neutral, polar neutral, and electrically charged side chains. Which of the following amino acids has a polar, neutral side chain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leucine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methionine

explanation.summary: Glutamine belongs to the polar, neutral group alongside serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine, and asparagine.
