explanation.whyCorrect: Grouped by the chemical nature of the R-group, the polar neutral side chains are serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine, asparagine, and glutamine. Glutamine's amide-containing side chain is polar but carries no charge, placing it in this category.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutamate is an electrically charged (acidic, negatively charged) amino acid, not a neutral one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leucine is grouped with the nonpolar, neutral side chains along with glycine, alanine, valine, and isoleucine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysine is an electrically charged (basic, positively charged) amino acid, not a neutral one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methionine's sulfur-containing side chain is classified as nonpolar and neutral, not polar.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A student learns that NADH and FADH2, the reduced molecules generated during energy metabolism, are required for many enzyme-catalyzed reactions and are carbon-based structures derived from B vitamins. Which of the following statements about how these molecules are classified is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are coenzymes, and every coenzyme is also a cofactor

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are coenzymes, and every cofactor is also a coenzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are inorganic cofactors, and every inorganic cofactor is also a coenzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are prosthetic groups, and every prosthetic group is also a coenzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are substrates, and every substrate is also a cofactor

explanation.summary: A coenzyme is an organic cofactor: all coenzymes are cofactors, but not all cofactors are coenzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: A coenzyme is an organic (carbon-containing) cofactor. It is a special type of cofactor, and the relationship is like saying all dalmatians (coenzymes) are dogs (cofactors) but not all dogs (cofactors) are dalmatians (coenzymes). The reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2 are excellent examples; these vitamin B derivatives are carbon-based and required to carry out enzyme-catalyzed metabolic reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The relationship runs one way: every coenzyme is a cofactor, but a cofactor such as Mg++ is not a coenzyme because it lacks carbon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADH and FADH2 contain carbon and are therefore organic, not inorganic cofactors; inorganic cofactors are metal ions like Zn++, Mg++, and Ca++.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A prosthetic group is a cofactor covalently linked to the protein (e.g., heme); NADH and FADH2 are not described as covalently attached, and prosthetic groups are not defined as coenzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These molecules are non-protein helpers required for enzyme activity, which is the definition of a cofactor, not of a substrate.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with a known genetic defect of the renal transporter for neutral amino acids has been lost to follow-up and receives no supplementation. She now presents with chronic diarrhea, a scaly dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, and new cognitive decline. Which of the following best explains the development of these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of lysine and arginine in the blood impairs collagen hydroxylation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of glutamate and aspartate in the urine disrupts ionic salt bridges in tissue proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of histidine in the urine eliminates buffering capacity of the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retention of neutral amino acids in the kidney leads to pathological protein aggregation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary loss of tryptophan depletes NAD+, producing pellagra

explanation.summary: Untreated Hartnup disease leads to pellagra because neutral amino acid loss depletes NAD+.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hartnup disease is caused by a genetic defect of a kidney transporter that reabsorbs neutral amino acids, so affected individuals lose too many neutral amino acids in the urine (hyperaminoaciduria). If left untreated, Hartnup disease leads to pellagra due to depletion of NAD+. Pellagra is characterized by the 4 D's: diarrhea, dementia, dermatitis, and eventually death if unresolved. Tryptophan, a neutral amino acid, is among those lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lysine and arginine are positively charged, not neutral, and the transporter defect causes urinary loss, not accumulation; collagen hydroxylation depends on vitamin C, not these amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate and aspartate are negatively charged and are not handled by the neutral amino acid transporter, so they are not lost in Hartnup disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histidine is positively charged, not neutral, and is not the amino acid wasted by this transporter defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is failure of reabsorption with loss in urine, not retention; protein aggregation is a feature of mechanical stress and misfolding, not of Hartnup disease.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: Myoglobin (Mb), when fully folded, contains 8 distinct alpha-helices arranged in three dimensions along a single protein chain with one N-terminus and one C-terminus. Which is the highest level of protein structure that myoglobin exhibits?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prosthetic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quaternary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tertiary

explanation.summary: Myoglobin is a monomer whose highest structural level is tertiary; it lacks quaternary structure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tertiary structure describes all the secondary structural elements that occur on a single polypeptide (one N- and one C-terminus). When Mb is fully folded it contains 8 distinct alpha-helices on a single protein chain. Quaternary structure requires multiple protein subunits (numerous N- and C-termini); Mb is a monomer and lacks quaternary structure, whereas Hb contains four distinct globin subunits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Primary structure is only the linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds from N- to C-terminus; myoglobin is folded well beyond this level.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A prosthetic group is a covalently bound cofactor such as heme, not a level of protein structure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Quaternary structure occurs when multiple subunits with numerous N- and C-termini interact; myoglobin is a monomer and lacks this level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary structure refers to individual alpha-helices or beta-pleated sheets, not to the arrangement of 8 helices together on one chain.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A secreted protein retains several covalent cross-links between distant parts of its single polypeptide chain even after the protein is heated enough to disrupt its hydrogen bonds and ionic salt bridges. Which of the following best describes how these cross-links are formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen bonding between two threonine hydroxyl groups

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ionic attraction between a lysine and a glutamate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidation of two cysteine residues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylation of two serine residues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient dipoles between two leucine residues

explanation.summary: Disulfide bonds are covalent S-S links formed when two cysteines are oxidized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the forces stabilizing tertiary structure, disulfide bonds are S-S covalent links formed when two cysteines are oxidized. Because they are covalent, they persist alongside the peptide backbone when heat disrupts the weaker forces such as hydrogen bonds, ionic salt bridges, and van der Waals interactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrogen bonds are specialized dipole-dipole interactions, not covalent bonds, and the stem states they were disrupted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An ionic salt bridge between positively and negatively charged side chains is a weak force that heat disrupts; the stem specifies these were lost.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group to a hydroxyl and is a signaling modification, not a covalent cross-link between two residues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transient, spontaneous dipoles describe van der Waals interactions, which are weak, noncovalent, and disrupted by heat.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A neuropathologist examines brain tissue from a patient who died of a prion disease. The prion protein normally has a physiological structure and function in the body, but in this patient it adopted an abnormal fold. Which of the following best explains why the misfolded prion is pathogenic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes an effective buffer that shifts intracellular pH

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes too stable to be destroyed by normal cellular turnover

choices.label: C
choices.text: It gains excessive flexibility and changes conformation without any energy input

choices.label: D
choices.text: It loses all covalent bonds and is rapidly hydrolyzed into free amino acids

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires a large energy investment to bind its heme prosthetic group

explanation.summary: Misfolded prions are 'bunker' proteins: excessively stable, they cannot be destroyed and cause disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteins need to change shape slightly, so their structure relies on a collection of weaker forces rather than an indestructible covalent 'bunker.' Proteins that are like bunkers are pathogenic. Prions, the causative agent of 'Mad Cow' disease, have a normal function and structure in the body, but when misfolded they become too stable and are unable to be destroyed, resulting in disease. There must be a mix of stability with adaptability in protein structure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Buffering at physiological pH is a property of histidine side chains, not the mechanism of prion pathogenicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Misfolded prions are pathogenic because they are too rigid and stable, the opposite of excessive flexibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The problem with misfolded prions is excessive stability and failure to be destroyed, not rapid hydrolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heme is the prosthetic group of hemoglobin; prion pathology is not described in terms of prosthetic group binding.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted with a body temperature of 41.5 C (106.7 F). Her physician is concerned that the very high temperature will cause loss of function of critical proteins. As kinetic energy increases within these proteins, which of the following interactions is most likely to remain intact?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disulfide bonds between oxidized cysteines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms of an alpha-helix

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between polar side chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ionic salt bridges between charged side chains

choices.label: E
choices.text: Van der Waals interactions between nonpolar side chains

explanation.summary: Heat disrupts the weaker forces of protein structure while covalent peptide backbone and disulfide bonds persist.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heat increases kinetic energy, which disrupts the weaker forces that stabilize protein structure. The stronger covalent forces such as the peptide backbone and disulfide bonds persist, but the weaker forces are sufficiently compromised at higher temperatures to cause a loss of function. This is one of the concerns of a very high body temperature.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrogen bonds stabilizing secondary structure are weak dipole-dipole interactions that heat readily disrupts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Side-chain hydrogen bonds, like backbone hydrogen bonds, are weak interactions that do not withstand high temperatures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ionic salt bridges are among the weaker, noncovalent forces of tertiary structure that are compromised by heat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Van der Waals interactions arise from transient dipoles and are weak forces easily disrupted by increased kinetic energy.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A researcher places a purified enzyme into a strongly alkaline buffer and observes complete loss of activity. Gel analysis shows the polypeptide is still full length, and no cysteines are present in the enzyme. Which of the following best explains the loss of activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alkaline conditions reduce disulfide bonds and unfold the tertiary structure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deprotonation of lysine and arginine side chains neutralizes their charge and disrupts ionic salt bridges

choices.label: C
choices.text: High pH removes the hydrogen from nonpolar side chains, abolishing van der Waals interactions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxide ions hydrolyze the peptide bonds that hold the primary structure together

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protonation of glutamate and aspartate side chains gives them a positive charge that repels one another

explanation.summary: pH changes alter only charged side chains, neutralizing one partner of an ionic salt bridge.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only the amino acids with charged side chains are altered by pH conditions. Changes in pH alter ionic salt bridges by neutralizing the charge on one of the amino acids involved in the interaction. Protonation of glutamate and aspartate or the deprotonation of histidine, arginine, and lysine will neutralize their respective charges to disrupt salt bridges. In an alkaline buffer, the positively charged lysine and arginine lose protons and their charge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states no cysteines are present, so disulfide bonds cannot be involved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonpolar side chains are uncharged and are not altered by pH; only charged side chains are affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The polypeptide is still full length; peptide bonds are covalent and require a protease, not a pH change, to be hydrolyzed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alkaline conditions deprotonate rather than protonate, and protonation of glutamate or aspartate would make them uncharged, not positively charged.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has taken a medication for several years that markedly raises the pH of his stomach. He now has laboratory evidence of vitamin B12 deficiency despite a diet rich in animal protein. Which of the following best explains the impaired absorption of nutrients contained within his dietary protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of the acidic environment allows lysosomal enzymes to degrade dietary proteins before they can be absorbed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the acidic environment leaves dietary proteins undenatured, so digestive proteases cannot access the peptide

choices.label: C
choices.text: The higher pH chelates the Ca++ cofactor that digestive proteases require, leaving them present but inactive

choices.label: D
choices.text: The higher pH deprotonates histidine residues on dietary proteins, causing them to form insoluble aggregates

choices.label: E
choices.text: The higher pH hydrolyzes dietary proteins into free amino acids before they reach the small intestine

explanation.summary: Stomach acid denatures dietary protein so proteases can reach the peptide; raising gastric pH impairs nutrient absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Select denaturation of proteins is warranted. A high protein meal is only beneficial if the amino acids can be absorbed from the dietary tract, which requires the protein to be denatured so that the peptide is readily accessible by digestive proteases. This is one of the purposes of the acidic environment of the stomach. Increasing the pH milieu of the stomach can prevent proper absorption of nutrients contained within dietary protein sources, such as amino acids and vitamin B12.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lysosome is an intracellular organelle for internalized proteins and does not act on dietary protein in the gut lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ca++ is the cofactor discussed for the blood coagulation cascade, and pH changes do not chelate metal ions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The problem is a failure to denature dietary proteins, not aggregation of them; aggregation is described with mechanical stress and misfolding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: pH changes disrupt weak forces but do not hydrolyze covalent peptide bonds; proteases are required for that.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol consumption develops multiple vitamin deficiencies despite an adequate diet. Which of the following best explains how alcohol impairs vitamin absorption in the digestive tract?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol acts as a protease, hydrolyzing the peptide backbone of intestinal transport proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol chelates the metal ion cofactors that intestinal transport proteins require for uptake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol forms a micelle-like sphere that traps hydrophobic vitamins away from the absorptive surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alcohol hydroxyl groups hydrogen bond with protein side chains, denaturing proteins required for absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alcohol lowers the intestinal pH, protonating the glutamate and aspartate side chains of transport proteins

explanation.summary: Organic solvents such as alcohol denature digestive-tract proteins through hydrogen bonding by their hydroxyl groups.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lifestyle choices or accidental chemical exposures to organic solvents can have detrimental effects on protein structure. Chronic consumption of alcohol adversely impacts vitamin absorption because the hydroxyl groups (-OH) can hydrogen bond with select protein side chains and denature proteins in the digestive tract that are required for absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only hydrolytic enzymes (proteases) can cleave the covalent peptide backbone; alcohol disrupts weak forces instead.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metal chelation is the mechanism of agents like EDTA and EGTA, not of alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Forming a sphere with a polar head group and hydrophobic core describes detergents (soap), not alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alcohol acts as an organic solvent through hydrogen bonding, not by altering pH to protonate acidic side chains.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A hospital infection-control program emphasizes handwashing with soap as an effective preventive measure against the spread of viruses and bacteria. Which of the following best explains why soap is effective against these pathogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its acidic pH protonates pathogen surface proteins, neutralizing their charge and their function

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its chelating groups sequester the Ca++ that pathogen surface enzymes require for activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its heat of dissolution raises kinetic energy and disrupts the hydrogen bonds within pathogen proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its hydroxyl groups hydrogen bond with the pathogen's side chains and then cleave their peptide bonds outright

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its polar charged end and hydrophobic portion denature pathogen proteins while allowing removal with water

explanation.summary: Detergents have a dual polar/hydrophobic nature that denatures pathogen proteins and washes them away with water.
explanation.whyCorrect: Detergents have a dual nature: a very polar, charged end and a hydrophobic portion. The soap can form a sphere with a polar head group that interacts with water while the core is hydrophobic to trap components like body oil. This is why handwashing is an effective preventive measure: the soap can denature the proteins of pathogens to prevent infection while also allowing their removal with water.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Soap's action depends on its dual polar/hydrophobic structure, not on an acidic pH altering charged side chains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chelation of Ca++ is the mechanism of EDTA and EGTA in blood collection tubes, not of soap.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heat disrupts weak forces by increasing kinetic energy, but soap works through its detergent structure, not by generating heat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrogen bonding by hydroxyl groups describes organic solvents like alcohol, and no denaturing agent cleaves covalent peptide bonds; that requires a protease.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 55-year-old retired professional boxer dies after years of progressive cognitive decline. Autopsy of his brain reveals abundant insoluble protein aggregates consistent with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Which of the following agents or conditions is most directly responsible for the protein misfolding underlying this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detergent exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extreme pH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heat

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mechanical stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: Organic solvent exposure

explanation.summary: Repeated physical trauma (mechanical stress) promotes protein misfolding and aggregation in CTE.
explanation.whyCorrect: Weak forces are unable to be maintained upon physical agitation. A high-profile example is the identification of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in brains of athletes like boxers or NFL players. Repeated physical trauma can promote protein misfolding, aggregation, and impaired clearance, contributing to pathological protein accumulation. Denatured proteins often form insoluble aggregates, a common histological finding in the brain tissue of individuals with CTE.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Detergents disrupt proteins through their dual polar/hydrophobic nature and are not implicated in CTE.
whyWrongByChoice.B: pH changes alter charged side chains and salt bridges but are not the mechanism of trauma-related protein aggregation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heat denatures proteins by increasing kinetic energy, as in very high body temperature, but is not the cause of CTE in athletes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Organic solvents such as alcohol denature proteins via hydrogen bonding of hydroxyl groups, which is unrelated to repetitive head trauma.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A glycoprotein is analyzed and found to carry a carbohydrate chain attached through the oxygen atom of an amino acid side-chain hydroxyl group. Which of the following amino acids could serve as the attachment site for this modification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asparagine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Threonine

explanation.summary: O-linked glycosylation requires a hydroxyl group, so serine, threonine, and tyrosine are its targets.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two main forms of glycosylation are O-linked and N-linked, named for the atom to which the sugar moiety is covalently linked. Much like phosphorylation, a hydroxyl (-OH) group is required for O-linked glycosylation, so serine, threonine, and tyrosine contain such modifications. Threonine's alcohol-containing side chain provides the oxygen for this linkage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asparagine is the only amino acid targeted for N-linked glycosylation, where the sugar attaches to nitrogen rather than to a hydroxyl oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate has a carboxylic acid side chain and lacks the hydroxyl group required for O-linked glycosylation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysine's side chain contains an amine that is the attachment site for ubiquitin, not a hydroxyl for O-linked sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proline is hydroxylated in collagen, but it is not described as an O-linked glycosylation target; the targets are serine, threonine, and tyrosine.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A polyubiquitinated cytosolic protein is unfolded in an ATP-dependent manner, translocated into the catalytic core of the proteasome, and hydrolyzed. Which of the following best describes the fate of the ubiquitin molecules and the substrate protein after this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both ubiquitin and the substrate are hydrolyzed into free amino acids inside the catalytic core

choices.label: B
choices.text: The substrate is reduced to small peptides that supply amino acids, while ubiquitin is recycled

choices.label: C
choices.text: The substrate is released intact while ubiquitin is degraded to supply amino acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ubiquitin is trafficked to the lysosome while the substrate is exported intact from the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ubiquitin remains covalently bound to the small peptides that are released

explanation.summary: The proteasome hydrolyzes the tagged protein into small peptides for biosynthesis while ubiquitin is recycled.
explanation.whyCorrect: Polyubiquitination tags and traffics the protein to the proteasome, a multi-subunit complex that uses ATP-dependent unfolding to denature and translocate ubiquitinated proteins into its catalytic core, which hydrolyzes the protein. Small peptides are produced that can provide amino acids for biosynthesis, while the ubiquitin is recycled.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ubiquitin is not consumed; it is recycled after the substrate is degraded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is the tagged substrate, not ubiquitin, that is hydrolyzed into small peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ubiquitin-proteasome pathway handles intracellular cytosolic proteins and does not route ubiquitin to the lysosome or export the substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitin is released and reused rather than staying attached to the peptide products.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A cell biologist is tracing the degradation of several different molecules within a fibroblast. Which of the following would be expected to be degraded by lysosomal turnover rather than by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cytosolic pro-apoptotic protein degraded by a multiple myeloma cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cytosolic protein that has been unfolded in an ATP-dependent manner

choices.label: C
choices.text: A damaged cytosolic signaling enzyme tagged with a chain of ubiquitin

choices.label: D
choices.text: A misfolded cytosolic protein that has been polyubiquitinated on a lysine

choices.label: E
choices.text: An extracellular matrix glycosaminoglycan internalized by the cell

explanation.summary: Lysosomes degrade internalized extracellular material, including proteins, lipids, and glycosaminoglycans; the proteasome handles cytosolic proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysosomal protein turnover is typically used for extracellular proteins that are internalized. The lysosome is a single lipid bilayer organelle with an acidic interior (pH 4.5-5.0) whose lysosomal-specific enzymes are activated within the acidic environment to degrade biomolecules including proteins, lipids, and glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides), the long unbranched polysaccharides of the matrix and connective tissue. Autophagy also delivers whole organelles such as mitochondria to the lysosome. In contrast, the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway degrades and recycles intracellular cytosolic proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Multiple myeloma cells rapidly ubiquitinate and degrade pro-apoptotic proteins through the proteasome, which is why bortezomib is effective.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ATP-dependent unfolding is the mechanism the proteasome uses to translocate ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins into its catalytic core.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ubiquitin-tagged cytosolic enzyme is trafficked to the proteasome, not the lysosome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyubiquitination on lysine is the signal that directs a cytosolic protein to the proteasome.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with a severely restricted diet develops bleeding gums, easy bruising, and joint pain. His prolyl hydroxylase is present and properly folded but lacks the small organic, carbon-containing molecule it requires to hydroxylate proline within collagen. Which of the following most precisely classifies this missing molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoenzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coenzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inorganic cofactor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prosthetic group

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substrate

explanation.summary: Vitamin C is an organic cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, which makes it a coenzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is required for the function of prolyl hydroxylase, the enzyme that post-translationally modifies collagen for tissue integrity. In scurvy, nothing is inherently wrong with the enzyme; it just requires a nonprotein component for function. Such factors are broadly known as cofactors, and because vitamin C is organic in nature (contains carbon), it is also accurately classified as a coenzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The apoenzyme is the protein portion lacking its cofactor, which here is the intact prolyl hydroxylase itself, not the missing molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inorganic cofactors lack carbon (e.g., Zn++, Mg++, Ca++); vitamin C is a carbon-based organic molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A prosthetic group is covalently linked to the protein and its removal often denatures the enzyme; in scurvy the enzyme remains properly folded, so vitamin C is not a prosthetic group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The substrate is proline within collagen, the molecule the enzyme acts upon, not the required helper molecule.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a fasting glucometer reading within her target range on the morning of her clinic visit, yet her HbA1c is markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains why these two measurements can disagree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HbA1c forms by equilibrium-driven glycation over the RBC's roughly 120-day lifespan, reflecting the preceding 3 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbA1c is a phosphorylated form of Hb whose level depends on the patient's insulin signaling that day

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbA1c is produced enzymatically only during periods of hyperglycemia and is cleared within hours of normalization

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbA1c measures glucose bound to plasma albumin, which turns over within 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbA1c reflects glucose taken up by hepatocytes, which have a lifespan of about 3 months

explanation.summary: HbA1c is a non-enzymatic glycated Hb whose level tracks glucose exposure across the ~120-day RBC lifespan.
explanation.whyCorrect: Post-translational modification is used for diagnostic purposes. Unlike a glucometer, which is a current snapshot of blood glucose, HbA1c is a specific glycated form of Hb. This modification is driven by equilibrium and not enzymatic activity: the more glucose an RBC is exposed to, the more HbA1c is produced. Because an RBC has a functional lifespan of about 120 days, an HbA1c measurement reflects glucose management over the preceding 3 months, so a single normal morning glucose does not lower it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HbA1c is a glycated (sugar-modified) form of Hb, not a phosphorylated one, and its level does not depend on a single day's signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbA1c formation is driven by equilibrium, not enzymatic activity, and it persists for the life of the RBC rather than clearing within hours.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbA1c is a modification of hemoglobin within RBCs, not of plasma albumin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 3-month window derives from the ~120-day lifespan of the RBC carrying the glycated Hb, not from hepatocytes.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A research fellow finds that contaminating nucleases are degrading DNA samples. A lab mate suggests storing the DNA in a Tris-EDTA solution. After switching, the DNA remains well preserved even though the nucleases are still present in the sample. Which of the following best explains why the DNA is protected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: EDTA acts as a detergent that denatures the nucleases through hydrophobic interactions

choices.label: B
choices.text: EDTA covalently binds the DNA backbone, blocking nuclease access to the substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: EDTA hydrolyzes the peptide bonds of the nucleases, destroying their primary structure

choices.label: D
choices.text: EDTA lowers the solution pH, protonating glutamate residues in the nuclease active site

choices.label: E
choices.text: EDTA sequesters the Zn++ cofactor the nucleases require, leaving the enzymes present but inactive

explanation.summary: Nucleases require a Zn++ cofactor; EDTA chelates the metal so the intact enzyme cannot function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The success of the experiment depends on the fact that the contaminating nucleases require a Zn++ cofactor. Metal ions like Zn++ are inorganic cofactors that can easily be removed by agents to prevent protein activity. EDTA is a metal chelator that binds and coordinates positively charged metals; the contaminating enzyme is still present, but its function is inhibited when Zn++ is sequestered by EDTA, preserving the DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Detergents have a dual polar/hydrophobic nature; EDTA is a metal chelator, not a detergent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EDTA coordinates metal ions; it does not covalently modify DNA to shield it from enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only a protease can hydrolyze peptide bonds; EDTA is a chelator and does not destroy primary structure, which is consistent with the enzymes still being present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: EDTA's protective effect comes from chelating metal cofactors, not from altering the pH of the solution.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I

questions.stem: A newborn develops a hemolytic crisis in the first days of life and is found to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On a later rotation, an otherwise healthy 53-year-old man is diagnosed with the exact same enzyme deficiency, yet this is his first-ever hemolytic episode. Which of the following best explains the difference in age at initial presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G6PD enzyme activity naturally increases with age, protecting older patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced glutathione is only required in neonatal red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The adult's red blood cells contain mitochondria that compensate for the defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: The older adult acquired the deficiency later in life rather than inheriting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: The two patients carry different G6PD variants that differ in residual enzyme activity

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency is a spectrum disorder whose severity depends on which of the many variants a patient carries.
explanation.whyCorrect: Over 200 pathogenic G6PD variants (and 400+ variant enzymes) are described, and the disease occurs along a spectrum of severity. Some variants cause hemolysis within days of birth, while others may never cause a crisis unless the right oxidative stressor is introduced. The age of presentation is entirely dependent on the specific mutation and how it impacts enzyme function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme activity does not rise with age; residual activity is set by the inherited variant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced glutathione is required throughout life in all red blood cells, not only in neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mature red blood cells lack mitochondria entirely, which is precisely why they depend on pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G6PD deficiency is an inherited X-linked disorder present from birth, not something acquired in adulthood.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department with abnormally dark urine after starting a sulfa drug for a urinary tract infection. Blood work shows a low hematocrit with an increased reticulocyte count, indicating hemolytic anemia. This patient's condition is most likely due to failure of which of the following functions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degradation of lysosomal cargo

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutralizing oxidative agents

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of the amino acid cysteine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proper elastin formation

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency prevents NADPH production, so red blood cells cannot regenerate reduced glutathione to neutralize oxidative agents.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sulfa drug is a classic oxidative stressor that triggers hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Without G6PD, red cells cannot make NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway, so they cannot reduce glutathione and neutralize accumulating oxidizing species, leading to red-cell destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure to degrade lysosomal cargo describes lysosomal storage disorders such as Hurler or I-cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxidative phosphorylation would be reduced by anemia, but a decrease in ATP production is not what causes the hemolysis here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired cysteine production reflects cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency (homocystinuria), not G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective elastin formation is the problem in Marfan syndrome, not a cause of hemolytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy of Mediterranean descent develops jaundice and dark urine one day after eating fava beans. A peripheral blood smear shows red cells with membrane "bites" removed and inclusions of denatured hemoglobin. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrillin-1 of connective tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic cystathionine beta-synthase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lysosomal alpha-L-iduronidase

explanation.summary: Favism with Heinz bodies and bite cells is the classic picture of G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fava beans are a well-known oxidative trigger in G6PD deficiency, which is common in individuals of Mediterranean heritage. The inclusions of oxidatively denatured hemoglobin are Heinz bodies, and the bite cells form when macrophages remove those Heinz-body regions from the red cell membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrillin-1 is defective in Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria, presenting with thrombosis and lens dislocation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU, presenting with a mousy odor and developmental delay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome, a lysosomal storage disorder, not acute hemolysis.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have a musty, mousy body odor. Over the following months the infant develops progressive developmental delay and unusually fair skin and hair. Which of the following enzymatic conversions is most likely impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of homocysteine to cysteine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degradation of glycosaminoglycans

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of neutrophil elastase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regeneration of reduced glutathione

explanation.summary: Classic PKU results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, which normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine.
explanation.whyCorrect: In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates to neurotoxic levels (causing developmental delay) and generates metabolites that produce a mousy odor. Because melanin synthesis requires tyrosine, affected patients are typically fair-complected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Impaired conversion of homocysteine to cysteine occurs in homocystinuria, which does not cause a mousy odor or fair skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure to degrade glycosaminoglycans describes Hurler syndrome, a lysosomal storage disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of neutrophil elastase inhibition describes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and its lung disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure to regenerate reduced glutathione describes G6PD deficiency and its hemolytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A child with a milder form of phenylketonuria (PKU) shows partial clinical improvement when supplemented with a specific organic cofactor used by phenylalanine hydroxylase. Which of the following is this cofactor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cobalamin

choices.label: B
choices.text: FAD

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADPH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin

explanation.summary: Phenylalanine hydroxylase uses tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), and some milder PKU variants respond to BH4 supplementation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylalanine hydroxylase uses the GTP-derived organic cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) to hydroxylate phenylalanine to tyrosine. When a variant enzyme binds its cofactor poorly, raising cofactor concentration can drive binding and partially restore function, which is why some milder PKU forms are BH4-responsive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cobalamin (B12) participates in homocysteine remethylation, not phenylalanine hydroxylation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FAD (from vitamin B2) serves glutathione reductase, not phenylalanine hydroxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADPH is produced by the pentose phosphate pathway and used to reduce glutathione, not by phenylalanine hydroxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) is the cofactor for cystathionine beta-synthase in homocystinuria, not for phenylalanine hydroxylase.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has coarse facial features, joint stiffness, developmental delay, and increased urinary mucopolysaccharides. Enzyme testing reveals deficient alpha-L-iduronidase, confirming Hurler syndrome. Which of the following features would best distinguish this disorder from Hunter syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presence of coarse facial features

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presence of corneal clouding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progressive developmental delay

explanation.summary: Corneal clouding is present in Hurler but absent in Hunter syndrome, making it a key distinguishing feature.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hurler and Hunter syndromes both accumulate heparan and dermatan sulfate and share many features, but Hunter syndrome is distinct in that there is no corneal clouding, it is X-linked, it includes aggressive behavior, and it is due to iduronate sulfatase deficiency. The presence of corneal clouding therefore points to Hurler.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfate is shared by both Hurler and Hunter syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both disorders result from deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme, so this is not distinguishing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coarse facial features occur in both disorders and cannot distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progressive developmental delay is a shared manifestation of both syndromes.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An infant has severe developmental delay, coarse facial features, and failure to thrive. Cultured fibroblasts contain dense intracellular inclusion bodies. Laboratory testing shows markedly ELEVATED lysosomal hydrolase levels in the plasma with normal urinary mucopolysaccharides. Which of the following processes is defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of the mannose-6-phosphate tag

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degradation of glycosaminoglycans by alpha-L-iduronidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxylation of phenylalanine to tyrosine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multimerization of tropoelastin into elastin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction of oxidized glutathione

explanation.summary: I-cell disease results from defective GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, which fails to add mannose-6-phosphate, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of delivered to lysosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In I-cell disease, GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase cannot form mannose-6-phosphate on lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi. Without this tag, trans-Golgi receptors cannot route the hydrolases to lysosomes, so the enzymes spill into the circulation (elevated plasma levels) while undegraded material accumulates as dense inclusion bodies. Urinary mucopolysaccharides are not increased, unlike in Hurler syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Deficient alpha-L-iduronidase causes Hurler syndrome, which raises urinary mucopolysaccharides and affects only one enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective phenylalanine hydroxylation causes PKU, not a lysosomal trafficking disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective tropoelastin multimerization reflects fibrillin-1 dysfunction in Marfan syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure to reduce glutathione causes G6PD-related hemolytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A tall, thin 17-year-old has long fingers with positive thumb and wrist signs and is found to have upward-and-outward dislocation of the ocular lens along with aortic root dilation. Which of the following genes is most likely mutated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FBN1

choices.label: B
choices.text: G6PD

choices.label: C
choices.text: IDUA

choices.label: D
choices.text: PAH

choices.label: E
choices.text: SERPINA1

explanation.summary: Marfan syndrome arises from mutation of the fibrillin-1 gene, FBN1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tall stature, arachnodactyly (positive thumb and wrist signs), upward-and-outward lens dislocation, and aortic root dilation are classic for Marfan syndrome. Marfan arises from an autosomal dominant mutation of FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1, the scaffold protein for elastin in connective tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: G6PD mutations cause hemolytic anemia, not a connective tissue phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IDUA mutations cause Hurler syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PAH mutations cause PKU.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SERPINA1 mutations cause alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with lung and liver disease.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: In Marfan syndrome, mutation of fibrillin-1 produces a defective elastin scaffold in connective tissue. Which of the following secondary molecular changes is chiefly responsible for the aortic pathology seen in these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of homocysteine in the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased transforming growth factor beta activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin within red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity in the lung

explanation.summary: In Marfan syndrome, FBN1 mutation secondarily increases TGF-beta activity, which drives the aortic pathology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond producing defective elastin, the FBN1 mutation secondarily increases the levels and activity of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta), a signaling protein. Abnormal TGF-beta activation is what primarily drives the aortic dissection and aneurysm risk associated with Marfan syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulation of homocysteine is the mechanism in homocystinuria, a biochemically distinct disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of mannose-6-phosphate tagging is the defect in I-cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin occurs in G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity underlies alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought in for a decline in her speaking ability. She has intellectual delay, long thin extremities, and vision problems from a downward-and-inward dislocation of the ocular lens. Which of the following proteins is most likely defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-L-iduronidase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrillin-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase

explanation.summary: Homocystinuria, most commonly from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, presents with intellectual disability, marfanoid habitus, and downward-and-inward lens dislocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of intellectual disability, marfanoid long limbs, and a down-and-in (inferonasal) lens dislocation is characteristic of homocystinuria. The most common enzyme deficiency causing homocystinuria is cystathionine beta-synthase, which normally consumes homocysteine to make cysteine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome, presenting in infancy with coarse features and corneal clouding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, in which the lens dislocates up and out and intellect is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, not lens dislocation and intellectual disability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU, which does not feature lens dislocation.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria share several clinical features despite having unrelated biochemical causes. Which of the following findings points specifically to homocystinuria rather than Marfan syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adverse cardiovascular events

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired vision from lens dislocation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intellectual disability

choices.label: E
choices.text: Long limbs and appendages

explanation.summary: Intellectual disability and thrombotic risk are specific to homocystinuria, whereas long limbs, vision problems, and cardiovascular events are shared with Marfan syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria share long appendages, impaired vision, and adverse cardiovascular events. Homocystinuria is distinguished by intellectual disability (when untreated) and a high risk of thrombosis leading to early myocardial infarction or stroke, features not seen in Marfan syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adverse cardiovascular events occur in both conditions and therefore do not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance describes Marfan syndrome, not homocystinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired vision from lens dislocation occurs in both, differing only in the direction of dislocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Long limbs and appendages (marfanoid habitus) are a shared feature of both disorders.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a minimal smoking history has early-onset emphysema affecting the lower lobes of the lungs. He is also found to have cirrhosis with elevated liver enzymes. Genetic testing reveals that he is homozygous for the Z allele (Glu342Lys) of the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene. Which of the following best explains his liver involvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of AAT protein production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycosaminoglycans accumulate within hepatic lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homocysteine accumulation causes hepatic vein thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Misfolded AAT accumulates in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutrophil elastase digests the hepatic extracellular matrix

explanation.summary: The Z allele produces a misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin that accumulates in the hepatocyte ER, causing cellular stress and liver disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Z allele replaces a glutamate with lysine (Glu342Lys), a nonconservative change that causes AAT to misfold within the liver endoplasmic reticulum. This misfolded protein induces cellular stress and hepatocyte death, producing cirrhosis, elevated liver enzymes, decreased protein production, and increased hepatic cancer risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rarer null variants make minimal or no AAT and, lacking misfolding stress, spare the liver while still causing lung disease; this patient's Z allele does produce protein that misfolds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycosaminoglycan accumulation in lysosomes describes Hurler syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homocysteine-related thrombosis is a feature of homocystinuria, not AAT deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil elastase drives the lung disease by degrading the alveolar extracellular matrix, not the liver pathology.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemist is characterizing the tripeptide that promotes and maintains oxidative/reductive balance within red blood cells. She notes that the molecule cycles between a reduced (GSH) and an oxidized (GSSG) form. Which of the following amino acid residues of this tripeptide is responsible for allowing it to cycle between these two forms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cysteine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histidine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methionine

explanation.summary: The cysteine residue of glutathione allows it to cycle between reduced (GSH) and oxidized (GSSG) forms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. It is the cysteine residue that allows glutathione to cycle between the reduced (GSH) and oxidized (GSSG) forms, and this cycling is critical for cellular redox balance. In G6PD deficiency, the lack of NADPH prevents regeneration of the reduced form.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate is one of the three residues of glutathione, but it is not the residue responsible for redox cycling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycine is one of the three residues of glutathione, but it does not participate in the reduced/oxidized cycling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histidine is not a component of the glutathione tripeptide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methionine is not a component of glutathione; it is the product formed when homocysteine is remethylated.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with chronic liver disease has laboratory testing that reveals a markedly increased ratio of oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to reduced glutathione (GSH) in his cells. An enzymatic assay confirms normal glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity. Which of the following best interprets these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Additional oxidative stress from his hepatic disease is outpacing the reduction of glutathione

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutathione reductase is inactive because of an underlying riboflavin deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: He carries a mild G6PD variant that the enzymatic assay failed to detect

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADPH production from the pentose phosphate pathway is completely blocked in his cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total glutathione abundance is reduced because hepatic synthesis of the tripeptide has failed

explanation.summary: The GSSG/GSH ratio is an index of cellular oxidative stress that can be elevated by conditions such as cancer or liver disease even when G6PD is fully functional.
explanation.whyCorrect: The relative abundance of GSSG and GSH can be measured clinically and serves as an index of cellular oxidative stress. An inability to reduce glutathione, as in G6PD deficiency, causes GSSG to accumulate, but other imbalances occur when additional oxidative stress is produced, such as in cancer or liver disease, even when G6PD is functional. With a normal G6PD assay, the liver disease itself is the source of the oxidative burden.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nothing indicates riboflavin deficiency, and even in ariboflavinosis the glutathione reductase pathway is not really compromised.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The assay confirms normal enzyme activity; the elevated ratio is explained by his liver disease rather than an occult variant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normal G6PD assay indicates NADPH production from the pentose phosphate pathway is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The abnormality is in the form of glutathione (oxidized versus reduced), not its total abundance.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase is expressed in a wide array of tissues because the pentose phosphate pathway is required by many cell types. Nevertheless, a patient with G6PD deficiency experiences hemolysis without clinically evident dysfunction of hepatocytes or skeletal muscle. Which of the following best explains why red blood cells are uniquely affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are exposed to far higher concentrations of circulating oxidizing agents than any other cell type

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cannot obtain glucose 6-phosphate from glycolysis to supply the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: They lack glutathione altogether and therefore rely solely on NADPH to neutralize oxidizing agents

choices.label: D
choices.text: They rely on a red cell-specific G6PD isoform and, lacking mitochondria, depend entirely on PPP-derived NADPH

choices.label: E
choices.text: They survive longer than other cells, allowing oxidative damage to accumulate before repair occurs

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency affects red blood cells because they express a specific G6PD isoform and, lacking mitochondria, depend entirely on pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although G6PD is expressed widely, the disease is caused by a lack of a specific isoform of G6PD expressed in RBCs. In addition, RBCs are uniquely affected because they lack mitochondria and depend entirely on PPP-derived NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione and neutralize oxidizing agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vulnerability lies in the red cell's inability to regenerate NADPH, not in a greater exposure to oxidants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pentose phosphate pathway obtains its substrates from glycolysis in red cells; that supply is not the defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red blood cells contain glutathione; the problem is generating the reduced form, not a lack of the tripeptide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell longevity is not the explanation given; the lack of mitochondria and isoform-specific deficiency are.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is found to have a normocytic anemia. An assay of red-cell glutathione reductase activity establishes a diagnosis of ariboflavinosis (vitamin B2 deficiency). A colleague suggests that her anemia, like that of G6PD deficiency, results from a failure to neutralize oxidizing agents within red blood cells. Which of the following best explains the actual cause of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A secondary effect of riboflavin deficiency impedes the absorption of iron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the FAD-dependent step diverts glucose 6-phosphate away from the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADPH production is blocked because glutathione reductase cannot regenerate NADP+

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidized glutathione accumulates and produces Heinz bodies that trigger hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced glutathione is degraded because its cysteine residue cannot be maintained

explanation.summary: In ariboflavinosis the glutathione reductase assay is only diagnostic; the pathway is not really compromised, and the normocytic anemia is due to a secondary effect that impedes iron absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The FAD-requiring glutathione reductase is used to diagnose riboflavin deficiency, but the pathway itself is not really compromised and the enzyme remains functional. The normocytic anemia that results with ariboflavinosis is instead due to a secondary effect that impedes iron absorption, which is entirely different from the hemolytic mechanism of G6PD deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 6-phosphate is not diverted; the redox pathway remains functional in ariboflavinosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In ariboflavinosis the enzyme is functional and the pathway is not really compromised, so NADPH production is not blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heinz body formation and hemolysis characterize G6PD deficiency, not the anemia of riboflavin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cysteine residue and glutathione itself are not degraded; the pathway is intact and the anemia arises from impaired iron absorption.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with known G6PD deficiency develops hemolysis after an infection. On the peripheral smear, in addition to classic bite cells, the pathologist also notes blister cells. Which of the following best describes how these blister cells form?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A macrophage attempts to remove a Heinz body but fails to remove the full membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bilirubin deposits within the membrane cause it to separate from the cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heinz bodies precipitate directly beneath an intact, undamaged membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidized hemoglobin polymerizes and deforms the cell into a rigid shape

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retained RNA remnants push the membrane outward as the cell matures

explanation.summary: Blister cells arise by the same phagocytic phenomenon as bite cells, but the macrophage fails to remove the full membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: As Heinz bodies form, they are perceived as non-self, prompting phagocytic macrophages to selectively remove chunks of membrane and cytoplasm, producing bite cells. The same phenomenon can cause blister cells, in which the full membrane fails to be removed by the macrophage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilirubin is released after hemolysis and accounts for jaundice, not for membrane blistering.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heinz bodies are oxidatively damaged Hb aggregates, but the blister results from macrophage action on the membrane, not from precipitation alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polymerization of oxidized hemoglobin into a rigid shape is not the mechanism described for blister cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA remnants are a feature of reticulocytes and do not produce blister cells.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with G6PD deficiency develops yellowing of the whites of his eyes two days after a febrile illness. Which of the following properties of the accumulating molecule best accounts for the yellow discoloration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conjugated ring system with alternating double and single bonds that absorbs light

choices.label: B
choices.text: A heme-iron complex that reflects yellow wavelengths once the iron is oxidized

choices.label: C
choices.text: A porphyrin ring that remains bound to globin and fluoresces in daylight

choices.label: D
choices.text: A water-soluble pigment that deposits selectively within scleral collagen fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: An insoluble aggregate of oxidatively denatured hemoglobin deposited in the sclera

explanation.summary: Bilirubin is a conjugated ring system that absorbs light, so its accumulation turns the skin and sclerae yellow (scleral icterus).
explanation.whyCorrect: Fragile red cells lyse and release abnormal amounts of porphyrin from hemoglobin, leading to abnormal levels of bilirubin. Bilirubin is a conjugated ring system, a cyclic structure with alternating double and single bonds, that absorbs light, so the patient's skin or the whites of the eyes may appear yellow (scleral icterus).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The yellow color arises from light absorption by the conjugated ring of bilirubin, not from an iron complex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The porphyrin released from hemoglobin gives rise to bilirubin; it is not a globin-bound fluorescent pigment that colors the eye.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The discoloration is explained by bilirubin's light-absorbing ring structure, not by selective deposition in collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insoluble aggregates of denatured hemoglobin are Heinz bodies, which are found within red blood cells, not in the sclera.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Three days after a hemolytic episode, a 30-year-old woman has a reticulocyte percentage well above normal as her bone marrow attempts to recover the loss of red blood cells. Which of the following characteristics distinguishes the cells being counted from mature red blood cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are released from the marrow only after blood loss, never after hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: They contain Heinz bodies that mature red cells lack

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain mitochondria that mature red cells lack

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contain remnants of RNA that mature red cells lack

choices.label: E
choices.text: They require 1-2 weeks in circulation to fully mature

explanation.summary: Reticulocytes are newly formed immature blood cells that still contain remnants of RNA, which mature red blood cells lack.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reticulocytes are newly formed immature blood cells released into circulation that fully mature within 1-2 days. They still contain remnants of RNA that mature RBCs lack. After a hemolytic event, their number or percent increases as the bone marrow attempts to recover the loss of RBCs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reticulocyte count rises after hemolysis; general blood loss is another factor that can also increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heinz bodies are oxidatively damaged hemoglobin aggregates seen in G6PD deficiency, not a defining feature of reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red blood cells lack mitochondria; the distinguishing feature of reticulocytes is retained RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reticulocytes fully mature within 1-2 days, not weeks.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical student notes that many newly identified G6PD variants are named after geographic regions, such as G6PD Mediterranean. G6PD deficiency is commonly associated with genetic heritages from regions where which of the following is endemic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatitis B

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iodine deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Malaria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Riboflavin deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tuberculosis

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked disease commonly associated with heritages from malaria-endemic regions.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and is commonly associated with genetic heritages from regions where malaria is endemic, such as Asia (especially Southeast Asia), the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Africa. As new variants are identified they are often named after the geographic region, for example G6PD Mediterranean.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis B is not the endemic disease associated with G6PD deficiency heritage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iodine deficiency is not the endemic condition linked to the distribution of G6PD variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency is diagnosed with a glutathione reductase assay but has no link to the geographic distribution of G6PD variants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculosis is not associated with the geographic distribution of G6PD deficiency.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency shows a marked fall in plasma homocysteine after starting high-dose pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Which of the following best explains why supplementation restores partial enzyme function in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pyridoxine directly donates a methyl group to homocysteine, bypassing the defective enzyme entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pyridoxine induces increased transcription of the mutant gene, raising total enzyme abundance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyridoxine is converted into tetrahydrobiopterin, replacing the organic cofactor the enzyme lacks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxine prevents the variant enzyme from misfolding and being degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raising the coenzyme concentration drives binding to a variant enzyme with reduced coenzyme affinity

explanation.summary: When a variant enzyme binds its coenzyme with reduced affinity, supplementing the coenzyme drives the equilibrium toward binding and partially restores function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cystathionine beta-synthase uses a modified form of vitamin B6, pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). If an enzyme's sequence is altered so that it fails to bind its required coenzyme with the required affinity, supplementing the coenzyme increases its concentration, driving the equilibrium to favor coenzyme binding and partially restoring function. This strategy aids roughly 25% of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency cases, much like BH4 supplementation for select PKU variants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methyl donation to homocysteine occurs via methyl-B12 in the remethylation pathway, not via pyridoxine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The rescue works by favoring coenzyme binding to the existing variant enzyme, not by increasing gene transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tetrahydrobiopterin is the GTP-derived cofactor of phenylalanine hydroxylase; cystathionine beta-synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Misfolding and ER stress describe the Z allele of alpha-1 antitrypsin, not the mechanism of B6-responsive homocystinuria.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is started on pyridoxine. His physician also prescribes folate and cobalamin even though he has no dietary deficiency of either vitamin. Which of the following is the most likely rationale for adding these two vitamins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To augment the other pathways that consume homocysteine

choices.label: B
choices.text: To correct the anemia that accompanies cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: To increase synthesis of cysteine downstream of the enzymatic block

choices.label: D
choices.text: To provide the cofactor required by cystathionine beta-synthase itself

choices.label: E
choices.text: To reduce the intestinal absorption of dietary methionine

explanation.summary: Folate and cobalamin are supplemented in homocystinuria to maximize all pathways that consume homocysteine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B9 (folate) and vitamin B12 (cobalamin) regulate homocysteine levels through the remethylation pathway, in which methyl-FH4 transfers a methyl group to B12, which then converts homocysteine to methionine. In cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, folate and cobalamin are usually supplemented alongside pyridoxine to maximize and augment all pathways that consume homocysteine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: No anemia is described as part of homocystinuria; the vitamins are given to lower homocysteine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cysteine is made downstream of cystathionine beta-synthase; folate and cobalamin act on the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine instead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cystathionine beta-synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), which is why pyridoxine is given; folate and cobalamin serve a different pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vitamins do not act on intestinal absorption; they support the enzymatic consumption of homocysteine.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Hurler syndrome results from an inability to degrade glycosaminoglycans, also known as mucopolysaccharides. Which of the following best describes the structure of these accumulating molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linear polymers assembled from a single repeating amino acid residue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long, unbranched polysaccharide chains usually built from two repeating carbohydrate units

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secreted glycoproteins carrying a mannose 6-phosphate tag added within the Golgi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Short, highly branched oligosaccharide chains covalently attached to membrane lipids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small tripeptides composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine residues

explanation.summary: Glycosaminoglycans are long, unbranched polysaccharide chains usually made of two repeating carbohydrate units.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hurler syndrome is caused by a genetic deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase (IDUA gene), which degrades glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). GAGs are long, unbranched chains of polysaccharides usually comprised of two repeating carbohydrate units; heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate accumulate in the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GAGs are carbohydrate polymers, not amino acid polymers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mannose 6-phosphate-tagged proteins are the lysosomal hydrolases mis-trafficked in I-cell disease, not GAGs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GAGs are long and unbranched, not short branched chains attached to lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine describes glutathione, not a glycosaminoglycan.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a normal examination at birth. At 9 months of age she is brought in for a prominent forehead, enlarged gums and lips, and stiff joints, and her parents ask why she seemed healthy at birth. Enzyme testing of her tissues confirms deficient alpha-L-iduronidase activity. Which of the following best explains the delayed onset of her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her lysosomal enzymes are only secreted into the circulation after infancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal enzyme crossing the placenta protected her until the time of birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Symptoms require an oxidative stressor to be introduced before they appear

choices.label: D
choices.text: The IDUA gene is not normally transcribed until after the first year of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: The intracellular buildup of heparan and dermatan sulfate takes time to manifest

explanation.summary: Children with Hurler syndrome appear unaffected at birth because the abnormal buildup of GAGs takes time to manifest, with complications appearing between 6-12 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Hurler syndrome the abnormal buildup of GAGs within the cell, namely heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, takes time to manifest, so children appear unaffected at birth. Between 6-12 months a wide range of complications begin to appear and worsen over time, including coarse gargoyle-like facial features (prominent forehead, enlarged gums/lips), joint stiffness, corneal clouding, cardiomyopathy, developmental delay, hearing loss, and respiratory issues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spillage of lysosomal enzymes into the circulation is the hallmark of I-cell disease, not Hurler syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Placental transfer of maternal enzyme is not the mechanism described; accumulation of substrate simply takes time.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidative stressors trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and are unrelated to Hurler syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The enzyme deficiency is genetic and present from birth; the delay reflects time needed for GAGs to accumulate, not delayed transcription.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has coarse facial features, joint stiffness, hearing loss, and developmental delay that are milder than those of a cousin with Hurler syndrome. Unlike his cousin, he has clear corneas and displays marked aggressive behavior. His mother's brother had a similar condition. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-L-iduronidase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase

choices.label: C
choices.text: GlcNAc 1-phosphotransferase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
