choices.text: Iduronate sulfatase

explanation.summary: Hunter syndrome is an X-linked deficiency of iduronate sulfatase presenting with mild Hurler-like symptoms, no corneal clouding, and aggressive behavior.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hunter syndrome is often confused with Hurler syndrome because both accumulate heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Hunter presents with mild Hurler symptoms but is distinct in that there is no corneal clouding, inheritance is X-linked (consistent with an affected maternal uncle), aggressive behavior is present, and the deficient enzyme is iduronate sulfatase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency is Hurler syndrome, which includes corneal clouding and is the cousin's diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria with marfanoid habitus and lens dislocation, not coarse features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GlcNAc 1-phosphotransferase deficiency causes I-cell disease, a more pronounced disorder with death usually in the first decade.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G6PD deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, not a lysosomal storage phenotype.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Two infants present with nearly identical coarse facial features, developmental delay, and skeletal abnormalities. Infant 1 is diagnosed with Hurler syndrome and Infant 2 with I-cell disease. Which of the following best characterizes how the course of Infant 2's disease is expected to differ from that of Infant 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corneal clouding will be absent because the disorder is inherited in X-linked fashion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disease will be more pronounced, with death usually occurring within the first decade

choices.label: C
choices.text: Symptoms will be milder because only a single lysosomal enzyme is affected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symptoms will regress once the mannose 6-phosphate tag is added later in childhood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary mucopolysaccharides will rise to much higher levels than in Infant 1

explanation.summary: I-cell disease is more severe than Hurler syndrome because the Golgi defect impacts all lysosomal enzymes, with death usually within the first decade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike Hurler and Hunter, in which a single enzyme is deficient, the lysosomal dysfunction in I-cell disease originates in the Golgi and impacts all lysosomal enzymes. Although the clinical presentations are very similar, I-cell disease is characterized by more pronounced issues, with death usually occurring within the first decade, and mucopolysaccharides are not increased in urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent corneal clouding with X-linked inheritance describes Hunter syndrome, not I-cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: I-cell disease affects all lysosomal enzymes, not just one, and is therefore more severe rather than milder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GlcNAc 1-phosphotransferase defect is permanent; the disease is progressively debilitating and does not regress.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mucopolysaccharides are not increased in the urine in I-cell disease; that biomarker belongs to Hurler syndrome.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Lysosomal hydrolases synthesized in a fibroblast receive a mannose 6-phosphate tag as a posttranslational modification and are subsequently bound by a receptor that traffics them to the lysosome. In which of the following locations does this receptor bind the tagged enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cis-Golgi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysosomal lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nuclear envelope

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: E
choices.text: trans-Golgi

explanation.summary: Receptors in the trans-Golgi bind mannose 6-phosphate-tagged proteins to traffic them to lysosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: GlcNAc 1-phosphotransferase catalyzes the formation of mannose 6-phosphate on translated proteins within the Golgi apparatus. Mannose 6-phosphate is required to properly route degradative hydrolytic enzymes to the lysosome because receptors in the trans-Golgi bind proteins carrying this posttranslational modification and traffic them to lysosomes. Without the tag, as in I-cell disease, the enzymes spill into the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The tag is added in the Golgi, but the receptor-mediated sorting occurs in the trans-Golgi rather than the cis-Golgi.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lysosome is the destination of the trafficked enzymes, not the site of receptor binding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nuclear envelope plays no role in lysosomal enzyme trafficking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rough ER is where the hydrolases are translated, not where the M6P receptor sorts them.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has severe aortic root dilation and marked skeletal findings. His 15-year-old daughter carries the identical FBN1 mutation but has only mild arachnodactyly and a normal aorta. Which of the following genetic concepts best explains the difference in their disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic heterogeneity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Variable expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked inheritance

explanation.summary: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, so two people with the same defective gene can differ in disease severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Marfan syndrome is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion but is known to have variable expressivity. This means that even if two people have the same defective gene, there are differences in how severe their disease will be, much like G6PD deficiency and PKU, which occur along a spectrum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation is not described for Marfan syndrome, and the younger generation here is less severely affected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both patients carry the identical FBN1 mutation, so different genes are not involved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The daughter does show features of the disease, so the gene is expressed; the difference is in severity, not in whether it manifests at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, not X-linked.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies connective tissue from a patient with Marfan syndrome and finds that the elastin is structurally defective even though its precursor protein is synthesized in normal amounts. Which of the following steps is most likely disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cross-linking of the precursor by a vitamin B6-dependent synthase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydroxylation of the precursor by a BH4-dependent enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multimerization of tropoelastin on a fibrillin scaffold

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protection of the precursor from neutrophil elastase by alpha-1 antitrypsin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transport of the precursor to the lysosome via a mannose 6-phosphate tag

explanation.summary: Fibrillin forms a scaffold for elastin and is responsible for proper multimerization of tropoelastin, so FBN1 mutation yields defective elastin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Marfan syndrome arises from a mutation of the fibrillin 1 gene (FBN1), which forms a scaffold for elastin in connective tissue. Fibrillin is responsible for proper multimerization of tropoelastin, the precursor of elastin. Mutation of FBN1 therefore results in defective elastin, and the mutation secondarily increases TGF-beta levels and activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A vitamin B6-dependent synthase describes cystathionine beta-synthase in the cysteine pathway, not elastin assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BH4-dependent hydroxylation is the phenylalanine hydroxylase reaction in PKU, unrelated to elastin assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1 antitrypsin restrains neutrophil elastase in the lung; its deficiency causes emphysema, not the defective elastin of Marfan syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mannose 6-phosphate tagging routes lysosomal hydrolases; it is disrupted in I-cell disease, not Marfan syndrome.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with suspected Marfan syndrome is asked to wrap her hand around her opposite wrist. Which of the following findings would constitute a positive wrist sign?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The distal phalanx of the adducted thumb extends beyond the ulnar border of the palm

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fingers cannot fully encircle the wrist because of stiffness of the finger joints

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thumb and the fifth finger fail to meet on the far side of the wrist

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tip of the thumb covers the entire fingernail of the fifth finger

choices.label: E
choices.text: The wrist hyperextends beyond 90 degrees while the fingers are wrapped around it

explanation.summary: The wrist sign is positive when the tip of the thumb covers the entire fingernail of the fifth finger wrapped around the contralateral wrist.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arachnodactyly in Marfan syndrome is commonly assessed by two distinct signs. The wrist sign is positive when the tip of the thumb covers the entire fingernail of the fifth finger when wrapped around the contralateral wrist. The thumb sign is positive when the entire distal phalanx of the adducted thumb extends beyond the ulnar border of the palm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes a positive thumb sign, the other assessment of arachnodactyly, not the wrist sign.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marfan patients have hyperflexible joints and long digits; failure to encircle the wrist is the opposite of the positive finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A positive sign requires overlap of thumb over fifth fingernail, not failure of the digits to meet.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wrist hyperextension is not part of the wrist sign as defined.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with long arms and legs, joint laxity, and a high-arched palate suffers an acute myocardial infarction. Angiography shows a thrombus occluding a coronary artery. Examination reveals ocular lenses dislocated inferonasally. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased NADPH within red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased homocysteine in the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased lysosomal hydrolases in the plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased mucopolysaccharides in the urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased phenylalanine in the plasma

explanation.summary: Marfanoid habitus with a down-and-in lens dislocation and early thrombosis indicates homocystinuria, with accumulation of homocysteine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homocystinuria produces a marfanoid habitus (long arms and legs with joint laxity and hypermobility, high-arched palate), visual problems from a down-and-in (inferonasal) lens dislocation, and a high risk of thrombosis leading to early myocardial infarction or stroke, usually before the second decade of life. Unlike the non-thrombotic aortic events of Marfan syndrome, this thrombotic infarction reflects accumulation of homocysteine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased red-cell NADPH occurs in G6PD deficiency and causes hemolysis, not lens dislocation or thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysosomal hydrolases in the plasma indicate I-cell disease, not a marfanoid thrombotic disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased urinary mucopolysaccharides is the biomarker of Hurler syndrome, which presents with coarse features in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated phenylalanine characterizes PKU, which presents with a mousy odor and developmental delay.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Neutrophil elastase is a fairly nonspecific protease that protects the lung against pathogens but can also insult and destroy host proteins. The needed balance is accomplished by an enzyme inhibitor, alpha-1 antitrypsin. Which of the following organs produces this inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spleen

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is produced by the liver, which is why certain SERPINA1 mutations cause hepatic complications.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT, sometimes A1AT) is an enzyme inhibitor produced by the liver that restrains neutrophil elastase. Because AAT is made in hepatocytes, mutations such as the Z allele that cause misfolding within the liver ER lead to liver complications in addition to lung disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow produces neutrophils, not the inhibitor of their elastase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney is not the source of AAT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lung is where neutrophil elastase acts and where AAT deficiency causes emphysema, but the inhibitor is not made there.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen is not the source of AAT.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old nonsmoking woman has early-onset emphysema of the lower lobes. Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin is nearly undetectable. Liver enzymes are normal and imaging shows no cirrhosis. Genetic testing shows she is homozygous for a rare SERPINA1 variant rather than the common Z allele. Which of the following best explains why her liver is spared?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatocytes express a separate AAT isoform encoded by a gene other than SERPINA1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minimal or no AAT protein is translated, so no misfolding stress occurs in the hepatocyte ER

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophil elastase is confined to the lung and never reaches hepatic extracellular matrix

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant carries a conservative substitution that permits normal folding in the ER

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant protein is secreted normally from hepatocytes and inhibits hepatic proteases

explanation.summary: Rarer SERPINA1 variants that produce minimal or no AAT lack liver presentations because there is no misfolding stress, but lung disease persists.
explanation.whyCorrect: Other less common SERPINA1 variants cause minimal to no AAT protein to be translated. Because there is no stress from misfolding, these rarer variants lack liver presentations, but lung issues persist since neutrophil elastase remains unopposed and degrades the alveolar extracellular matrix. This illustrates how differing mutations of the same protein can impact a single organ or multiple organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AAT is encoded by the single SERPINA1 gene; there is no separate hepatic isoform.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver disease of AAT deficiency is due to intracellular misfolding, not elastase; elastase confinement is not the reason the liver is spared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normally folded, secreted AAT would not leave serum levels nearly undetectable; the variant produces little or no protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her AAT level is nearly undetectable, so the protein is not being secreted normally.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man homozygous for the Z allele of SERPINA1 asks why his pulmonologist insists that he never smoke. Which of the following best describes how smoking worsens lung disease in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts the normal M allele product into the misfolding Z form

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depletes reduced glutathione so alveolar cells can no longer regenerate NADPH

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases neutrophil elastase release and oxidatively damages AAT to inhibit its function

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates hepatocytes to retain more AAT within the endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates TGF-beta signaling that drives remodeling of the alveolar walls

explanation.summary: Smoking increases neutrophil elastase release and oxidatively damages AAT, compounding the deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Smoking is a major factor in individuals with AAT deficiency because it increases neutrophil elastase release and oxidatively damages AAT to inhibit its function, tipping the balance further toward extracellular matrix destruction. Importantly, individuals homozygous for the Z allele can still develop complications earlier than individuals with M alleles even if they are nonsmokers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Z allele is a fixed genetic substitution (Glu342Lys); smoking does not alter the allele a person carries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Depletion of reduced glutathione and NADPH describes the red-cell defect of G6PD deficiency, not the effect of smoking on AAT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ER retention of misfolded AAT is a property of the Z variant itself, not an effect of smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abnormal TGF-beta activation drives the aortic pathology of Marfan syndrome, not smoking-related lung injury in AAT deficiency.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man homozygous for the Z allele of SERPINA1 has established cirrhosis. He now reports easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. Which of the following best explains this new complaint?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulated homocysteine is promoting vascular fragility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycosaminoglycans are accumulating within the vessel walls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Misfolded AAT is directly inhibiting the coagulation proteases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophil elastase is degrading platelet surface proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: The damaged liver is producing fewer coagulation proteins

explanation.summary: Z-allele liver disease reduces hepatic protein production, including coagulation proteins and albumin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Z allele causes AAT misfolding within the liver ER, inducing cellular stress and cell death. The resulting liver complications include cirrhosis, decreased protein production (for example coagulation proteins or albumin), increased liver enzyme biomarkers, and increased hepatic cancer risk. Reduced synthesis of coagulation proteins by the damaged liver accounts for the bleeding tendency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homocysteine accumulation causes thrombosis in homocystinuria, the opposite problem, and is unrelated to AAT deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycosaminoglycan accumulation describes Hurler and Hunter syndromes, not AAT deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Misfolded AAT causes harm by accumulating in the hepatocyte ER, not by inhibiting coagulation proteases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil elastase degrades the alveolar extracellular matrix in the lung; it is not described as acting on platelets.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Protein-based diseases can arise by several distinct principles. Which of the following pairs of disorders best illustrates two different proteins that, because they are functionally related, compromise the same biological process when defective and therefore produce very similar clinical presentations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G6PD deficiency and phenylketonuria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hurler syndrome and I-cell disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylketonuria and homocystinuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Z-allele and null-variant alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

explanation.summary: Hurler syndrome and I-cell disease involve different proteins that are functionally related, so both compromise lysosomal function and present similarly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hurler syndrome (alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency) and I-cell disease (GlcNAc 1-phosphotransferase deficiency) disrupt distinct proteins, yet because those proteins are functionally related, both compromise the same biological process, degradation within the lysosome, and produce very similar clinical presentations. They are distinguished by molecular biomarkers: urinary mucopolysaccharides in Hurler versus lysosomal enzymes spilled into the plasma in I-cell disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G6PD deficiency and PKU illustrate a different principle: disease occurring along a spectrum depending on the protein variant expressed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria share presentations but arise from disruption of proteins that lack a shared biochemical pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PKU and homocystinuria involve unrelated pathways (phenylalanine hydroxylation versus cysteine synthesis); their only link is cofactor-responsive rescue of select variants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two AAT variants illustrate how differing mutations of the same protein can impact a single organ or multiple organs.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher measures the equilibrium constant of a reversible reaction with and without a purified enzyme present. The enzyme dramatically increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached. Which of the following is the enzyme most likely to leave unchanged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The activation energy required for the reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: The overall equilibrium of the reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rate at which the transition state is formed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rate of the forward reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: The time required to reach equilibrium

explanation.summary: Enzymes accelerate reaction rates (kinetics) but do not alter thermodynamics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enzymes are catalysts that lower the activation energy and speed the rate at which a reaction proceeds, but they do not change whether the reaction is thermodynamically favorable or shift its equilibrium position. A catalyzed reaction reaches the same equilibrium as an uncatalyzed one, only faster.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lowering the activation energy is the defining action of an enzyme, so this is changed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzymes favor formation of the transition state, accelerating its appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: By lowering activation energy the enzyme increases the forward rate, so this is changed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Because the enzyme increases the rate, equilibrium is reached in less time.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy patient develops fasting hypoglycemia after weeks of eating raw eggs, which sequester biotin. The impaired reaction adds CO2 to pyruvate to form oxaloacetate in an ATP-dependent step of gluconeogenesis. Which class of enzyme catalyzes this diminished reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isomerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ligase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lyase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidoreductase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferase

explanation.summary: A biotin-dependent carboxylase that covalently joins two substrates using ATP is a ligase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ligases form a covalent bond between substrates in an ATP-dependent manner; the carboxylase subclass adds CO2 to a substrate to form a carboxylic acid and requires biotin (vitamin B7). Pyruvate carboxylase adding CO2 to pyruvate fits this exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The molecular formula changes between substrates and product, so this is not a simple isomerization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lyase breaks bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation; here a bond is being formed with ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No oxidation-reduction (electron transfer) occurs in this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No functional group is being swapped between two substrates; a new covalent bond is being created.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle, an enzyme uses free inorganic phosphate (Pi) to cleave a glucose unit from glycogen, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. Which term best describes this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isomerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphatase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphoglucomutase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphorylase

explanation.summary: A phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate to break a bond and generate a phosphorylated product.
explanation.whyCorrect: A phosphorylase adds phosphate onto a substrate but, unlike a kinase, it uses free inorganic phosphate (Pi) rather than ATP to break bonds. Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves glycogen with Pi to liberate glucose-1-phosphate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An isomerase rearranges a substrate without adding phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP, not from free inorganic phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A phosphatase removes a phosphate using water; here phosphate is being added.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphoglucomutase relocates a phosphate on the sugar (glucose-1-P to glucose-6-P) rather than cleaving glycogen with Pi.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 20-year-old athlete reports painful muscle cramps that occur only during intense exercise. Muscle biopsy shows abnormal glycogen accumulation in skeletal muscle, and testing reveals deficiency of the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase. Which of the following best explains the exertional symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ammonia accumulates because transamination is impaired

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysosomal enzymes are mistrafficked out of the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Muscle cannot liberate glucose substrates from glycogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Muscle glycogen synthesis is blocked, depleting glycogen stores

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes red-cell hemolysis

explanation.summary: McArdle disease (type V glycogen storage disease) results from muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deficiency of the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase (McArdle disease) prevents breakdown of glycogen, so glycogen accumulates and engorges the muscle. During exertion the muscle cannot provide sufficient glucose-derived substrate for ATP production, producing painful cramps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ammonia buildup relates to impaired transamination, not glycogen phosphorylase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mistrafficking of lysosomal enzymes describes I-cell disease, a defect of post-translational mannose-6-phosphate tagging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is in glycogen breakdown, not synthesis; glycogen accumulates rather than depletes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase deficiency affects red blood cells and causes hemolytic anemia, not exertional muscle cramps.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A patient develops jaundice, fatigue, and pallor after eating fava beans and is found to have an underlying red-cell enzyme deficiency causing acute hemolysis. Which plasma biomarker is most likely to be elevated as a result of the red-cell destruction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosomal enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)

explanation.summary: LDH is highly enriched in red blood cells, so hemolysis releases it into plasma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactate dehydrogenase is present in many tissues but is highly enriched in red blood cells, which depend on interconversion of lactate and pyruvate. When RBCs lyse (as in G6PD deficiency triggered by fava beans), circulating LDH rises.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GGT is a marker of hepatobiliary or pancreatic membranes, not red-cell lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipase indicates pancreatic pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysosomal enzymes in the circulation point to I-cell disease, not hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a marker of prostate tissue, not red-cell turnover.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with acute crushing chest pain. The clinician wants an enzyme biomarker that is relatively specific for cardiac muscle injury. Which of the following is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alanine transaminase (ALT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pancreatic alpha-amylase

explanation.summary: CK-MB isoforms are a biomarker of cardiac (heart) injury such as myocardial infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Creatine kinase-MB isoforms serve as a biomarker of the heart, and their rise in plasma indicates myocardial injury such as a myocardial infarction, matching this presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALT is a marker of liver injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ALP reflects liver or bone disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GGT indicates hepatobiliary (and sometimes pancreatic) disease, not myocardial injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic alpha-amylase points to pancreatic pathology.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Two isozymes, A and B, act on the same substrate and have nearly identical Vmax values (~200 umol/L/s). Isozyme A reaches half of Vmax at a substrate concentration of 10 mM, whereas isozyme B reaches half of Vmax at 5 mM. Which isozyme has the higher affinity for the substrate, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isozyme A, because it has the larger Km

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isozyme A, because it has the smaller Km

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isozyme B, because it has the larger Km

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isozyme B, because it has the smaller Km

choices.label: E
choices.text: They have equal affinity because their Vmax values are equal

explanation.summary: Km is the substrate concentration at half of Vmax, and a lower Km means higher affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Km equals the substrate concentration when velocity is one-half of Vmax. Isozyme B reaches half-Vmax at a lower substrate concentration (5 mM vs 10 mM), so it has the smaller Km. Because Km and affinity are inversely related, the smaller Km reflects higher affinity for the substrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A larger Km indicates lower, not higher, affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isozyme A has the larger Km, not the smaller one, so this reasoning is wrong.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isozyme B has the smaller Km, not the larger one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Affinity is determined by Km, not by Vmax, so equal Vmax values do not imply equal affinity.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A student assumes that raising the substrate concentration to 10 times an enzyme's Km will drive a Michaelis-Menten reaction all the way to Vmax. For an enzyme obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics, what velocity is actually achieved when [S] = 10 x Km?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.15 Vmax

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.33 Vmax

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.50 Vmax

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.91 Vmax

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exactly Vmax

explanation.summary: Because Vmax is an asymptote, even [S] = 10 x Km reaches only about 91% of Vmax.
explanation.whyCorrect: Using V0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with [S] = 10Km gives V0 = (Vmax x 10Km)/(Km + 10Km) = 10Vmax/11 = 0.91 Vmax. Vmax is only a theoretical asymptote that the curve approaches, so high substrate concentrations never fully reach it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the velocity; at 10x Km the enzyme is well past the low-substrate range.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.33 Vmax would correspond to a substrate concentration well below Km.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 0.50 Vmax occurs when [S] equals Km, not 10 times Km.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vmax is an asymptote and is only truly reached at infinite substrate; it cannot be achieved at a finite concentration.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An investigator plots reaction velocity against substrate concentration for an enzyme with quaternary structure and obtains a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve rather than a hyperbolic one. Which property best explains why this enzyme does not obey Michaelis-Menten kinetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An unusually high turnover number

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition by product

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cooperativity between subunits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Covalent modification by phosphorylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Irreversible denaturation at high substrate

explanation.summary: Michaelis-Menten kinetics apply only to enzymes that lack cooperativity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Michaelis-Menten kinetics only apply to enzymes that lack cooperativity. Multi-subunit enzymes with quaternary structure can show allostery between subunits, generating a sigmoidal curve (like hemoglobin's oxygen binding), whereas a non-cooperative monomer (like myoglobin) gives a hyperbolic curve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high turnover number affects how fast product forms, not the shape of the curve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Product inhibition alters apparent kinetics but does not itself produce a sigmoidal cooperativity curve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphorylation is a regulatory modification but is not what makes the velocity curve sigmoidal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Denaturation would reduce activity rather than create a cooperative S-shaped curve.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A pharmacologist uses a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot to characterize how a drug alters enzyme kinetics. On this plot, which parameter is represented by the x-intercept?

choices.label: A
choices.text: -1/Km

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1/Vmax

choices.label: C
choices.text: Km

choices.label: D
choices.text: Km/Vmax

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vmax

explanation.summary: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot the x-intercept equals the negative reciprocal of Km.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Lineweaver-Burk plot is a double reciprocal of the Michaelis-Menten plot. On it, the x-intercept equals -1/Km, the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax, and the slope equals Km/Vmax. This makes changes in Km and Vmax easier to detect when studying drugs that alter kinetics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 1/Vmax is the y-intercept, not the x-intercept.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Km is obtained as the negative reciprocal of the x-intercept, not the x-intercept value itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Km/Vmax is the slope of the line, not an intercept.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vmax itself is not read directly off an intercept; it is the reciprocal of the y-intercept.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An enzyme's active site is lined with several aspartate and glutamate residues. Which of the following is the most likely chemical feature of its preferred substrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydrophobic core that excludes water entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: A region composed of several acidic (negatively charged) amino acid residues

choices.label: C
choices.text: A region composed of several basic (positively charged) amino acid residues

choices.label: D
choices.text: A region composed of several bulky, aromatic nonpolar residues

choices.label: E
choices.text: A region composed of several small, nonpolar residues

explanation.summary: An active site rich in acidic residues favors binding a positively charged (basic) substrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspartate and glutamate have negatively charged, acidic side chains, so the active site is negatively charged. This favors recognition and binding of a positively charged substrate, such as one enriched in basic residues like lysine and arginine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The active site is polar and charged here, so a purely hydrophobic, water-excluding substrate would not bind well.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An acidic substrate would carry the same negative charge as the active site, causing repulsion instead of attraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bulky nonpolar residues would not favor association with the polar, negatively charged active site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small nonpolar residues also lack the positive charge needed to complement an acidic active site.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: After moderate drinking, blood ethanol reaches 10-20 mM, while alcohol dehydrogenase has a Km of about 1-2 mM for ethanol. Because [S] far exceeds Km, which factor is the rate-limiting determinant of ethanol clearance, and why does blood alcohol accumulate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperativity between alcohol dehydrogenase subunits at high substrate levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme turnover, because the enzyme is saturated and operating near Vmax

choices.label: C
choices.text: Substrate availability, because the enzyme is far from saturation at these levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: The activation energy, which rises as ethanol accumulates in the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Km of alcohol dehydrogenase, which increases as more ethanol is consumed

explanation.summary: When [S] greatly exceeds Km the enzyme is saturated, so enzyme turnover becomes rate-limiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: When substrate concentration exceeds Km, enzyme turnover (how fast the enzyme can operate) is the rate-limiting factor. Because ethanol (10-20 mM) far exceeds the Km of alcohol dehydrogenase (1-2 mM), the enzyme is saturated and working near Vmax, so alcohol builds up in the blood faster than it can be cleared.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rate limitation here reflects saturation kinetics, not subunit cooperativity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Substrate availability is rate-limiting only when [S] is below Km; here [S] is well above Km.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Activation energy is a fixed property lowered by the enzyme and does not rise with substrate accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Km is an intrinsic constant of the enzyme and does not increase simply because more ethanol is consumed.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A biochemist measures the rate of a metabolic reaction in a test tube with and without a purified enzyme. Relative to the uncatalyzed reaction, by roughly how much is the enzyme-catalyzed reaction expected to be accelerated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 to 5 times faster

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10 to 100 times faster

choices.label: C
choices.text: 10^2 to 10^3 times faster

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10^20 to 10^30 times faster

choices.label: E
choices.text: 10^6 to 10^14 times faster

explanation.summary: Enzymes accelerate reactions by 10^6 to 10^14-fold compared with the uncatalyzed reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enzymes are protein-based catalysts that accelerate reaction rates so they proceed fast enough to sustain life. A catalyzed reaction occurs 10^6 to 10^14 times faster than the same reaction without the enzyme, which is why the energy in food is not left waiting years to be converted to ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few-fold acceleration would be far too small to sustain biological viability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 10- to 100-fold increase vastly underestimates the rate enhancement enzymes provide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzymatic rate enhancements are many orders of magnitude greater than 10^2 to 10^3.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the range; enzymatic acceleration falls between 10^6 and 10^14-fold.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A first-year student notices that most enzymes end in the suffix '-ase', yet the proteolytic enzymes thrombin and trypsin do not. Which of the following best explains this naming?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are cofactors rather than catalysts and so use a different suffix

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are isozymes named according to the substrate they prefer

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are nonenzymatic transport proteins named for their tissue of origin

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are transition-state analogues rather than true enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: They retain older names that predate the standard '-ase' nomenclature

explanation.summary: Standard enzyme nomenclature uses '-ase', but select older enzyme names end in '-in'.
explanation.whyCorrect: With few exceptions, standard enzyme nomenclature uses the suffix '-ase' to denote an enzyme. Some enzymes discovered earlier kept older names ending in '-in', such as thrombin and trypsin; these are still true enzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are enzymes themselves, not cofactors that assist enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isozymes are isoforms of the same enzyme with different primary sequences; the '-in' ending reflects historical naming, not isozyme status.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombin and trypsin are catalytic enzymes, not transport proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transition-state analogues are drugs that bind enzymes tightly; thrombin and trypsin are enzymes, not analogues.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An investigator determines how many substrate molecules a single molecule of a purified enzyme can convert to product each second when it is fully saturated with substrate. Which of the following terms describes this value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allostery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Michaelis constant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specificity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turnover number

explanation.summary: The turnover number is the maximum number of substrate molecules acted upon by one enzyme molecule per unit time.
explanation.whyCorrect: Turnover number is defined as the maximum number of substrate molecules acted upon by one molecule of enzyme per unit time, exactly what the investigator measured.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation energy is the energy barrier the enzyme lowers, not a measure of how many molecules are processed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allostery is regulation by noncovalent binding at a site distinct from the active site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Michaelis constant (Km) is the substrate concentration at which velocity is one-half of Vmax, not a per-enzyme rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Specificity describes the limitation of an enzyme's activity to a particular substrate, which can be broad or narrow.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An enzyme isolated from a cell uses water to cleave the phosphoester bonds that link nucleotides within a strand of DNA. Which of the following best classifies this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolase, lipase subclass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrolase, nuclease subclass

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase, carboxylase subclass

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lyase, decarboxylase subclass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferase, kinase subclass

explanation.summary: Nucleases are hydrolases that use water to break phosphoester bonds within nucleic acids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydrolases break bonds with water. The major subclasses are proteases (peptide bonds in proteins), lipases (esters within lipids), and nucleases (phosphoesters within nucleic acids). Cleaving the phosphoester backbone of DNA with water is the work of a nuclease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipases are hydrolases, but they cleave esters within lipids, not phosphoesters in nucleic acids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligases form covalent bonds in an ATP-dependent manner; a carboxylase adds CO2 to a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lyases break bonds by means other than hydrolysis or oxidation; a decarboxylase removes CO2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP onto a substrate rather than cleaving a bond with water.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has an isolated elevation of a plasma enzyme. The clinician notes that this particular biomarker can indicate dysfunction in either the liver or the bone, so additional testing is needed to localize the source. Which of the following enzymes was most likely elevated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alkaline phosphatase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspartate transaminase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creatine kinase-MB

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate-specific antigen

explanation.summary: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is a biomarker of both liver and bone disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the summary chart of enzyme biomarkers, alkaline phosphatase is listed with potential dysfunction of the liver or bone disease. Because it is not specific to one tissue, a slate of biomarkers must be cross-referenced to get an accurate clinical picture.

whyWrongByChoice.B: AST is a marker of liver dysfunction and does not indicate bone disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CK-MB isoforms indicate heart injury such as a myocardial infarction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipase points to pancreatic dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a biomarker of the prostate.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who tolerated dairy products as a child now develops symptoms after ingesting milk and is diagnosed with lactose intolerance. Which of the following mechanisms governing enzyme activity best accounts for her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric inhibition of lactase by lactose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased expression of lactase over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of mannose 6-phosphate tagging on lactase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylation-mediated suppression of lactase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Poly-ubiquitination of lactase after each meal

explanation.summary: Lactose intolerance develops when lactase expression decreases, leaving insufficient enzyme to degrade ingested lactose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Altering the abundance of an enzyme is one of the three main ways enzyme activity is governed. When a person's lactase expression decreases over time, they develop lactose intolerance because there is an insufficient amount of enzyme to properly degrade the ingested carbohydrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allosteric regulation acts on previously translated enzyme; lactose intolerance reflects too little enzyme, not inhibition of existing enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of mannose 6-phosphate tagging mistrafficks lysosomal enzymes, as in I-cell disease, and is unrelated to lactase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Post-translational modification such as phosphorylation acts on existing protein and is not the basis of lactose intolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitin-mediated destruction is a post-translational fate of intracellular enzymes, not the mechanism behind reduced lactase.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical team designs an inhibitor that mimics the structure of the high-energy intermediate formed from the substrate of a target enzyme. Which of the following best explains why this design strategy produces a potent drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Molecules resembling the intermediate raise the activation energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Molecules resembling the intermediate shift the reaction equilibrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzyme binds the transition state more tightly than any other species

choices.label: D
choices.text: The intermediate is rapidly converted to product by the enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: The intermediate is the most stable, lowest-energy species in the pathway

explanation.summary: Transition state analogues are effective drugs because the transition state has the highest affinity for the enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: The transition state is the high-energy intermediate formed from the substrate. It has the highest affinity for and binds most tightly to the enzyme. Transition state analogues are therefore used as drugs because they bind tightly to the enzyme target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The potency of an analogue comes from tight binding to the enzyme, not from changing the activation energy of the reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enzymes and their inhibitors act on kinetics; they do not alter the thermodynamic equilibrium of a reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The true transition state is converted to product, but an analogue is not; it occupies the enzyme because of its tight binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The transition state is the high-energy intermediate, not the lowest-energy species.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A newborn has hemolytic anemia caused by deficiency of the red blood cell-specific isoform of pyruvate kinase. The infant's other tissues function normally. Which of the following best explains why this patient is viable, whereas global loss of pyruvate kinase activity is not compatible with life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other tissues bypass the reaction through allosteric activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Other tissues degrade the defective enzyme via the proteasome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other tissues do not require pyruvate kinase for their metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other tissues express a distinct isozyme that catalyzes the same reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other tissues increase transcription of the RBC isoform

explanation.summary: Isozymes are tissue-specific enzyme isoforms with unique primary sequences that catalyze the same reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Isozymes are enzyme isoforms with unique primary sequences that catalyze the same biological reaction and are often expressed in a tissue-specific manner. Deficiency of the RBC-specific pyruvate kinase isoform produces hemolytic anemia, but other tissues rely on their own isoforms and remain functional. Global loss of pyruvate kinase activity, in contrast, is not compatible with life.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allosteric regulation modulates an existing enzyme; it cannot substitute for a missing enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Proteasomal degradation removes protein; it does not restore the catalytic activity the tissue needs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate kinase activity is essential; global loss is lethal, so other tissues clearly require it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RBC isoform is the defective one; other tissues rely on a different isoform, not on more of the RBC isoform.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A metabolite binds noncovalently to a pocket on an enzyme that is distinct from the active site, inducing a conformational change that increases the enzyme's catalytic activity. Which of the following terms best describes this regulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Covalent modification

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzyme induction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Substrate saturation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transition state stabilization

explanation.summary: Allostery is regulation by noncovalent binding at a site distinct from the active site that changes enzyme conformation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allostery is the ability to influence enzymatic activity by noncovalently binding to a site distinct from the active site, inducing conformational changes that either activate or inhibit the enzyme. Here the change increases activity, so it is positive allosteric regulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Covalent modification, such as phosphorylation, is post-translational modification; the binding here is noncovalent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Induction changes enzyme abundance through expression, not the activity of an existing enzyme molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saturation describes all active sites being occupied by substrate, not regulation at a separate site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transition state stabilization is how the active site itself lowers activation energy, not binding at a distinct regulatory site.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A student compares the energy diagrams of an uncatalyzed reaction and the same reaction catalyzed by an enzyme and notes that the peak of the catalyzed curve is lower. Which of the following best describes how the enzyme achieves this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It positions substrates in close proximity and proper orientation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It raises the free energy of the substrates above the products

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the equilibrium of the reaction toward products

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stabilizes the substrate in its lowest-energy ground state

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies the free energy that makes the reaction spontaneous

explanation.summary: Enzymes lower activation energy by bringing substrates together in the right orientation to favor the transition state.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like positioning a toddler just right to pull off a sweater, enzymes bring substrates into close proximity and in the right orientation to favor formation of the high-energy transition state, which is then rapidly converted to more favorable, lower-energy products. This lowers the activation energy (Ea) required for the reaction to proceed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Raising substrate energy is not how catalysis works; the enzyme lowers the barrier to the transition state.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium position of a reaction, only how fast it is reached.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stabilizing the ground state would make the substrate less reactive; enzymes instead favor the transition state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzymes accelerate kinetics; they do not alter thermodynamics or supply energy to make a reaction spontaneous.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use has a deficiency of vitamin B1 (thiamine). The oxidative decarboxylation reactions of the TCA cycle are impaired. Which of the following enzyme classes is most directly affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isomerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lyase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidoreductase

explanation.summary: Oxidative decarboxylation in the TCA cycle is an oxidoreductase (dehydrogenase) reaction that requires vitamin B1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxidoreductases catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions; the dehydrogenase and oxidase subclasses are its major members. The oxidative decarboxylations common in the TCA cycle are oxidoreductase reactions and carry a commonly tested vitamin B1 requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolases break bonds with water and are not vitamin B1-dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isomerases rearrange a substrate without changing its molecular formula.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligases form covalent bonds in an ATP-dependent manner; the carboxylase subclass requires vitamin B7, not B1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lyase decarboxylase removes CO2 without oxidation, whereas these TCA reactions are oxidative and involve electron transfer.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A patient with a dietary deficiency of vitamin B6 has reduced activity of the enzymes that move an amino group from one carbon backbone to another. Which of the following enzyme classes is affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ligase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lyase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidoreductase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferase

explanation.summary: Transaminases (aminotransferases) are transferases that move an amino group between substrates and require vitamin B6.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transferases interchange functional groups between substrates. The transaminase (aminotransferase) subclass transfers an amino group and has a commonly tested vitamin B6 requirement, so B6 deficiency impairs this transferase activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolases break bonds with water and do not transfer amino groups.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ligases form covalent bonds using ATP; the carboxylase subclass requires vitamin B7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lyases break bonds by means other than hydrolysis or oxidation, often forming a double bond or ring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidoreductases carry out oxidation-reduction reactions; their tested vitamin requirement is B1.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An enzyme removes carbon dioxide from a substrate, generating a product with a new double bond. The reaction does not involve water, oxidation, ATP, or vitamin B7. Which of the following best classifies this enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isomerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lyase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidoreductase

explanation.summary: A decarboxylase that breaks a bond without hydrolysis or oxidation is a lyase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lyases catalyze the breaking of various chemical bonds by means other than hydrolysis and oxidation, often forming a new double bond or a new ring structure. The decarboxylase subclass, which removes CO2 from a substrate, is the major example.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolases break bonds with water, which is not used here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isomerases rearrange a substrate without losing an atom; here CO2 is removed, changing the molecular formula.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ligase carboxylase does the opposite, adding CO2 in an ATP- and vitamin B7-dependent manner.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidoreductases require oxidation-reduction; this reaction explicitly involves no oxidation.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During fasting, hepatocytes convert glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose that is released into the blood, with generation of inorganic phosphate (Pi). Which of the following best describes the enzyme that catalyzes this final step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydrolase that uses water to cleave a phosphoester

choices.label: B
choices.text: A kinase that transfers the phosphate onto ADP

choices.label: C
choices.text: A phosphorylase that uses Pi to cleave a bond

choices.label: D
choices.text: A transferase that moves the phosphate to another sugar

choices.label: E
choices.text: An isomerase that relocates the phosphate within the sugar

explanation.summary: Glucose-6-phosphatase is a hydrolase that removes a phosphate with water and releases inorganic phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: To remove a phosphate from a substrate, a phosphatase is utilized. This class of hydrolase removes a phosphate group from a carbon by using water to cleave a phosphoester, generating an unphosphorylated product and inorganic phosphate (Pi). In liver glycogen degradation, glucose-6-phosphatase performs this step to produce free glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A kinase moves phosphate from ATP onto a substrate; the phosphatase removes phosphate and does not reattach it to any recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A phosphorylase uses free Pi to break bonds and generates a phosphorylated product, the opposite of what occurs here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phosphatase does not transfer the phosphate to another molecule; it releases it as Pi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relocating the phosphate from carbon 1 to carbon 6 is the job of phosphoglucomutase, the earlier step in the pathway.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A hepatocyte must increase the activity of a metabolic enzyme in response to a new stimulus. Which of the following regulatory mechanisms would take the longest to change the enzyme's activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric activation by a metabolite

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allosteric inhibition by a pathway product

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dephosphorylation of the enzyme by a phosphatase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased transcription and translation of the enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphorylation of the existing enzyme by a kinase

explanation.summary: Changing expression levels is the slowest way to govern enzyme activity because new enzyme must be transcribed and translated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enzyme activity is governed by expression levels, post-translational modification, and allosteric regulation. Expression changes take the longest because the cell requires time for transcription and translation to produce newly synthesized enzymes; the other methods act on previously translated proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allosteric activation acts rapidly on previously translated enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allosteric inhibition likewise modifies existing enzyme without new synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dephosphorylation is a post-translational change to an existing protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphorylation is a post-translational modification that acts on enzyme that already exists.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An intracellular enzyme is covalently tagged with a chain of small proteins and is subsequently degraded. Which of the following best describes this outcome of post-translational modification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric inhibition by a bound metabolite

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mannose 6-phosphate tagging for lysosomal trafficking

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorylation that suppresses catalytic activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poly-ubiquitination routing the enzyme to the proteasome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced transcription of the enzyme's gene

explanation.summary: Post-translational modification can destroy an enzyme: poly-ubiquitination routes intracellular proteins to the proteasome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Post-translational modification can result in activation, suppression, localization, or destruction of an enzyme. Destruction occurs because intracellular enzymes are proteins that can be poly-ubiquitinated to route them to the proteasome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allosteric inhibition is noncovalent and reduces activity without destroying the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mannose 6-phosphate tagging governs localization of lysosomal enzymes, not their destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphorylation can activate or suppress an enzyme but does not by itself target it for degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced transcription lowers the amount of new enzyme made; it does not degrade enzyme already present.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An investigator is studying an enzyme that obeys Michaelis-Menten kinetics with a fixed amount of enzyme. Which of the following interventions will increase the Vmax of the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding a transition state analogue to the reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adding an allosteric inhibitor of the enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adding more enzyme to the reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raising the substrate concentration to 100 times Km

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switching to a substrate with a lower Km

explanation.summary: The only way to increase Vmax is to increase the amount of enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vmax is the plateau reached when all enzyme sites are occupied (saturation); it is only theoretical because the Michaelis-Menten formula produces an asymptote. The only way to increase Vmax is to increase the amount of enzyme, which is why producing more enzyme is one way cells regulate enzyme activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A transition state analogue binds the enzyme tightly and would reduce, not increase, available activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An allosteric inhibitor decreases enzyme activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing substrate brings velocity closer to Vmax but never raises the asymptote itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A lower Km reflects higher affinity, which affects how quickly half of Vmax is reached, not the value of Vmax.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Kinetic data for an enzyme are transformed into a Lineweaver-Burk plot. The line crosses the y-axis at 0.02 L*s/umol. Which of the following is the Vmax of the enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.02 umol/L/s

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.5 umol/L/s

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 umol/L/s

choices.label: D
choices.text: 50 umol/L/s

choices.label: E
choices.text: 500 umol/L/s

explanation.summary: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, Vmax is the reciprocal of the y-intercept.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Lineweaver-Burk plot graphs 1/[S] versus 1/V, so the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax. Vmax is therefore the reciprocal of the y-intercept: 1 / 0.02 = 50 umol/L/s. This transformation is used because accurately assessing Vmax on a Michaelis-Menten plot is difficult.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.02 is the y-intercept (1/Vmax) itself, not Vmax.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.5 does not correspond to the reciprocal of 0.02.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5 would be the reciprocal of a y-intercept of 0.2, not 0.02.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 500 would require a y-intercept of 0.002.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman who has never smoked is diagnosed with panacinar emphysema, and genetic screening reveals alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency with the ZZ genotype. Because the ZZ variant produces severely misfolded AAT, the physician is concerned about cirrhosis and orders ALT, AST, and GGT. Which of the following additional plasma measurements would best assess the liver's synthetic function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin and clotting factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate and pyruvate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactate dehydrogenase and creatine kinase-MB

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipase and pancreatic alpha-amylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate-specific antigen and alkaline phosphatase

explanation.summary: Beyond leaked enzymes, liver function is monitored with proteins the liver produces, such as albumin and clotting factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated liver enzyme markers such as ALT, AST, and GGT suggest perturbation of liver function through inflammation (e.g. hepatitis) or scarring (e.g. cirrhosis). Because the ZZ variant produces severely misfolded AAT, cirrhosis from cell stress is a concern, and additional markers such as clotting factors and albumin, proteins produced by the liver, would be monitored.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate and pyruvate are metabolites interconverted by LDH, not indicators of liver protein synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LDH is enriched in multiple tissues including RBCs and heart, and CK-MB indicates myocardial injury; neither reflects liver synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipase and pancreatic alpha-amylase are markers of pancreatic dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a prostate marker; ALP is a leaked enzyme marker of liver or bone disease, not a product of hepatic synthetic function.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During a transaminase reaction, aspartate donates its amino group to an acceptor carbon backbone without generating free ammonia. Which of the following alpha-keto acids is formed from the carbon backbone of aspartate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alanine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-ketoglutarate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxaloacetate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate

explanation.summary: Aspartate and oxaloacetate share the same carbon backbone and differ only by an amino versus a ketone group.
explanation.whyCorrect: The carbon backbones of amino acid/alpha-keto acid pairs are identical; they differ only in whether there is an amino functional group or a ketone functional group. Transaminases transfer these groups between different carbon backbones to obtain amino acids or alpha-keto acids without producing toxic ammonia. The pairs are alanine and pyruvate, glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate, and aspartate and oxaloacetate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine is an amino acid formed when pyruvate accepts an amino group.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the alpha-keto acid partner of glutamate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamate is an amino acid, not an alpha-keto acid; it is formed when alpha-ketoglutarate accepts an amino group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate is the alpha-keto acid partner of alanine, not aspartate.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a newly diagnosed pancreatic tumor has an elevated plasma gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) while his ALT and AST are within normal limits. Which of the following best explains the elevated GGT in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GGT hydrolyzes ester bonds within the lipids of pancreatic acinar cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: GGT is highly enriched in red blood cells that lyse near the tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: GGT is released from bone in response to metastatic disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: GGT is synthesized only in hepatocytes and leaks with any liver injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: GGT sits in membranes of secretory and absorptive cells, including the pancreas

explanation.summary: GGT is localized to membranes of cells with robust secretory and absorptive capacity, so pancreatic tumors also raise circulating GGT.
explanation.whyCorrect: GGT adds a gamma-glutamyl group donated from the tripeptide glutathione to amino acids and peptides to promote their transport across cellular membranes. Because of this role in membrane transport, GGT is localized to the membranes of cells with robust secretory and absorptive capacity such as the liver, kidneys, and pancreas. GGT therefore must not be interpreted in isolation; pancreatic tumors also increase circulating GGT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolysis of lipid esters is the function of lipase, a separate pancreatic biomarker; GGT transfers gamma-glutamyl groups.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate dehydrogenase, not GGT, is the enzyme highly enriched in red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alkaline phosphatase is the biomarker linked to bone disease; GGT is not a bone marker.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GGT is not exclusive to hepatocytes; it is also found in kidney and pancreatic cell membranes.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A clinical laboratory confirms a suspected enzyme deficiency by measuring the activity of the enzyme in a patient's sample. The assay is deliberately run with substrate and the coenzyme NAD+ present at saturating concentrations. Which of the following best explains the rationale for these conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperativity between enzyme subunits is prevented

choices.label: B
choices.text: Km can be read directly from the initial rate under these conditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Substrate availability becomes the rate-limiting factor of the assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: The initial rate then equals Vmax and can be compared to a reference range

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reaction reaches thermodynamic equilibrium more rapidly

explanation.summary: Clinical enzyme assays use saturating substrate so the initial rate equals Vmax and results are comparable across labs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coenzymes such as NAD+ or FAD should be viewed as substrates of the reaction. Most clinical assays used to assess enzymatic function are run under saturating substrate concentrations so that the initial rate is equivalent to Vmax. These test conditions are standardized so that all labs can compare results to a reference range for activity, which is commonly how enzyme deficiencies are initially diagnosed or confirmed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Saturating conditions standardize the rate; they do not eliminate cooperativity in multi-subunit enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Km is the substrate concentration at half of Vmax; it cannot be read from a single saturating-rate measurement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: At saturating substrate, enzyme turnover, not substrate availability, is rate-limiting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzyme assays measure initial rate (kinetics), not the position or speed of reaching equilibrium.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration of carbon dioxide to carbonic acid with a Km of 12 mM, and the reverse dehydration of carbonic acid to carbon dioxide with a Km of 26 mM. In a region of the kidney where carbon dioxide and carbonic acid are present at equal concentrations, which of the following best describes the behavior of the enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neither direction is favored, because the substrate concentrations are equal

choices.label: B
choices.text: The forward reaction proceeds, because carbon dioxide has the larger Km

choices.label: C
choices.text: The forward reaction proceeds, because the substrate with the lowest Km reacts first

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reverse reaction proceeds, because bicarbonate always exceeds carbon dioxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reverse reaction proceeds, because the higher Km indicates higher affinity

explanation.summary: When one enzyme acts on two substrates, the reaction with the substrate that has the lowest Km happens first.
explanation.whyCorrect: If an enzyme acts on more than one substrate, the reaction with the substrate that has the lowest Km happens first. With a forward Km of 12 mM and a reverse Km of 26 mM, carbonic anhydrase preferentially proceeds in the forward direction when carbonic acid and carbon dioxide concentrations are equal. To get the reverse reaction to occur, the concentration of carbonic acid (or bicarbonate) must greatly exceed that of carbon dioxide, which is what happens in a different region of the kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Equal concentrations do not produce a tie; the lower-Km substrate wins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The forward substrate, carbon dioxide, has the smaller Km (12 mM), and a smaller Km is what favors it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bicarbonate exceeds carbon dioxide only in specific regions; in the region described the concentrations are equal, and the forward reaction is favored.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Km and affinity are inversely related; the higher Km of the reverse reaction indicates lower affinity.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Two isozymes catalyze the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, the first step of glycolysis. Enzyme X has a Km of 0.05 mM for glucose, and enzyme Y has a Km of 5 mM. Which of the following statements about these enzymes is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzyme X is glucokinase, which is found only in cells of the liver and pancreas

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme X selectively metabolizes glucose in the postprandial state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzyme Y ensures glucose metabolism in neurons when glucose is scarce

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzyme Y is glucokinase, which promotes hepatic glucose storage in times of abundance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enzyme Y is hexokinase, which is widely distributed among tissues

explanation.summary: Hexokinase (Km 0.05 mM) works at low glucose in RBCs and neurons; glucokinase (Km 5 mM) acts in liver and pancreas after meals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hexokinase has a Km of 0.05 mM and glucokinase a Km of 5 mM with respect to glucose, so enzyme Y is glucokinase. Glucokinase is found only in cells of the liver and pancreas and selectively metabolizes glucose in the postprandial state when plasma glucose is elevated and abundant. This allows glucose sparing in times of fasting but promotes storage in the liver in times of abundance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme X, with the low Km of 0.05 mM, is hexokinase, not glucokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Postprandial, high-glucose metabolism is the role of glucokinase (enzyme Y); hexokinase functions even when glucose availability is limited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metabolizing glucose at low concentrations in glucose-dependent cells such as RBCs and neurons is the role of the low-Km hexokinase, enzyme X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzyme Y has the high Km of glucokinase; hexokinase is the widely distributed, low-Km isozyme (enzyme X).

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A researcher compares two isozymes that both catalyze the first step of glycolysis. Enzyme X, found in red blood cells and neurons, becomes half-maximally active at a very low glucose concentration, whereas enzyme Y, found in hepatocytes, requires a much higher glucose concentration to reach half-maximal activity. Which property best explains why enzyme X can phosphorylate glucose even during fasting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzyme X binds glucose at an allosteric site rather than the active site

choices.label: B
