choices.text: Enzyme X has a high Km, reflecting low affinity for glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzyme X has a higher Vmax than enzyme Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzyme X has a low Km, reflecting high affinity for glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enzyme X is only expressed when blood glucose is high

explanation.summary: Hexokinase's low Km gives it high glucose affinity, letting glucose-dependent cells trap glucose even at low blood levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: A low Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a low substrate concentration, i.e., high affinity for glucose. Hexokinase (enzyme X) is expressed in neurons and RBCs, which rely on circulating glucose, so its low Km permits rapid conversion of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate even when blood glucose is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both hexokinase and glucokinase phosphorylate glucose at the active site, not an allosteric site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high Km indicates low affinity and describes glucokinase (enzyme Y), which cannot phosphorylate glucose efficiently when levels are low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hexokinase actually has a lower Vmax than glucokinase; this prevents overaccumulation rather than explaining low-glucose function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Being active only at high glucose describes the liver's glucokinase, not the RBC/neuron enzyme.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: In the liver, glucokinase (hexokinase IV) has both a higher Km and a higher Vmax than the hexokinase found in most other tissues. During a period of glucose abundance after a large meal, what is the physiological advantage of this kinetic profile for hepatocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows the liver to trap glucose even when blood glucose concentrations are very low during fasting

choices.label: B
choices.text: It ensures the liver competes with neurons for the scarce glucose available during fasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: It makes the liver's rate of glucose phosphorylation independent of the blood glucose concentration entirely

choices.label: D
choices.text: It permits rapid, high-volume conversion of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate only when glucose is plentiful

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents the liver from ever forming glucose 6-phosphate from the glucose it absorbs

explanation.summary: Glucokinase's high Km plus high Vmax lets the liver phosphorylate glucose rapidly, but only when glucose is abundant, feeding storage pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The high Km means glucokinase only becomes substantially active at elevated glucose (e.g., postprandial), which spares blood glucose during fasting. The high Vmax then allows fast, efficient accumulation of glucose 6-phosphate to supply anabolic storage pathways such as glycogen and lipid synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trapping glucose at very low concentrations describes low-Km hexokinase, not high-Km glucokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The high Km specifically spares blood glucose for other tissues during fasting rather than competing with neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucokinase activity is strongly dependent on glucose concentration; it rises steeply as glucose increases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucokinase does form glucose 6-phosphate; it simply restricts this to high-glucose conditions.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A pharmacologist studies a drug that binds reversibly and noncovalently to the active site of an enzyme and structurally resembles the natural substrate. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, adding this drug shifts the x-intercept to be less negative but leaves the y-intercept unchanged. Which type of inhibitor is this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric activator

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible (suicide) inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Noncompetitive inhibitor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncompetitive inhibitor

explanation.summary: A reversible active-site inhibitor that resembles substrate, raises apparent Km, and leaves Vmax unchanged is competitive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate at the active site and commonly mimic its structure. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, Vmax (y-intercept) is unchanged because excess substrate can still overcome the inhibitor, while the apparent Km rises, seen as a less negative x-intercept (-1/Km).

whyWrongByChoice.A: An activator would increase activity, not inhibit; it would not raise apparent Km.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irreversible/suicide inhibitors bind covalently, are not overcome by dilution, and decrease Vmax without changing Km.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Noncompetitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, leave Km unchanged, and decrease Vmax (increased y-intercept).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncompetitive inhibitors decrease both Km and Vmax and bind only after substrate is bound.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An enzyme is exposed to an inhibitor that binds an allosteric site, does not resemble the substrate, and cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration. The enzyme-substrate complex still forms normally. Which pair of kinetic changes is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Km decreased, Vmax decreased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Km increased, Vmax increased

choices.label: C
choices.text: Km increased, Vmax unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: Km unchanged, Vmax decreased

choices.label: E
choices.text: Km unchanged, Vmax unchanged

explanation.summary: Noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged and decrease Vmax.
explanation.whyCorrect: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site, changes enzyme shape, and reduces product formation regardless of substrate concentration. Because it does not compete at the active site, the enzyme-substrate complex forms normally and Km is unchanged, but Vmax falls because functional catalysis is reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased Km and decreased Vmax describes an uncompetitive inhibitor, which binds only after substrate is bound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No inhibitor increases Vmax; that would be activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased Km with unchanged Vmax describes a competitive inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unchanged Km and Vmax would mean no inhibitory effect at all.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A toxicology exam asks which single feature is shared by a reversible competitive inhibitor and an irreversible suicide inhibitor acting on the same enzyme. Which of the following is that shared feature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are relieved by dilution

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both bind at an allosteric site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both bind at the active site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both increase the apparent Km of the enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both leave Vmax unchanged

explanation.summary: Competitive and suicide inhibitors both act at the active site and resemble the substrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both a competitive enzyme inhibitor and an irreversible suicide inhibitor bind the active site, and to do so they chemically resemble the substrate to some extent. Their key difference is the bond formed: competitive inhibitors bind noncovalently and reversibly, while suicide inhibitors bind covalently and irreversibly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the reversible competitive inhibitor is relieved by dilution; covalent suicide inhibition is not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither binds an allosteric site; both act at the active site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only the competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km; the suicide inhibitor leaves Km unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged, but the suicide inhibitor decreases Vmax.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after ingesting an organophosphate pesticide. This class of poison, along with drugs such as allopurinol and aspirin, acts by binding covalently to an enzyme's active site so that the inhibition cannot be reversed by dilution. What is the expected effect on the enzyme system's kinetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both Km and Vmax are increased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme function is fully restored by simply diluting the inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Km is decreased and Vmax is unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vmax is lowered while the affinity (Km) is unchanged

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vmax is unchanged while Km is increased

explanation.summary: Irreversible (suicide) inhibitors covalently remove functional enzyme, lowering Vmax without changing the Km of the remaining enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irreversible inhibitors bind covalently and effectively subtract functional enzyme molecules from the mixture, so Vmax drops. The enzyme copies that remain unbound behave normally, so their affinity for substrate (Km) is unchanged. Organophosphates, allopurinol, and aspirin are cited as suicide inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increasing both Km and Vmax is not a recognized inhibition pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Covalent irreversible inhibition is not removed by dilution; recovery requires synthesis of new enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased Km with unchanged Vmax does not describe irreversible inhibition (it partially resembles uncompetitive inhibition).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unchanged Vmax with increased Km describes a reversible competitive inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During a lecture on hepatic drug metabolism, phase I and phase II reactions are contrasted. Which statement most accurately distinguishes them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phase I and phase II reactions both must occur strictly in sequence and cannot occur independently

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phase I reactions conjugate polar groups; phase II reactions oxidize substrates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phase I reactions decrease water solubility, while phase II reactions decrease it further

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phase I reactions oxidize/hydrolyze substrates, while phase II reactions covalently add polar groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phase II enzymes generate reactive oxygen species using NADPH, while phase I enzymes do not

explanation.summary: Phase I enzymes (CYP450) oxidize/hydrolyze xenobiotics; phase II enzymes conjugate polar groups to boost water solubility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase I reactions transform molecules chiefly by oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, or hydroxylation and are largely catalyzed by CYP450 enzymes. Phase II reactions are conjugations in which polar molecules such as glutathione, glucuronate, or sulfate are covalently linked to the substrate, increasing water solubility for excretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick states the pattern is generally sequential but that broad specificity allows phase II to occur apart from phase I in some cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the two phases; oxidation is phase I and conjugation is phase II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both phases increase water solubility to promote excretion, not decrease it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ROS generation and NADPH use are hallmarks of the CYP450 (phase I) enzymes, not phase II.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A member of the CYP450 enzyme family is described as containing a heme prosthetic group, requiring NADPH as a coenzyme, being associated with ER membranes and mitochondria, and being inducible by substrate abundance. Which additional property is characteristic of all CYP450 enzymes and contributes to their potential cytotoxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They add glucuronate to bilirubin during phase II conjugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind their substrate irreversibly and cannot be induced by it

choices.label: C
choices.text: They conjugate glutathione onto substrates during phase II metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: They generate a free-radical/reactive oxygen intermediate

choices.label: E
choices.text: They phosphorylate glucose to glucose 6-phosphate in hepatocytes

explanation.summary: All CYP450 enzymes generate a free-radical/ROS intermediate that can be cytotoxic when it accumulates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists that all CYP450 members oxidize substrate while reducing oxygen, require NADPH to produce a reduced active oxygen species that can form reactive oxygen species, and generate a free-radical intermediate that upon accumulation can be cytotoxic. This underlies liver damage from ethanol oxidation via CYP2E1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucuronate addition to bilirubin is done by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, a phase II enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP450 enzymes are inducible by substrate abundance, so this statement is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione conjugation is a phase II reaction performed by glutathione S-transferase, not CYP450.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose phosphorylation is done by hexokinase/glucokinase, unrelated to CYP450.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with heavy chronic alcohol use is being counseled about medication safety. He notes that at high levels of alcohol intake, a larger proportion of ingested ethanol is handled by CYP2E1 rather than alcohol dehydrogenase. Which statement about CYP2E1 best explains this shift and its clinical consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CYP2E1 conjugates ethanol with sulfate to make it water soluble

choices.label: B
choices.text: CYP2E1 has a higher Km and is induced by ethanol, so heavy drinking increases toxic by-product formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: CYP2E1 has a lower Km for ethanol than alcohol dehydrogenase, so it acts first at low ethanol levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: CYP2E1 is a phase II enzyme that inactivates ethanol without generating any reactive species

choices.label: E
choices.text: CYP2E1 is inhibited by ethanol, so heavy drinking decreases its activity

explanation.summary: CYP2E1 has a higher Km for ethanol than ADH and is induced by ethanol, so heavy drinking shifts metabolism toward the microsomal system and its toxic by-products.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP2E1 has a much higher Km for ethanol (~10 mM) than ADH (~1 mM), so a greater fraction of ethanol is metabolized by CYP2E1 when levels are high. As a CYP450, it generates free-radical/toxic by-products, and because CYP2E1 is induced by ethanol, damage such as cirrhosis is enhanced with increased intake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sulfate conjugation is a phase II reaction (sulfotransferase), not the phase I oxidation performed by CYP2E1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP2E1 has a higher, not lower, Km than ADH, which is why it dominates only at high ethanol levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP2E1 is a phase I CYP450 and does generate reactive/free-radical species that damage the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CYP2E1 is induced by ethanol, so activity increases, not decreases, with heavier intake.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is stabilized on a benzodiazepine and a statin, both metabolized by CYP3A4. She begins drinking large amounts of fresh grapefruit juice daily. Which change in her drug metabolism is most likely, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grapefruit activates phase II conjugation, eliminating both of her drugs much faster

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grapefruit converts CYP3A4 into an irreversible inhibitor of hepatic hexokinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grapefruit has no effect because CYP3A4 metabolizes very few clinically used drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grapefruit induces CYP3A4, lowering the blood levels of both of her drugs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, raising blood levels of her CYP3A4-metabolized drugs

explanation.summary: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, so drugs cleared by CYP3A4 accumulate to higher blood levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Citrus fruits, especially grapefruit, contain components that inhibit the enzymatic contribution of CYP3A4. If a drug is predominantly inactivated by CYP3A4, inhibiting that enzyme reduces clearance and alters (raises) the drug's blood levels compared with previous experience. CYP3A4 acts on more drugs than any other CYP450 isoform.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grapefruit's effect is on CYP3A4 (phase I), not on accelerating phase II conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grapefruit does not turn CYP3A4 into a hexokinase inhibitor; these enzymes are unrelated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP3A4 alone accounts for over one-third of hepatic CYP450 and acts on more drugs than any other isoform, so the effect is clinically significant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grapefruit inhibits rather than induces CYP3A4; St. John's Wort is described as having an activating (inducing) effect.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought in with scleral icterus and elevated ALT and AST after taking a large amount of acetaminophen for muscle soreness. He denies alcohol use, and his HCT and MCV are normal. Testing later reveals a polymorphic, sub-optimal variant of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. Which mechanism best explains his jaundice and elevated liver enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CYP3A4 induction by acetaminophen destroys circulating red blood cells, releasing bilirubin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess glutathione directly damages hepatocytes, releasing ALT and AST into the blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: His defective phase II conjugation cannot keep pace, so acetaminophen is shunted to NAPQI

choices.label: D
choices.text: His hexokinase cannot phosphorylate glucose, causing hemolysis and resulting jaundice

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfotransferase overactivity converts bilirubin into a toxic free radical species

explanation.summary: A weak UDP-glucuronosyltransferase variant overwhelmed by high acetaminophen impairs bilirubin conjugation and shunts drug to NAPQI, producing jaundice and liver injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin for excretion; a suboptimal variant plus an abundant xenobiotic (acetaminophen) prevents adequate bilirubin conjugation, causing jaundice. With conjugation overwhelmed, more acetaminophen is oxidized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, and elevated liver enzymes reflect hepatic damage. Alcohol can potentiate this but is not required in individuals with such variants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP3A4 is a drug-metabolizing phase I enzyme and does not lyse red blood cells; his RBC indices are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione is protective, neutralizing NAPQI; it does not directly damage hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: His normal HCT and MCV argue against hemolysis, and hexokinase deficiency is not the described mechanism; the defect is in phase II conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfotransferase is a normal phase II route; it does not convert bilirubin into a toxic radical.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A patient with a large acetaminophen overdose develops rising liver enzymes because the toxic metabolite NAPQI is accumulating. Which agent is the appropriate antidote, and by what mechanism does it work?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allopurinol, because it competitively conjugates NAPQI with sulfate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ethanol, because it inhibits CYP2E1 and stops NAPQI formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose, because hexokinase converts NAPQI to glucose 6-phosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grapefruit juice, because it induces UDP-glucuronosyltransferase

choices.label: E
choices.text: N-acetylcysteine, because it rapidly replenishes glutathione stores

explanation.summary: N-acetylcysteine replenishes GSH, which glutathione S-transferase uses to conjugate and detoxify NAPQI.
explanation.whyCorrect: NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione by glutathione S-transferase (forming mercapturic acid), but this system is easily saturated in overdose, letting NAPQI bind cellular cysteines and cause damage. N-acetylcysteine rapidly replenishes GSH stores to counteract NAPQI accumulation, restoring the protective conjugation pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allopurinol is a suicide inhibitor of xanthine oxidase and does not conjugate NAPQI with sulfate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ethanol induces CYP2E1, which would increase NAPQI formation; it is not an antidote here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose, not NAPQI; this pathway is unrelated to detoxification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 and does not induce UDP-glucuronosyltransferase; it would not detoxify NAPQI.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A first-year medical student asks why glucose that enters a red blood cell and is converted to glucose 6-phosphate cannot diffuse back out of the cell, whereas free glucose can move across the membrane. Which property of glucose 6-phosphate best explains its retention inside the cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds irreversibly to the membrane glucose transporter

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is immediately polymerized into glycogen within the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is rapidly converted to lipid before it can be exported

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its negatively charged phosphate prevents transport out of the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hydrophobic character of its phosphate group prevents it from crossing the membrane

explanation.summary: Phosphorylation of glucose adds a negative charge that traps glucose 6-phosphate inside the cell for intracellular metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hexokinase and glucokinase transfer a phosphate from ATP onto glucose in the first step of glycolysis. Addition of a negatively charged phosphate to glucose prevents its transport out of the cell, effectively trapping it for intracellular metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose 6-phosphate does not bind the transporter irreversibly; it simply cannot be transported because of its charge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cells are incapable of storing glucose as glycogen; retention is due to the charge of the phosphate, not polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red blood cells cannot convert glucose into lipids; retention occurs immediately upon phosphorylation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The phosphate makes the molecule more charged and polar, not hydrophobic.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A biochemist compares the maximal velocities of the glucose-phosphorylating enzymes from erythrocytes and hepatocytes and finds that the erythrocyte enzyme has a markedly lower Vmax. Which statement best explains the physiological advantage of the lower Vmax in erythrocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows erythrocytes to store excess glucose as glycogen for later use

choices.label: B
choices.text: It ensures glucose 6-phosphate is exported to the liver for lipid synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It permits phosphorylation only when blood glucose is abundant

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents the cell from trapping more glucose than it can use

choices.label: E
choices.text: It raises the affinity of the enzyme for glucose during fasting

explanation.summary: Hexokinase's low Vmax keeps glucose 6-phosphate production slow enough that cells unable to store glucose do not overaccumulate it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Vmax of hexokinase is lower than that of glucokinase. This slower production of glucose 6-phosphate ensures the cell does not trap more glucose inside than can be used, which matters because the fate of glucose in RBCs and neurons is limited: they are incapable of storing glucose as glycogen or fat. The low Vmax therefore prevents overaccumulation or waste.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes cannot store glucose as glycogen; that limitation is precisely why a low Vmax is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 6-phosphate is trapped inside the cell and is not exported to the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Restriction of activity to high glucose is a property of glucokinase's high Km, not hexokinase's low Vmax.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vmax describes maximal rate, not affinity; affinity is reflected by Km, and hexokinase's Km is already low.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Using kinetic curves of hexokinase and glucokinase plotted against glucose concentration, a student notes that the Km of glucokinase is about 10 mmol/L while the Km of hexokinase is close to 0 mmol/L. In a fasting patient whose blood glucose is approximately 5 mmol/L, which statement best describes the activity of the two enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both enzymes are operating below half-maximal activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both enzymes are operating near their respective Vmax values

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucokinase is operating near its Vmax while hexokinase is below half-maximal activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hexokinase activity is zero because the concentration is below its Km

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hexokinase is operating near its Vmax while glucokinase is below half-maximal activity

explanation.summary: At fasting glucose (~5 mmol/L), hexokinase is saturated near its Vmax while glucokinase, with a Km near 10 mmol/L, is well below half-maximal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal activity. Because hexokinase's Km is near 0 mmol/L, it is essentially saturated and near its (low) Vmax at 5 mmol/L glucose. Glucokinase's Km is about 10 mmol/L, so at 5 mmol/L it has not yet reached half-maximal activity, which is how it spares blood glucose during fasting for other tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hexokinase reaches near-maximal activity at very low glucose because of its very low Km.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucokinase is far from its Vmax at fasting glucose; its activity rises steeply only when glucose exceeds its Km.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two enzymes; glucokinase is the one that is below half-maximal at fasting glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 5 mmol/L is above hexokinase's Km, and even at concentrations below Km an enzyme retains partial activity rather than zero.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A researcher isolates hexokinase IV from human tissue samples. Which pair of tissues is expected to express this isozyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocytes and pancreas

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney and adipose tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver and pancreas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons and erythrocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle

explanation.summary: Hexokinase IV is glucokinase, which is expressed by the pancreas and liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucokinase (i.e., hexokinase IV) is the high-Km isozyme expressed by the pancreas and liver. Its high Km prevents production of glucose 6-phosphate from glucose during fasting, sparing blood glucose for other cells and tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes express hexokinase rather than glucokinase, so this pair is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kidney and adipose tissue are not identified as glucokinase-expressing tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurons and erythrocytes express low-Km hexokinase, not glucokinase, because they rely on circulating glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle is not identified as a site of glucokinase (hexokinase IV) expression.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Glucose transporters (GLUTs) isolated from two tissues are compared. The transporter from neurons has a very low Km for glucose, whereas the transporter from hepatocytes has a high Km. Which statement best describes the functional significance of the hepatocyte transporter's kinetic profile?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks glucose entry into hepatocytes after a carbohydrate meal

choices.label: B
choices.text: It complements the low Km of hepatic glucokinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lets glucose enter hepatocytes only when glucose is abundant

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lets hepatocytes import glucose preferentially during fasting

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lets hepatocytes import glucose regardless of blood glucose level

explanation.summary: High-Km GLUTs on liver and pancreas admit glucose only when it is abundant, matching the high Km of glucokinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteins other than enzymes also have Km values. GLUTs expressed on the liver and pancreas have a high Km to ensure glucose only enters these cell types when glucose is abundant. In many tissues GLUT affinity complements the kinetic properties of hexokinase or glucokinase, coordinating glucose uptake with intracellular metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: After a meal glucose is abundant, which is exactly when the high-Km transporter permits entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic glucokinase has a high Km, not a low one; the transporter matches that high Km.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A high Km means low affinity, so the liver does not preferentially import glucose when levels are low during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Import independent of glucose concentration describes neither transporter; the high-Km transporter is strongly concentration dependent.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: An enzyme preparation loses activity when a test compound is added. When the mixture is diluted, full enzyme activity returns. Which type of interaction between the compound and the enzyme is most consistent with this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Covalent modification of a residue within the active site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of a covalent disulfide bond with a cysteine residue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Noncovalent binding through hydrogen bonds or ionic bonds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Permanent removal of the enzyme's heme prosthetic group

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proteolytic cleavage of the enzyme's peptide backbone

explanation.summary: Reversible inhibitors bind noncovalently via weak hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, or ionic bonds and are easily removed by dilution.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reversible enzyme inhibitors bind noncovalently to enzymes by weak hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, or ionic bonds. These types of inhibitors are easily removed by dilution, which is the defining observation here. They are subclassified as competitive, noncompetitive, or uncompetitive based on their effect on kinetic parameters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Covalent modification of the active site characterizes irreversible inhibitors, which are not removed by dilution.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A covalent disulfide bond would not be reversed by dilution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of a prosthetic group would not be restored simply by diluting the mixture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cleavage of the backbone destroys the enzyme; activity could not return with dilution.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A graduate student measures the kinetics of an enzyme with and without a reversible active-site inhibitor that resembles the substrate. She reports that the inhibitor "lowered the enzyme's affinity for substrate." Her mentor says this description is imprecise. Which statement most accurately describes what the inhibitor did?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It altered the enzyme's shape so that substrate could no longer bind

choices.label: B
choices.text: It left the intrinsic Km unchanged but raised the apparent Km

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowered both the intrinsic Km and the Vmax of the enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lowered the intrinsic Km while leaving the apparent Km unchanged

choices.label: E
choices.text: It permanently raised the intrinsic Km of the enzyme

explanation.summary: A competitive inhibitor does not change the enzyme's intrinsic Km; it increases the apparent Km observed experimentally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fight for binding to the active site between substrate and competitive inhibitor makes the enzyme look like it has reduced affinity for the substrate. This is reflected as an increase in the apparent Km on a Lineweaver-Burk plot. The intrinsic Km of the enzyme is unchanged, but the presence of the competitive inhibitor increases the apparent Km observed in the plotted values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Changing the whole enzyme's shape describes allosteric noncompetitive inhibition; substrate can still bind and overcome a competitive inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreasing both Km and Vmax describes uncompetitive inhibition, and a competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the relationship; the intrinsic Km is unchanged and the apparent Km rises.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The intrinsic Km is unchanged, and a reversible inhibitor produces no permanent change.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Two inhibitors of the same enzyme are characterized. Inhibitor 1 binds the active site reversibly and is overcome by raising substrate concentration. Inhibitor 2 binds an allosteric site and is not overcome by raising substrate concentration. In pharmacodynamic terms, which effects on the substrate's response are expected from inhibitor 1 and inhibitor 2, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased efficacy; decreased efficacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased efficacy; decreased potency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased potency; decreased efficacy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased potency; decreased potency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased potency; decreased efficacy

explanation.summary: Reversible competitive inhibitors decrease potency, whereas noncompetitive (and irreversible) inhibitors decrease efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the summary comparison of inhibitors, reversible competitive inhibitors are overcome by increasing substrate, leave Vmax unchanged, and pharmacodynamically decrease potency (more substrate is needed for the same effect). Noncompetitive inhibitors cannot be overcome by substrate, decrease Vmax, and therefore decrease efficacy (the maximal response is lowered).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The competitive inhibitor still allows the full maximal response at high substrate, so efficacy is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the pairing; the competitive inhibitor lowers potency and the noncompetitive inhibitor lowers efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The noncompetitive inhibitor lowers the achievable maximum, which is a loss of efficacy, not potency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No inhibitor increases potency; the competitive inhibitor decreases it.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A rarely used drug binds its target enzyme only after the substrate has already bound, attaching at an allosteric site and preventing product formation. Compared with the uninhibited enzyme, which changes are expected on a Lineweaver-Burk plot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less negative x-intercept and increased y-intercept

choices.label: B
choices.text: Less negative x-intercept and unchanged y-intercept

choices.label: C
choices.text: More negative x-intercept and increased y-intercept

choices.label: D
choices.text: More negative x-intercept and unchanged y-intercept

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged x-intercept and increased y-intercept

explanation.summary: Uncompetitive inhibitors decrease both Km and Vmax, giving a larger negative x-intercept and an increased y-intercept.
explanation.whyCorrect: Uncompetitive inhibitors are reversible inhibitors that bind the enzyme only when substrate is already bound, attach to an allosteric site, and prevent product formation. They decrease both Km and Vmax, which is seen as a larger negative x-intercept (-1/Km) and an increased y-intercept (1/Vmax) on a Lineweaver-Burk plot. This type is rarely encountered in medicine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A less negative x-intercept would indicate an increased Km, but uncompetitive inhibitors decrease Km.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A less negative x-intercept with unchanged y-intercept is the pattern of a competitive inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The y-intercept must rise because Vmax is decreased by an uncompetitive inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An unchanged x-intercept with increased y-intercept describes noncompetitive inhibition (Km unchanged, Vmax decreased).

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: In a metabolic cascade, rising concentrations of the final product cysteine reduce the activity of enzymes earlier in its own synthesis pathway, contributing to the accumulation of homocysteine. Which type of regulation does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Irreversible suicide inhibition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Negative feedback

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive feedforward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Substrate-level induction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncompetitive inhibition

explanation.summary: End products reversibly inhibiting enzymes in their own synthesis cascade is negative feedback.
explanation.whyCorrect: In metabolism, many end products are reversible inhibitors of the enzymes that produce them, especially in synthesis cascades; the product may inhibit the direct enzyme that produced it or another in the cascade. This is negative feedback. Cysteine inhibits its own synthesis cascade, so cysteine production cannot compensate for rising homocysteine as a protective measure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Suicide inhibition is covalent and irreversible; end-product feedback is reversible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Positive feedforward is when a substrate speeds up an enzyme in a cascade, as with PRPP and purine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Induction by substrate abundance describes CYP450 enzyme expression, not end-product inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncompetitive inhibition is a kinetic classification, not the regulatory concept of an end product inhibiting its pathway.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During de novo purine synthesis, an abundance of PRPP increases the rate of the committed step of the pathway. Which regulatory mechanism best describes this effect of a substrate on a downstream enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allosteric inhibition by end product

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative feedback

choices.label: D
choices.text: Noncompetitive inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive feedforward

explanation.summary: A substrate speeding up an enzyme in a cascade, as PRPP does at the committed step of purine synthesis, is positive feedforward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Positive feedforward describes a substrate that speeds up an enzyme in a cascade. The brick's example is PRPP and the committed step of purine de novo synthesis, contrasting with negative feedback in which end products inhibit their own synthesis pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: End-product inhibition is negative feedback, the opposite of the acceleration described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive inhibition also reduces activity, and PRPP is a substrate, not an inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative feedback involves an end product inhibiting, not a substrate accelerating, the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Noncompetitive inhibition reduces activity; here activity is increased.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 32-year-old soldier is exposed to sarin gas. Days later, after the agent has been cleared from his circulation, laboratory testing shows that activity of the targeted enzyme remains markedly reduced. Which process is required for his enzyme activity to recover?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation of the inhibitor with glucuronate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilution of the inhibitor by increased fluid intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Displacement of the inhibitor by excess substrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous dissociation of the inhibitor from the active site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis of new, unbound enzyme molecules

explanation.summary: Covalently bound irreversible inhibitors such as sarin can only be overcome by producing additional free enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nerve agents such as sarin gas act as suicide (irreversible) inhibitors that bind covalently to the enzyme's active site. If the bond to the active site cannot be broken, the only way to recover enzyme function is to produce additional free, unbound enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phase II conjugation of a xenobiotic does not restore enzyme that has already been covalently modified.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Irreversible inhibitors are not removed by dilution because their modification is covalent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unlike competitive inhibitors, irreversible inhibitors are not overcome by increasing substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The covalent bond does not spontaneously dissociate; that is what makes the inhibition irreversible.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: During a lecture on hepatic detoxification, the term xenobiotic is introduced. Which of the following best defines a xenobiotic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A foreign compound that is nonnutritive

choices.label: B
choices.text: A nutrient absorbed from the diet

choices.label: C
choices.text: A polar conjugate produced by phase II enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reactive oxygen species generated by CYP450

choices.label: E
choices.text: An endogenous hormone synthesized by CYP450

explanation.summary: A xenobiotic is any foreign, nonnutritive compound that the body must biologically transform for elimination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipophilic drugs and other xenobiotics, defined as any foreign compound that is nonnutritive, are biologically transformed so they can be eliminated from the body. Detoxification is accomplished through phase I and phase II enzymes in the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A xenobiotic is specifically nonnutritive, so a dietary nutrient does not qualify.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugated metabolites are the products of detoxification, not the definition of the foreign compound itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ROS are by-products generated during CYP450 activity, not foreign compounds entering the body.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endogenous substances like steroid hormones are made by the body and are not foreign compounds.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A lipophilic drug is taken up by hepatocytes and processed by phase I and phase II enzymes. Which pair of outcomes represents the overall goal of hepatic transformation of this compound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion to glucose 6-phosphate and entry into glycolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased water solubility and activation of the compound

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased lipid solubility and enhanced tissue storage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased protein binding and prolonged circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased water solubility and inactivation of the compound

explanation.summary: Hepatic xenobiotic transformation aims to increase water solubility for excretion and to inactivate the foreign substance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The overall goal of hepatic xenobiotic transformation is twofold: increase water solubility to promote excretion, and inactivation of the foreign substance. Phase I oxidation and phase II conjugation progressively increase the polar nature and water solubility of the compound.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose phosphorylation is a glycolytic step unrelated to xenobiotic detoxification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both phases increase water solubility; the goal is inactivation rather than activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Detoxification increases polarity and water solubility, not lipid solubility or storage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolonging circulation opposes the goal of promoting excretion.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to name the most common phase I reaction and the enzyme family that catalyzes it. Which answer is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucuronidation by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutathionylation by glutathione S-transferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxylation by the cytochrome P450 family

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylation by hexokinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfation by sulfotransferase

explanation.summary: The most common phase I reaction is hydroxylation catalyzed by the CYP450 enzyme family.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase I biochemically transforms a molecule predominantly by reduction, oxidation, hydrolysis, or hydroxylation. The most common phase I reaction is hydroxylation catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme family, which oxidizes lipophilic compounds to alter or terminate their activity and increase polarity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation reaction, not a phase I reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathionylation is a phase II conjugation reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphorylation of glucose is a glycolytic step, not a detoxification reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfation is a phase II conjugation reaction.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Beyond metabolizing xenobiotics, CYP proteins catalyze reactions required for the synthesis of certain endogenous molecules. Which of the following are synthesized with the help of CYP enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bile acids and steroid hormones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutathione and glucuronate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen and triglycerides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin and myoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purines and pyrimidines

explanation.summary: CYP proteins also catalyze reactions in the synthesis of cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D, and steroid hormones.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to oxidizing lipophilic xenobiotics, CYP proteins play an important role in catalyzing reactions involved in synthesizing endogenous substances like cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D, and steroid hormones.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione and glucuronate are the polar groups added by phase II enzymes, not products of CYP synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen and triglyceride synthesis are storage pathways of the liver, not CYP-catalyzed processes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin and myoglobin are sources of heme that is broken down to bilirubin; CYPs do not synthesize them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Purine synthesis is discussed in the context of PRPP feedforward, not CYP enzymes.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops jaundice. Her physician explains that the yellow pigment is a substance normally conjugated with an acidic sugar before it can be excreted. This pigment is derived from the breakdown of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaminophen oxidized by the CYP2E1 isoform

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cholesterol released from damaged hepatocyte membranes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucuronate generated by the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutathione consumed during hepatic detoxification reactions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heme from hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes

explanation.summary: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme from Hb, Mb, and cytochromes, and must be conjugated with glucuronate to be excreted.
explanation.whyCorrect: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin, a breakdown product of heme derived from hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes, to increase its water solubility so it can be excreted. Without addition of the acidic sugar glucuronate, bilirubin accumulates and results in jaundice; the color arises because bilirubin is a conjugated ring system that absorbs light.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2E1 oxidation of acetaminophen yields NAPQI, a toxic intermediate, not the pigment of jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholesterol is an endogenous molecule synthesized with CYP involvement; it is not the source of bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucuronate is the acidic sugar added to bilirubin, not the source of the pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione is a tripeptide used in conjugation; its consumption does not produce the jaundice pigment.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension has been well controlled on a calcium channel blocker for years. He recently began taking the herbal supplement St. John's Wort for low mood, and at follow-up his blood pressure is elevated. Which mechanism best explains the loss of blood pressure control?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of CYP3A4 increased metabolism of the calcium channel blocker

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of the drug at its receptor by the supplement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of glutathione prevented conjugation of the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of CYP3A4 raised blood levels of the calcium channel blocker

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saturation of sulfotransferase shunted the drug to CYP2E1

explanation.summary: St. John's Wort activates CYP3A4, accelerating metabolism of CYP3A4 substrates such as calcium channel blockers and lowering their levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcium channel blockers for blood pressure, statins, and benzodiazepines are metabolized by CYP3A4. CYP3A4 activity is influenced by lifestyle choices: in contrast to grapefruit, which inhibits CYP3A4, the supplement St. John's Wort can have an activating effect on CYP3A4. Faster inactivation of the calcium channel blocker lowers its effective level and blood pressure control is lost.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The interaction described in the brick is metabolic, via CYP3A4 activation, not receptor competition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione conjugation is relevant to NAPQI detoxification, not to the CYP3A4 clearance of this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of CYP3A4 (as with grapefruit) would raise drug levels and enhance, not diminish, the antihypertensive effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shunting to CYP2E1 upon phase II saturation describes acetaminophen toxicity, not this drug interaction.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is found through genetic testing to have a CYP450 expression profile that classifies her as a "supermetabolizer" for a drug she is about to start. Which is the most appropriate consideration when planning her treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She may require unique dosing or an alternative medication

choices.label: B
choices.text: She requires no adjustment because standard doses apply to everyone

choices.label: C
choices.text: She should avoid all drugs metabolized by phase II enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: She should be given grapefruit juice to inhibit CYP3A4

choices.label: E
choices.text: She should receive N-acetylcysteine with each dose

explanation.summary: Precision medicine tailors treatment to an individual's CYP450 profile; supermetabolizers may need unique dosing or alternative drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Precision medicine takes into consideration an individual's CYP450 expression profile to properly tailor treatment based on their specific metabolism. Some individuals can be classified as a supermetabolizer and may require unique dosing or alternative medications compared with an average patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The premise of precision medicine is that standard dosing may not suit individuals with atypical metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The supermetabolizer classification concerns CYP450 (phase I) expression, not a need to avoid phase II-metabolized drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deliberately inhibiting CYP3A4 with grapefruit is not the described strategy; treatment is tailored through dosing or drug choice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione for NAPQI accumulation; it is not a routine companion to CYP450 variation.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Phase II detoxification enzymes move polar groups from a donor molecule onto a target substrate. Based on this activity, most phase II enzymes belong to which enzyme class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isomerases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidoreductases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferases

explanation.summary: Phase II conjugation enzymes are largely transferases because they move polar groups from one carbon source to another.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase II enzymes catalyze conjugation reactions in which polar molecules are covalently linked to target substrates. Many of these enzymes are in the transferase class because they move polar groups from a carbon source to another, as reflected in their names: glutathione S-transferase, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, and sulfotransferase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolysis is a phase I type of reaction, not the group-transfer chemistry of conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isomerization does not add a polar group to a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligases are not the class named for phase II conjugation enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidation and reduction are phase I reactions carried out largely by CYP450 enzymes.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: Glutathione S-transferase attaches the tripeptide glutathione (glutamic acid, cysteine, glycine) to NAPQI during acetaminophen detoxification. Through which residue and bond is glutathione linked to NAPQI?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cysteine, through a sulfide link

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamic acid, through an ester bond

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamic acid, through its gamma-carboxyl group

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycine, through a peptide bond

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycine, through its alpha-amino group

explanation.summary: Glutathione is added to NAPQI through a sulfide link via the cysteine within the tripeptide.
explanation.whyCorrect: NAPQI serves as a substrate for glutathione transferase, which adds glutathione to NAPQI through a sulfide link via the cysteine within the glutathione tripeptide. This mirrors how, when the mechanism is saturated, NAPQI instead covalently links to cysteines within cellular proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.B: No ester bond with glutamic acid is involved; the attachment is a sulfide link.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The gamma-carboxyl of glutamic acid forms the internal linkage to cysteine within glutathione itself, not the bond to NAPQI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycine's peptide bond is internal to glutathione; it is not how NAPQI is attached.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycine's amino group is used in the tripeptide's own peptide bond, not in attachment to NAPQI.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man ingests a large quantity of acetaminophen. In addition to NAPQI binding to cysteine residues of cellular proteins, which additional consequence of heavy glutathione consumption during detoxification is expected in his hepatocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased Km of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase for acetaminophen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced sulfation of acetaminophen by sulfotransferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired neutralization of oxidative species within the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Induction of CYP3A4 expression by the accumulating conjugates

explanation.summary: Depleting GSH through detoxification also removes the cell's means of neutralizing oxidative species, disturbing oxidative balance.
explanation.whyCorrect: GSH is utilized to neutralize oxidative species as part of the pentose phosphate pathway and thereby maintains oxidative balance within the cell. In detoxification, GSH plays a different but equally critical role as the conjugate for NAPQI. Depletion of GSH by overuse in detoxification will adversely impact oxidative balance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Consuming glutathione does not alter the Km of a separate phase II enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sulfation is a saturable phase II route already overwhelmed in overdose; GSH depletion does not enhance it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bilirubin conjugation depends on UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and glucuronate, and in overdose this system is overwhelmed rather than enhanced.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CYP450 enzymes are induced by substrate abundance, not by accumulating phase II conjugates.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old woman who does not drink alcohol takes a single standard dose of acetaminophen for a headache. Which pathway is expected to handle the majority of the drug under these conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and sulfotransferase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjugation with glutathione by hepatic glutathione S-transferase enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Covalent binding to the cysteine residues of cellular proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxylation by CYP3A4 followed by glutathione conjugation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidation by CYP2E1 to the reactive intermediate NAPQI

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen is typically handled by the phase II enzymes UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and sulfotransferase; CYP2E1 acts only at decreased affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acetaminophen is typically acted upon by the phase II enzymes UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and sulfotransferase to increase water solubility, with the conjugates excreted by the kidney in urine. The phase I CYP2E1 enzyme can also act on acetaminophen but at a decreased affinity; the pathway shifts toward CYP2E1 only with alcohol consumption (which increases CYP2E1 expression) and/or excess acetaminophen, neither of which applies here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione conjugation handles NAPQI, the minor CYP2E1 product, not the bulk of the parent drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein binding by NAPQI occurs only when glutathione conjugation is saturated in overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP3A4 is not described as the acetaminophen-metabolizing isoform; the relevant CYP is CYP2E1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CYP2E1 has decreased affinity for acetaminophen and becomes significant only with ethanol induction or excess drug.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: In a patient recovering from acetaminophen overdose treated with N-acetylcysteine, the toxic metabolite NAPQI is conjugated with glutathione. What is the eventual fate of this conjugate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is converted to a glucuronate conjugate and excreted in bile

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is excreted by the kidney in urine as mercapturic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is hydrolyzed back to free acetaminophen and glutathione

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is reoxidized by CYP2E1 to regenerate the NAPQI

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is stored within hepatocytes bound to cellular proteins

explanation.summary: The glutathione-NAPQI conjugate forms mercapturic acid, which is eliminated by the kidney in urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the acetaminophen detoxification pathway, glutathione S-transferase adds GSH to NAPQI, producing the glutathione conjugate (mercapturic acid), which is then excreted by the kidney in urine. N-acetylcysteine supports this route by rapidly replenishing GSH levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucuronidation is a separate route acting on the parent acetaminophen, and the conjugate is excreted in urine, not bile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sulfide-linked conjugate is not hydrolyzed back to parent drug; it proceeds to urinary excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The conjugate is a detoxified product headed for excretion; it is not converted back to NAPQI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Binding to cellular proteins is the harmful fate of free NAPQI when GSH is depleted, not the fate of the conjugate.

questions.topicName: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders II

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a reactive HIV screening immunoassay. Following laboratory protocol, a confirmatory test is performed in which proteins are denatured, given a uniform negative charge, separated through a gel by size, transferred to a membrane, and then probed with labeled antibodies. Which of the following techniques is being used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flow cytometry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Western blot separates denatured proteins by size and detects them on a membrane with antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In western blotting, proteins are denatured, given a uniform negative charge by detergent, separated by size through a porous gel (largest proteins migrate least), transferred to a membrane, and probed with antibodies. HIV infection and Lyme disease still use western blotting as the confirmatory test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flow cytometry analyzes antigens on intact cells passed one at a time through a light source, not denatured proteins on a membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates proteins by charge and does not use antibodies or a membrane-transfer step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry stains antigens within a tissue biopsy examined by microscopy, not proteins run on a gel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ELISA uses an immobilized antigen and antibody binding in a plate; it does not separate proteins by size on a gel or membrane.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with HIV requires monitoring of her absolute CD4+ T-cell count to guide therapy. The most appropriate laboratory method passes intact cells one at a time past a light source and uses labeled antibodies against surface markers to quantify how many cells express a given antigen. Which of the following techniques is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzymatic assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flow cytometry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunofluorescence of a biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Flow cytometry uniquely analyzes and counts antigens on intact cells one at a time.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flow cytometry uses fluid dynamics to run individual cells past a light source; light scatter separates cells by size and granularity, and antibodies against markers such as CD4 quantify the number of cells expressing that antigen within a population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An enzymatic assay quantifies enzyme activity against a standard and does not enumerate cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunofluorescence localizes antigens within a fixed tissue biopsy by microscopy rather than counting cells in suspension.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ELISA measures the abundance of a soluble antibody or antigen but does not detect antigens on intact cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot analyzes denatured proteins for size and cannot examine or count intact whole cells.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: As part of school health protocols, a student has a reactive (positive) hepatitis B titer by ELISA and is told no follow-up is needed, while a classmate is negative and must complete a vaccination series. Which of the following best explains the significance of the student's positive titer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A protective concentration of anti-hepatitis B antibodies is present

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active hepatitis B viral replication is present and requires treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B viral surface protein was directly detected in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: The immune system has failed to respond to prior vaccination

choices.label: E
choices.text: The test measured the size of a hepatitis B protein

explanation.summary: A titer measures the relative concentration of a patient's antibody; a positive result reflects protective immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ELISA measures the relative quantity of anti-hepatitis B antibodies, not the virus. A reactive titer means the student has a sufficient antibody concentration for protection, so no booster is needed. The negative classmate lacks antibodies and requires vaccination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The titer detects antibodies, not the virus, so it does not indicate active viral replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The clinic is not measuring for the virus or its surface protein; it is measuring the patient's antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A positive titer indicates a successful, not failed, antibody response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ELISA measures antibody abundance; only western blot provides the size of a protein.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a family history of sickle cell disease undergoes evaluation. The disorder is caused by an alteration in the beta-globin chain of hemoglobin. Which of the following amino acid changes at position 6 of the beta subunit is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydrophobic leucine is replaced by a polar serine

choices.label: B
choices.text: A negatively charged glutamate is replaced by a neutral valine

choices.label: C
choices.text: A neutral glutamine is replaced by a positively charged arginine

choices.label: D
choices.text: A neutral valine is replaced by a negatively charged glutamate

choices.label: E
choices.text: A positively charged lysine is replaced by a neutral glycine

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease results from a single glutamate-to-valine substitution in beta-globin.
explanation.whyCorrect: In sickle cell disease a negatively charged glutamate is replaced by a neutral, nonpolar valine within the beta subunit at position 6. This exposes a hydrophobic residue that drives HbS polymerization when deoxygenated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leucine and serine are not the residues involved in the sickle mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamine and arginine are not the residues involved in the sickle mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the actual change; the normal glutamate is the residue lost, not gained.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysine and glycine are not the residues involved in the sickle mutation.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A hematology laboratory uses gel electrophoresis to distinguish normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) from sickle hemoglobin (HbS). Because HbA and HbS are otherwise very similar molecules, which of the following properties allows the two forms to be separated by this technique?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody specificity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Molecular size

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overall charge

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polarity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quaternary shape

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates HbA from HbS on the basis of a difference in charge.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrophoresis separates proteins by their charge at a selected pH. Because HbS lacks the negatively charged glutamate present in HbA, it carries a more positive (less negative) overall charge and migrates differently, allowing the variants to be distinguished.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin electrophoresis relies on charge migration and does not use antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The size difference between exchanging a glutamate for a valine is too small to resolve HbA from HbS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although there is a slight polarity difference, hemoglobin electrophoresis does not separate proteins by polarity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbA and HbS have the same tetrameric quaternary structure, so shape does not separate them.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 28-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes hemoglobin electrophoresis during pregnancy screening. Her gel shows two distinct bands: one comigrating with the HbA reference and a second, more slowly migrating HbS band. Which of the following is the most likely genotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent beta-globin (no hemoglobin produced)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-A / Beta-A (normal)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-A / Beta-S (sickle cell trait)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-S / Beta-S (sickle cell anemia)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two identical HbS alleles with no HbA

explanation.summary: A heterozygous carrier shows both HbA and HbS bands on electrophoresis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A sample with both HbA and HbS bands indicates a heterozygous carrier (sickle cell trait, Beta-A/Beta-S). Carriers express both the normal and variant beta-globin and are typically asymptomatic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent beta-globin production is not consistent with two visible hemoglobin bands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal Beta-A/Beta-A genotype would show only a single HbA band.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sickle cell anemia (Beta-S/Beta-S) produces only an HbS band, with no HbA band.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two HbS alleles with no HbA describes sickle cell anemia, which would lack the HbA band she displays.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: On a hemoglobin electrophoresis gel, the sample is loaded near the positive pole and proteins migrate toward the negative pole. Compared with HbA, the HbS band is observed to travel farther from the positive pole. Which of the following best explains this migration pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HbS carries a more positive (less negative) charge than HbA

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbS has a greater net negative charge and is drawn to the positive pole

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbS has already polymerized into an insoluble mass

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbS is a larger tetramer that moves faster through the gel

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbS is bound by antibodies that pull it toward the negative pole

explanation.summary: Because HbS lacks a negative glutamate, its more positive charge shifts it away from the positive pole.
explanation.whyCorrect: HbS lacks the negatively charged glutamate of HbA and therefore has a more positive overall charge. A less negative protein is drawn less strongly toward the positive pole, so HbS migrates farther from it (closer to the negative pole) than HbA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HbS is less negative than HbA, not more negative, so it is not pulled harder toward the positive pole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Migration on the gel reflects charge of the soluble protein, not polymerization state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The size difference between the variants is negligible and does not explain the migration; separation here is by charge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin electrophoresis does not use antibodies to move the protein.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents in a painful vaso-occlusive crisis after strenuous exercise. Understanding that the sickling process is driven by a hydrophobic interaction, which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism and a key therapeutic goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frameshift truncates beta-globin; treatment requires enzyme replacement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies against RBCs cause hemolysis; treatment requires immunosuppression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deoxygenated HbS exposes valine; treatment aims to raise oxygen saturation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutamate enters the hydrophobic pocket; treatment aims to reduce hydration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxygenated HbS polymerizes; treatment aims to lower oxygen saturation

explanation.summary: Deoxygenation exposes the sickle valine, driving HbS polymerization; increasing oxygenation reverses it.
explanation.whyCorrect: When Hb is deoxygenated, a hydrophobic pocket forms. In HbS the abnormal valine is exposed to the polar environment and binds an adjacent deoxy-Hb tetramer, causing polymerization and rigid sickled RBCs. Because sickling is favored at low oxygen, a major intervention is to increase oxygen saturation (e.g., nasal cannula) and reduce exertion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sickle cell disease is a point mutation, not a frameshift, and beta-globin is produced full length.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sickling is due to HbS polymerization, not antibody-mediated hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It is the neutral valine, not glutamate, that interacts with the hydrophobic pocket in HbS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerization occurs with deoxygenated, not oxygenated, HbS; oxygenation reverses sickling, so lowering oxygen would worsen it.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A pathologist evaluates a breast biopsy to determine the tissue and cellular localization of a specific antigen for cancer staging. Antibodies are applied to the tissue section, and stained cells are examined under the microscope. Which of the following techniques is being used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzymatic activity assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescent flow cytometry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect ELISA on serum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western immunoblot

explanation.summary: Immunohistochemistry uses antibody-stained tissue biopsies to reveal antigen localization by microscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence use a patient biopsy, apply antibodies, and examine the stained sample by microscopy to determine the relative localization of an antigen in tissue. These techniques are commonly used in pathology to stage cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An enzymatic assay measures enzyme activity and does not visualize antigen location in tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flow cytometry analyzes intact cells in suspension and does not preserve tissue architecture for localization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ELISA measures the abundance of a soluble antibody or antigen in a plate, not localization in tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot provides antigen size from a protein mixture, not tissue localization.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: In an indirect ELISA, a laboratory-produced viral antigen is immobilized on a plastic surface and a patient's serum is added and incubated. After washing, which of the following steps allows the bound patient antibodies to be detected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Applying a labeled anti-human antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Applying an electric field to migrate the antibodies by charge

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passing the sample one cell at a time past a laser

choices.label: D
choices.text: Separating the antibodies by size through a porous gel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staining a tissue section and viewing it by microscopy

explanation.summary: Indirect ELISA discloses bound patient antibody using a labeled anti-human antibody that generates a color signal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an indirect ELISA, after the patient's antibodies bind the immobilized antigen, a labeled anti-human antibody is added to disclose the bound antibodies; a substrate then produces a color change, with a positive test showing color and a negative test remaining clear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Charge-based migration in an electric field describes electrophoresis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Passing cells past a laser is flow cytometry, not ELISA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Size separation through a gel is a step in western blotting, not ELISA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staining and microscopy of a tissue section describes immunohistochemistry.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a routine liver panel that reports ALT and AST values. Unlike western blotting or flow cytometry, this measurement provides no direct visualization of the protein. Which of the following best describes how these values are obtained?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By counting the number of hepatocytes expressing the enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: By determining the molecular weight of each enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: By localizing the enzyme within a liver biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: By quantifying the enzyme's activity relative to a standard

choices.label: E
choices.text: By separating the enzymes on a charge-based gel

explanation.summary: Enzymatic assays report protein abundance as activity measured against a reference standard.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALT and AST in liver panels are measured by enzymatic assays tailored to detect and quantify a specific enzyme. The consumption or conversion of a substrate is measured, and protein abundance is based on the extent of enzyme activity referenced to a standard, without visualizing the protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Counting cells that express a marker is flow cytometry, not an enzymatic assay.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Molecular weight is provided by western blotting, not by an activity-based enzymatic assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Localizing an enzyme within a biopsy describes immunohistochemistry.
