whyWrongByChoice.E: Charge-based gel separation describes electrophoresis, not an enzymatic activity assay.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A researcher needs to confirm both the presence and the approximate molecular weight of a specific antigen within a complex protein mixture. Which of the following techniques is uniquely suited to provide the size of the detected antigen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flow cytometry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunofluorescence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Western blot uniquely reports the molecular weight (size) of a detected antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because proteins are separated by size before antibody detection, western blot is the only listed technique that provides the molecular weight of an antigen within a mixture, in addition to confirming its presence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flow cytometry quantifies antigens on intact cells and does not give protein molecular weight.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates by charge and is not used to report antigen size in a general protein mixture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunofluorescence shows antigen localization in tissue, not molecular weight.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ELISA reports the relative abundance of an antibody or antigen but not its size.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A laboratory prepares an antibody reagent for a protein detection assay by covalently linking a fluorescent molecule to the antibody. To preserve the antibody's ability to bind its target, the fluorescent tag is attached to which of the following regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigen-binding fragment (Fab)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigen-contact site of the heavy chain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Crystallizable fragment (Fc)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hinge between the two Fab arms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable region of the light chain

explanation.summary: The Fc (constant) region of an antibody can be chemically modified for detection without disrupting antigen binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies have an antigen-binding fragment (Fab) and a crystallizable fragment (Fc), also called the constant region. The Fc region can be chemically altered, for example by covalently linking a fluorescent molecule, without adversely impacting antigen binding, which allows visualization, detection, and quantification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Fab is the antigen-binding fragment; modifying it would risk impairing binding to the target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Altering the antigen-contact site would interfere with the specific antibody/antigen interaction the assay depends on.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The label is attached to the Fc constant region, not to the junction between the Fab arms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The variable region participates in antigen recognition and is not the site used for chemical labeling.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A western blot is run on a patient's serum protein mixture and the membrane is probed with an antibody that recognizes two related proteins. One band appears near the 75 kDa marker close to the sample wells, and a second band appears near the 25 kDa marker much farther down the membrane. Which of the following best describes the relationship between these two bands?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bands cannot be compared because western blot does not report size

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lower band is the larger protein because it carried more negative charge

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two bands are the same protein detected in two different charge states

choices.label: D
choices.text: The upper band is the larger protein because it migrated the least distance

choices.label: E
choices.text: The upper band is the smaller protein because it bound more antibody

explanation.summary: In western blotting, the largest proteins migrate the least distance from the point of origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Denatured proteins carrying a uniform negative charge are separated through a porous matrix based on size, with the largest proteins migrating the least distance from the origin. A band remaining near the wells at the 75 kDa marker is therefore the larger protein, while the band that traveled farther to the 25 kDa marker is smaller.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Western blot uniquely provides the size of the antigen detected, so the bands can be compared by molecular weight.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The detergent gives all proteins a uniform negative charge, so migration reflects size, not charge; the farther-migrating band is the smaller one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Charge is normalized in western blotting, so different positions reflect different sizes rather than charge states of one protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Position on the membrane is determined by size, not by how much antibody binds; the upper band is the larger protein.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: Before proteins are loaded onto the gel for a western blot, they are denatured and treated with a detergent. Which of the following is the primary purpose of the detergent in this technique?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To attach a fluorescent label to each protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: To block nonspecific antibody binding on the membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: To give all proteins a uniform negative charge

choices.label: D
choices.text: To separate proteins according to their native charge

choices.label: E
choices.text: To transfer the proteins onto the membrane

explanation.summary: Detergent normalizes protein charge so that western blot separation depends on size alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: In western blotting, proteins are denatured and given a uniform negative charge by the addition of a detergent. Because every protein carries a similar charge, movement through the porous gel is determined by size, with the largest proteins migrating the least distance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Detection labels are attached to antibodies used in the staining step, not added to the proteins by the detergent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The detergent acts on the proteins before electrophoresis; it is not a membrane-blocking step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Separation by native charge at a select pH describes electrophoresis of hemoglobin, which does not normalize charge; western blotting deliberately eliminates charge differences.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfer to a membrane is a separate step after electrophoresis and is not the function of the detergent.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: During the polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) step of a western blot, a detergent-treated protein mixture is loaded into wells at one end of the gel and an electric field is applied. Toward which electrode do the proteins migrate, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They remain at the wells, because the porous gel traps them

choices.label: B
choices.text: Toward the anode, because antibodies bound to them carry a positive charge

choices.label: C
choices.text: Toward the anode, because detergent-coated proteins are anions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toward the cathode, because denatured proteins become cations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toward the cathode, because the largest proteins are pulled hardest

explanation.summary: Detergent-coated proteins are anions and therefore migrate toward the positively charged anode during PAGE.
explanation.whyCorrect: The detergent gives the denatured proteins a uniform negative charge, making them anions. In the PAGE apparatus, the sample is loaded near the cathode and the direction of anion migration is toward the anode, with smaller proteins traveling farther through the porous gel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The porous gel slows proteins according to size but does not trap them at the wells; they migrate through it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies are applied only after transfer to the membrane; they play no role in migration through the gel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The detergent imparts a negative, not positive, charge, so proteins move away from the negatively charged cathode.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proteins move toward the anode, and the largest proteins migrate the least distance rather than being pulled hardest.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: In the antibody staining step of a western blot, two different antibodies are applied sequentially to the membrane. Which of the following best describes the role of the second antibody added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds the target protein directly at a second epitope

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carries the fluorophore and binds the primary antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: It denatures the transferred proteins so the epitope is exposed

choices.label: D
choices.text: It gives the target protein a uniform negative charge

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transfers the target protein from the gel to the membrane

explanation.summary: The secondary antibody carries the detectable label and recognizes the primary antibody bound to the target.
explanation.whyCorrect: In western blot antibody staining, a primary antibody binds the target protein on the membrane, and a labeled secondary antibody carrying the fluorophore then binds the primary antibody. This exposes the protein for antibody-mediated detection and visualization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct binding of the target is the job of the primary antibody; the secondary antibody recognizes the primary antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Denaturation occurs before electrophoresis, not during antibody staining.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The uniform negative charge is conferred by the detergent before the gel run, not by an antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gel transfer is a separate electrical step preceding staining and does not involve antibodies.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A medical student asks why western blotting, once a common clinical assay, is now reserved mainly for confirmatory testing in a limited number of infections. Which of the following best explains its reduced use in clinical laboratories?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be performed with labeled antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cannot detect one antigen within a protein mixture

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot provide information about protein size

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires intact cells instead of a serum sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other tests are more sensitive and less laborious

explanation.summary: Western blotting has been displaced in most clinical settings by tests that are more sensitive and less laborious.
explanation.whyCorrect: Western blotting is not as broadly used in clinical labs as other more sensitive and less labor-intensive tests now exist. It remains the confirmatory test for HIV infection and Lyme disease, but is otherwise uncommon in routine clinical work.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Western blot detection depends on labeled antibodies applied to the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Western blot does detect a specific antigen within a complex protein mixture on the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Western blot uniquely provides the size of the antigen detected; this is a strength, not the reason it fell out of favor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Western blot analyzes denatured proteins and does not require intact cells; flow cytometry is the technique that examines whole cells.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: Four adults immunized with the same vaccine have serum samples serially diluted (1:2, 1:4, 1:8, and so on) and tested by indirect ELISA against the immobilized vaccine antigen. Color change persists through 1:16 for patient W, through 1:128 for patient X, only at 1:2 for patient Y, and at no dilution for patient Z. Which of the following patients had the strongest antibody response to the vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient W

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient X

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient Z

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients W and X equally

explanation.summary: The longer an ELISA signal persists across serial dilutions, the higher the antibody concentration in the sample.
explanation.whyCorrect: A titer reflects the relative concentration of an antibody in a patient's sample. Because the sample is serially diluted before being added to the immobilized antigen, the patient whose color change persists to the highest dilution (1:128) has the highest antibody concentration and therefore the strongest response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A signal that stops at 1:16 indicates a lower antibody concentration than one persisting to 1:128.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Signal only in the least-diluted well indicates a weak antibody response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No color change at any dilution indicates the patient appears not to have developed antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two patients differ by several dilution steps, so their antibody concentrations are not equal.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: An indirect ELISA is performed for a patient who has never been exposed to a particular viral antigen. After all reagents including the labeled anti-human antibody and substrate have been added, the well remains clear. Which of the following best explains why no color develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No patient antibody bound, so the labeled anti-human antibody had nothing to bind

choices.label: B
choices.text: The labeled anti-human antibody bound the antigen directly and blocked the substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patient's antibodies bound but were too small to be detected

choices.label: D
choices.text: The substrate was inactivated by the patient's serum

choices.label: E
choices.text: The viral antigen failed to immobilize on the plastic surface

explanation.summary: A negative indirect ELISA stays clear because, without patient antibody on the antigen, the labeled anti-human antibody cannot be retained to convert the substrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an indirect ELISA the patient's antibodies must bind the immobilized antigen; the labeled anti-human antibody then discloses those bound antibodies and converts the substrate to produce a color change. If the patient has no antibodies against the antigen, nothing is retained for the anti-human antibody to bind, so a negative test remains clear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The anti-human antibody recognizes human antibodies, not the viral antigen, and it generates rather than blocks the color signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Detection does not depend on antibody size; if patient antibodies had bound, the labeled anti-human antibody would disclose them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing in the technique involves inactivation of the substrate by serum; color depends on retained labeled antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antigen immobilization is a lab-controlled step; the absence of color in an unexposed patient reflects a lack of patient antibody, not a failed coating.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman uses an over-the-counter urine pregnancy test that produces a visible line within minutes. Which of the following best describes the type of assay she is using?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A flow cytometry assay counting hCG-positive cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hemoglobin electrophoresis adapted to urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lateral flow immunoassay adapted from ELISA

choices.label: D
choices.text: A western blot detecting the size of hCG

choices.label: E
choices.text: An enzymatic assay measuring hCG activity

explanation.summary: Over-the-counter pregnancy tests are lateral flow immunoassays, a commonly used adaptation of the ELISA technique.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lateral flow immunoassays are a commonly used adaptation of ELISA and are the platform behind OTC pregnancy tests. They rely on anti-hCG antibodies and are described as rapid and specific.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flow cytometry analyzes intact cells one at a time in a laboratory instrument, not a soluble hormone on a test strip.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates Hb variants by charge and has no relation to hCG detection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Western blotting is a labor-intensive gel and membrane technique, not a rapid home test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzymatic assays quantify the activity of a specific enzyme such as ALT or AST; the pregnancy test detects hCG with antibodies.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A diagnostics company is developing a rapid lateral flow test for a newly characterized protein biomarker. Despite already having one antibody that binds the biomarker, the development timeline is prolonged. Based on how rapid tests such as the hCG pregnancy test are built, which of the following is the most likely reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fluorescent label must be attached to the Fab region of the antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: A second antibody that binds the biomarker simultaneously is needed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intact cells expressing the biomarker must be isolated for the strip

choices.label: D
choices.text: The biomarker must first be size-separated on a polyacrylamide gel

choices.label: E
choices.text: The test must be calibrated against serial dilutions of every patient

explanation.summary: Rapid lateral flow tests require two distinct antibodies that can bind the target at the same time, and generating compatible antibodies takes time.
explanation.whyCorrect: For the pregnancy test, two distinct anti-hCG antibodies that can bind hCG simultaneously must be generated. Each antibody is a unique protein whose features may or may not be compatible with the test even if it binds the target, so such tests take time and effort to obtain, as illustrated by the unreliable early COVID-19 rapid tests that improved as better reagents were produced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Labels are attached to the Fc region so antigen binding is preserved; labeling the Fab would impair binding and is not the described bottleneck.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lateral flow tests detect a soluble analyte with antibodies; analysis of intact cells is the domain of flow cytometry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Size separation on a gel is a feature of western blotting, not of lateral flow immunoassays.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serial dilution is how a titer is determined for an individual sample; it is not a requirement for building the test platform.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A blood sample is analyzed by flow cytometry using light scattering alone, without any antibodies. On the resulting plot, one cell population sits high on the side scatter (SSC) axis, well above the lymphocyte and monocyte clusters. Which of the following cell types most likely makes up this population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4-positive T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells and debris

explanation.summary: Side scatter reflects cell granularity/density, so the most granular leukocytes, granulocytes, occupy the highest SSC region.
explanation.whyCorrect: A CBC or WBC scan uses light scattering to separate a blood sample by cell granularity/density, known as side scatter (SSC), and by size, known as forward scatter (FSC). Granulocytes appear as the cluster with the highest SSC, above monocytes and lymphocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Identifying CD4-positive T cells requires antibodies against the CD4 marker; light scatter alone does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphocytes form a low-SSC, low-FSC cluster near the bottom of the plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes form a cluster with intermediate scatter, below the granulocyte population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trash, RBCs, and debris fall at the lowest corner of the plot with minimal scatter.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A flow cytometry plot of a lymphocyte sample has the CD4 marker on the vertical axis and the CD8 marker on the horizontal axis, dividing the plot into four quadrants. A cluster of cells appears in the upper right quadrant. Which of the following best describes these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double negative for CD4 and CD8

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double positive for CD4 and CD8

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive for CD4 but with high side scatter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single positive for CD4 only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single positive for CD8 only

explanation.summary: On a two-marker flow plot, the quadrant high on both axes contains cells double positive for both antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: A flow cytometry plot often has two axes each designated for a specific antigen, and the four quadrants represent double negative, single positive for one antigen, or double positive for both antigen signals. Cells in the upper right are high for both the CD4 (vertical) and CD8 (horizontal) markers, so they are double positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Double-negative cells occupy the lower left quadrant, low for both markers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Side scatter is not one of the axes on this marker plot; the axes are the two antibody signals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4 single-positive cells sit in the upper left quadrant, high on CD4 but low on CD8.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD8 single-positive cells sit in the lower right quadrant, high on CD8 but low on CD4.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: Two blood samples are analyzed by flow cytometry with antibodies against CD4 and CD8. Compared with the reference sample, the second sample shows a markedly smaller cluster in the CD4-high/CD8-low quadrant while the CD8-high/CD4-low and double-negative clusters are similar in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer CD4 T cells than the reference sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher serum anti-CD4 antibody titer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased CD8 T cells relative to the reference

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased granularity of the lymphocyte population

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the CD4 antibody's fluorescent label

explanation.summary: A shrunken CD4 single-positive cluster on a flow plot indicates a lower number of CD4 T cells in that sample.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies within flow cytometry provide the total number of CD4-specific T cells within a sample. Comparing two scatter plots, a sample whose CD4 single-positive quadrant contains far fewer events, with the other quadrants unchanged, is lower in CD4 T cells than the reference.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Flow cytometry measures antigens on intact cells; it does not report a serum antibody titer, which is an ELISA measurement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The CD8 single-positive cluster is described as similar in size, so CD8 T cells are not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granularity is measured by side scatter, which is not an axis on a CD4 versus CD8 marker plot.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A failed label would remove signal from every CD4-expressing cell, including double positives, rather than selectively shrinking one quadrant with a valid reference run on the same reagents.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with thrombocytopenia is scheduled for oral surgery. The surgeon requests a platelet count and an RBC/platelet ratio from a blood draw within a few days of the procedure to reduce the risk of prolonged bleeding. Which of the following techniques would be used to obtain this information?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flow cytometry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect ELISA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Flow cytometry is the technique that partitions and quantifies the various cells within a blood sample.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flow cytometry is the only technique listed that can separate or partition the different cells in a blood sample and quantify them. A complete blood count is obtained by running individual cells past a light source and separating them by scatter, which yields the counts and ratios the surgeon requires.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates Hb variants by charge and does not count cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry shows the location of an antigen relative to cellular structures in a biopsy, which is not relevant to a cell count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ELISAs detect and quantify soluble analytes such as proteins but cannot detect intact cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot is incapable of analyzing whole cells and is not considered quantitative in nature.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A pathologist performs immunohistochemistry on a pancreatic biopsy. After a primary antibody and a secondary antibody are applied, DAB is added and the antigen-expressing cells turn brown under the microscope. Which of the following is responsible for producing the brown precipitate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A detergent that denatures the tissue proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fluorophore covalently attached to the primary antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: An electric current applied across the tissue section

choices.label: D
choices.text: An HRP-polymer on the secondary antibody converting DAB

choices.label: E
choices.text: Light scattering from the granular cells

explanation.summary: In IHC, an HRP-polymer linked to the secondary antibody converts DAB into a brown precipitate at the site of the antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the immunohistochemistry assay, a primary antibody binds the antigen in the tissue layer, a secondary antibody carrying an HRP-polymer binds the primary antibody, and the HRP converts DAB into a brown precipitate. Stained cells therefore appear brown under the microscope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Detergent-based denaturation is part of western blotting; IHC preserves tissue architecture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fluorophore produces a fluorescent signal as in immunofluorescence; it does not generate a brown DAB precipitate, and the label here is on the secondary antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Electric fields are used in electrophoresis, not in staining a tissue section.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Light scattering is the basis of flow cytometry, not of the color reaction in IHC.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: In an immunofluorescence study of a tissue biopsy, in addition to the tagged antibody against the antigen of interest, the technologist applies separate stains that mark the nucleus, mitochondria, and cell junctions. Which of the following is the purpose of these additional stains?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To determine the molecular weight of the tagged antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: To give the antigen a uniform negative charge

choices.label: C
choices.text: To increase the total number of cells counted in the biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: To measure the antibody titer within the tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: To provide landmarks for referencing antigen expression

explanation.summary: IHC and IF use stains for cellular landmarks so the localization pattern of an antigen can be interpreted in context.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence provide tissue, cellular, and organelle context to the relative localization of an antigen. Different stains or tagged antibodies are used to demark landmarks such as the nucleus, mitochondria, and cell junctions for referencing antigen expression levels and patterns.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Molecular weight is provided only by western blotting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Charge normalization is a western blot step and has no role in tissue staining.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Quantifying cell numbers is the role of flow cytometry; IHC and IF are about localization, not counting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A titer is the relative antibody concentration in a serum sample measured by ELISA, not something measured in a biopsy.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is diagnosed with an inherited disorder caused by a mutation in the gene encoding one of the globin chains of hemoglobin, resulting in an abnormal Hb variant. Which of the following terms best describes this category of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzymopathy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobinopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemolytic disease of the newborn

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immunodeficiency

explanation.summary: A hemoglobinopathy is an inherited disease caused by a mutation in one of the globin chain genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: A hemoglobinopathy is an inherited disease in which there is a mutation in one of the globin chain genes. Hundreds of different hemoglobinopathies have been identified, and sickle cell disease, in which the beta globin chain is altered, is by far the most common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is antibody-mediated destruction of RBCs, not an inherited globin gene mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An enzymopathy concerns a defective enzyme, not a structural globin chain mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolytic disease of the newborn is caused by maternal antibodies against fetal RBCs, not by a globin mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunodeficiency refers to impaired immune function and is unrelated to hemoglobin structure.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: Genetic analysis of a patient with sickle cell disease shows that the beta-globin protein is produced at full length with a single amino acid substitution and no other alteration. Which of the following types of mutation is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frameshift mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large gene deletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonsense mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splicing mutation

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene that changes one amino acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin chain gene. A single glutamate is replaced by a single valine, and the rest of the protein is produced without alteration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A frameshift would alter every downstream amino acid rather than substituting one residue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A large deletion would remove sequence and would not produce a full-length protein with one substitution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A nonsense mutation would truncate the protein, whereas beta-globin in SCD is full length.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A splicing mutation cannot properly account for a single amino acid change.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: Deoxygenated hemoglobin naturally forms a small hydrophobic pocket. A student asks why normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) does not polymerize when deoxygenated, even though this pocket is present. Which of the following best explains the stability of deoxy-HbA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It remains fully oxygenated in all tissues at all times

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its beta subunit lacks the hydrophobic pocket entirely

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its glutamate stays in the hydrophilic cytosol, not the pocket

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its tetramers are too large to approach one another in the cytosol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its valine at position 6 is buried inside the tetramer core

explanation.summary: In HbA the charged glutamate stays in the hydrophilic RBC cytosol and never engages the hydrophobic pocket, so no polymerization occurs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hydrophobic pocket that appears during deoxygenated states of Hb is natural and present in all deoxy-Hb forms. In unaffected Hb tetramers, the glutamate interacts with the hydrophilic RBC cytosol and does not interact with the hydrophobic pocket. It is the disparate chemical nature of the valine in HbS that drives the interaction with an adjacent tetramer and causes sickling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HbA becomes deoxygenated normally; stability comes from the residue's chemistry, not from remaining oxygenated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pocket forms in all deoxy-Hb forms, including HbA; its presence alone does not cause polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbA and HbS tetramers are the same size and shape; size does not prevent polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbA has a glutamate, not a valine, at position 6; valine is the sickle substitution.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is treated during a crisis with supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula and rest. As oxygenated hemoglobin comes to predominate in his red blood cells, which of the following changes is expected in the sickled cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They convert HbS into HbA

choices.label: B
choices.text: They lyse and release free hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: They permanently retain the crescent shape

choices.label: D
choices.text: They polymerize further into rigid rods

choices.label: E
choices.text: They return to a normal biconcave morphology

explanation.summary: Sickled RBCs regain their biconcave shape once oxy-Hb predominates, which is why raising oxygen saturation is a therapeutic goal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickled RBCs once again exhibit normal biconcave morphology when the oxy-Hb form predominates, because the hydrophobic pocket that drives polymerization occurs with deoxy-Hb. Although cycling between sickled and biconcave shape is limited, increasing Hb oxygen saturation by nasal cannula and reducing physical exertion are major interventions during a crisis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxygen does not change the amino acid sequence; HbS remains HbS but is no longer polymerized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reoxygenation reverses polymerization rather than causing the cells to burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sickled shape is not permanent; it reverses when oxy-Hb predominates, although the cycling is limited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polymerization is favored by low oxygen states; raising oxygen saturation reduces it.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with sickle cell disease develops recurrent episodes of severe pain and is found to have progressive damage to the spleen. Which of the following sequences best explains how the HbS mutation leads to this organ injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against HbS coat the RBCs, which are then destroyed in the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enlarged RBCs are trapped because HbS increases the size of the Hb tetramer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free HbS in plasma binds splenic endothelium and triggers local inflammation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Highly soluble Hb polymers leak from RBCs and precipitate in splenic sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insoluble Hb polymers distort the membrane; rigid RBCs occlude small vessels

explanation.summary: HbS polymers are poorly soluble, distort the RBC membrane, and produce rigid cells that cannot pass small vessels, causing painful occlusions and organ damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hb polymers are far less soluble and cause membrane distortion resulting in inflexibility of the RBCs. Sickled RBCs can no longer be distorted sufficiently to pass through small vasculature, and a major concern in SCD is vascular occlusions, which are often painful and severely damage organs such as the spleen and brain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sickling is a polymerization process within the RBC, not an antibody-mediated destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The HbS tetramer is essentially the same size as HbA; the problem is polymerization and loss of flexibility, not tetramer size.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The injury arises from rigid cells occluding vessels, not from hemoglobin acting on endothelium in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hb polymers are far less soluble, not highly soluble, and the damage comes from rigid cells blocking vessels.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A whole blood sample is sent for hemoglobin electrophoresis to evaluate for sickle cell disease. Which of the following best describes what is loaded into the wells of the gel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tissue section fixed on a glass slide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free hemoglobin released from hemolyzed red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin that has been denatured and coated with detergent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intact red blood cells suspended in plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum antibodies directed against HbS

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin electrophoresis runs free hemoglobin from hemolyzed RBCs through a gel under an electric charge and then stains the gel.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hemoglobin electrophoresis, free hemoglobin from hemolyzed RBCs in a whole blood sample is loaded into wells in a gel. An electric charge is applied, the proteins move to different places based on their size and charge, and the gel is then stained to see where the respective proteins migrated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fixed tissue sections are used for immunohistochemistry, not for hemoglobin electrophoresis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Detergent denaturation to normalize charge is a western blot step; hemoglobin electrophoresis separates proteins by their native charge at a select pH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The RBCs must be hemolyzed to release the hemoglobin; intact cells are analyzed by flow cytometry, not electrophoresis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The test analyzes the patient's hemoglobin protein directly; it does not involve anti-HbS antibodies.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with recurrent painful episodes undergoes hemoglobin electrophoresis. The sample is loaded near the positive pole. His lane shows a single band that has migrated farther toward the negative pole than the HbA band in the adjacent normal reference lane, and no band comigrates with HbA. Which of the following is the most likely genotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-A / Beta-A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-A / Beta-S

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-A with a second, unrelated Hb variant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-S / Beta-S

choices.label: E
choices.text: Beta-S with a partial HbA band lost to hemolysis

explanation.summary: A single HbS band with no HbA on hemoglobin electrophoresis indicates homozygous sickle cell anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The genetic nature of the disease determines which form of Hb is detectable. A patient who only expresses the Hb variant (HbS) is Beta-S/Beta-S, sickle cell anemia; the lane shows one band that, because HbS is more positively charged, sits farther from the positive pole than the HbA reference, with no HbA band present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal Beta-A/Beta-A sample would show a single band comigrating with the HbA reference.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sickle cell trait produces two bands, HbA and HbS; this lane has only one band and it is not at the HbA position.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The band's position matches the expected HbS migration in a symptomatic child; there is no HbA band to support a Beta-A allele.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis is a required part of sample preparation and does not selectively remove HbA; the absence of an HbA band reflects the genotype.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection

questions.stem: A clinical laboratory evaluates a new antibody-based assay for an infectious disease. In validation, the assay correctly returns a negative result in nearly every sample from patients known not to have the infection. Which of the following test characteristics does this finding best describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Qualitative capacity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reagent availability

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sensitivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specificity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Titer

explanation.summary: Specificity is a test's ability to identify negatives; sensitivity is its ability to detect positives.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sensitivity and specificity are key factors in selecting a protein detection technique. Sensitivity is the ability to detect positives within a test, and specificity is the ability to identify negatives. ELISAs are a great example of a test that is both sensitive and specific because of the antibody/antigen interaction on which they are based.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Qualitative capacity refers to whether a test reports presence or absence rather than a quantity; it does not describe how well negatives are identified.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reagent availability concerns how readily the antibodies and platforms for a test can be obtained, not its accuracy on negative samples.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sensitivity describes the ability to detect positives, not the ability to correctly call negatives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A titer is the relative concentration of an antibody in a patient's sample, not a property of the test's accuracy.

questions.topicName: Biotechniques: Protein Detection
